title: Modeling (I Do)
description: Demonstrate a skill or concept step-by-step before students attempt it themselves, using clear verbal and visual cues.
howTo: Show your own thinking out loud while working a problem or example on the board. Point to visuals, narrate each decision, then hand control to students for guided practice.
sourceName: Instructure
videoTitle: Learning Strategies: Model the Strategy
example: Before students graph systems of linear equations, the teacher works one problem on the board aloud, saying things like "I need the same variable to cancel, so I'll multiply this equation by negative two" while circling the matching coefficients. Students watch the full problem solved, including a moment where the teacher catches and fixes a sign error out loud, before touching their own worksheet. Only after the demonstration do students try a nearly identical system on their own paper.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is students narrating your same think-aloud steps back correctly during guided practice.

title: Gradual Release: I Do, We Do, Pairs Do
description: Move students from teacher modeling to guided practice to independent or paired application in a structured sequence.
howTo: Model the process (I do), practice together with prompting (we do), then have students apply it with a partner while you circulate and assess (pairs do/you do).
sourceName: Edutopia
videoTitle: Gradual Release of Responsibility in Action: Classroom Video
example: In a unit on writing topic sentences, the teacher first writes one on the board about a Rosa Parks passage, narrating each choice (I do). The class then drafts a second topic sentence together about a different paragraph, with the teacher prompting and revising suggestions aloud (we do). Finally, pairs write their own topic sentence for a third passage while the teacher circulates and checks in before students finish independently.
weeklyProduct: No new artifact — the evidence is students completing the paired practice step correctly without you re-explaining the model.

title: Collaborative Learning Groups
description: Students work in intentionally selected groups to explore and discuss a topic together.
howTo: Form groups purposefully rather than randomly, set clear ground rules for listening and turn-taking, and give each group a specific task or question to solve together.
sourceName: Instructure
videoTitle: COLLABORATIVE LEARNING: AN EXAMPLE IN THE ...
example: For a unit on the causes of World War I, the teacher forms four mixed-readiness groups, each assigned one cause (alliances, imperialism, militarism, nationalism), and gives each group a folder of primary-source excerpts to analyze together. Ground rules are posted: one speaker at a time, and every member must contribute one idea to the group's poster before the class jigsaw discussion. Groups then present their cause's role in the outbreak of the war to the rest of the class.
weeklyProduct: A group's shared answer or solution to the assigned task, showing what the group agreed on together.

title: Inquiry-Based Learning
description: Spark curiosity with targeted questions, then give students time to research and lead their own exploration.
howTo: Open a unit with a compelling question instead of an answer. Provide time for student-led research and structure a class discussion around what they discover.
sourceName: Instructure
videoTitle: Inquiry Learning in the Classroom
example: Instead of announcing the definition of natural selection, the teacher opens a biology unit by showing students photos of peppered moths on sooty versus clean tree bark and asks, "Why did the population's color change over fifty years?" Students spend fifteen minutes in small groups generating hypotheses and researching using provided data tables before the class discussion builds toward the formal explanation of natural selection. The teacher only introduces the vocabulary term after students have argued through the mechanism themselves.
weeklyProduct: A recorded discussion where students answer the opening compelling question and explain their reasoning after independent research.

title: Differentiated Instruction
description: Tailor instruction, materials, or tasks to individual student needs rather than delivering one version to everyone.
howTo: Adjust reading level of a text, vary task complexity, or offer multiple ways to demonstrate mastery, based on what recent data shows about each student's readiness.
sourceName: Instructure
videoTitle: Differentiated Instruction in the Classroom at Mesquite ...
example: For a lesson on The Diary of Anne Frank, the teacher gives some students the unabridged text, others an adapted version with vocabulary glosses, and a third group an audio version paired with a graphic novel excerpt, all addressing the same central question about hope during hardship. Task complexity also varies: some students write a full analytical paragraph while others complete a structured response frame with sentence starters. The grouping is based on that week's running-record and comprehension-check data rather than a single fixed track.
weeklyProduct: No single artifact — the visible result is students working on different versions of a task matched to their readiness data.

title: Scaffolding
description: Provide temporary supports so every learner can build on existing knowledge or reach a new skill.
howTo: Break a complex task into smaller steps, provide sentence starters or worked examples, and remove supports gradually as students gain independence.
sourceName: Instructure
videoTitle: Scaffolding Examples & Explicit Instruction for the Classroom
example: When introducing persuasive essay writing, the teacher breaks the task into claim, then evidence, then counterargument, teaching and practicing each piece separately over three days rather than assigning the whole essay at once. Sentence starters like "One might argue X, but the evidence shows Y" are provided on a handout for the counterargument section. By the final essay of the unit, the sentence starters are removed and students draft the full argument independently.
weeklyProduct: A completed multi-step task where each student used sentence starters or worked examples to reach the target skill.

title: Teach Metacognition
description: Help students analyze their own thinking, including growth mindset versus fixed mindset, and reflect after assignments.
howTo: After a task, ask students what they learned, where they can still grow, and what emotions came up while solving the problem. Make reflection a regular routine, not a one-off.
sourceName: Instructure
videoTitle: How to Foster Metacognitive Skills for Independent Learning
example: After a test on solving quadratic equations, the teacher has students complete a short reflection sheet asking which problem type they got wrong, why they think they made that mistake, and whether they felt confident or anxious during the factoring section. Students set one specific goal for the next unit test based on their answers, such as "double-check my sign when factoring." The teacher repeats this same reflection routine after every unit test rather than only after major exams.
weeklyProduct: A short written reflection where each student names what they learned and where they still need to grow.

title: Technology Integration
description: Incorporate digital tools, ideally ones that work together, to deliver instruction in new and engaging ways.
howTo: Choose a small set of digital tools that integrate well with each other and use adaptive technology to further differentiate practice for individual students.
sourceName: Instructure
videoTitle: Integration of Technology in the Classroom
example: For a research project on climate change, the teacher has students use one shared platform where they collect sources, take notes, and draft an outline, rather than juggling separate apps for each step. An adaptive vocabulary tool assigns each student practice on the specific climate-science terms they missed on a pre-assessment. The teacher checks the platform's dashboard to see which students still need support before the next class period.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is students completing adaptive practice tasks inside the chosen digital tool.

title: Active Learning
description: Put students at the center of the learning process through hands-on activities like reciprocal questioning and peer teaching.
howTo: Replace some lecture time with structured activities: have students generate questions, teach a concept to a partner, or physically manipulate materials related to the content.
sourceName: Instructure
videoTitle: Inside Active Learning Classrooms
example: Rather than lecturing straight through a lesson on cell organelles, the teacher has students build a labeled 3D model of a cell using household materials, then teach their model to a partner from a different table group, explaining what each organelle does. Students who built the mitochondria correctly help peers who mislabeled theirs. The teacher circulates listening for misconceptions during the peer-teaching rather than just checking the finished models.
weeklyProduct: No single artifact — the visible result is students actively generating questions or teaching a peer instead of just listening.

title: Reciprocal Questioning
description: When introducing a new topic, have students describe the concept back in their own words through structured Q&A.
howTo: Pair students and give each a role: one asks a question about the new concept, the other answers in their own words, then they switch.
sourceName: Instructure
videoTitle: LEAP: Reciprocal Questioning
example: After introducing the concept of supply and demand, the teacher pairs students and gives one the role of asking a question about the concept ("What happens to price when supply drops?") while the other answers in their own words before they switch roles. Each pair must generate at least three question-answer rounds before rejoining the whole class. The teacher listens in on a few pairs to catch students who are only reciting the definition rather than explaining the mechanism.
weeklyProduct: A recorded exchange where each student verbally explains the new concept back in their own words to a partner.

title: Three-Step Interviews
description: Students explore a topic by interviewing one another through a structured three-step process.
howTo: In trios, one student interviews a partner about the topic, then roles rotate so everyone interviews and is interviewed once before sharing out.
sourceName: Instructure
videoTitle: Three Step Interview
example: During a unit on the Harlem Renaissance, trios rotate through interviewing each other about a poem they each researched — one poet per student. In round one, Student A interviews Student B about Langston Hughes; roles rotate until all three have interviewed and been interviewed once. The trio then shares out the most interesting insight from each poet to the whole class.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is each student verbally answering and asking questions once as interviewer and interviewee.

title: Peer Teaching
description: Students teach concepts or material to one another as an active-learning activity.
howTo: Assign each student or pair a sub-topic to master, then have them teach it briefly to a small group or the whole class.
sourceName: Instructure
videoTitle: Teachers! HOW to organise peer-to-peer learning in the ...
example: In a unit on types of chemical reactions, each pair of students is assigned one reaction type — synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, or double replacement — and given ten minutes to prepare a two-minute explanation with an example equation. Pairs then rotate to teach their reaction type to a new small group, so every student hears all four types explained by classmates rather than the teacher. The teacher spot-checks by asking a student from each new group to summarize what they just learned.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is each student verbally teaching their assigned sub-topic to a small group.

title: Problem-Based Learning
description: Introduce a real-world, complex problem and let students dissect and discuss it with peers instead of receiving all information upfront.
howTo: Present a case study, roleplay, or simulation. Ask students to hypothesize before giving them information, so they build knowledge through exploration.
sourceName: Instructure
videoTitle: Using a Problem-Based Task with Fourth Graders to Create ...
example: Instead of teaching ratios abstractly, the teacher presents students with a real classroom problem: the class is planning a pizza party and needs to figure out how many pizzas to order for 28 students with different topping preferences and a fixed budget. Students hypothesize an approach in small groups before the teacher hands out pricing information, then must revise their plan once they see the actual numbers. The lesson ends with each group defending why their order best fits the budget and preferences.
weeklyProduct: A recorded response where each student answers a higher-order hypothesis question about the real-world case before receiving new information.

title: Trauma-Informed Classroom
description: Consider trauma as a possible explanation for misconduct and intentionally cultivate a safe environment.
howTo: Respond to misbehavior with curiosity before consequence, teach resilience skills explicitly, and demonstrate consistent empathy when challenges arise.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: The Trauma-Informed Classroom, Part 1
videoChannel: Oregon State University College of Education
example: When a student who is usually engaged suddenly puts their head down and refuses to work, the teacher responds by quietly asking "Rough morning?" instead of immediately issuing a consequence for noncompliance. The teacher offers the student a five-minute reset at a calm corner desk before re-engaging with the assignment. Over the semester, the teacher explicitly teaches a simple breathing strategy the whole class can use when they notice themselves getting overwhelmed.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is calmer, more curious responses to misbehavior and fewer escalations.

title: Classroom Environment of Safety
description: Make the classroom a consistent place of physical and emotional safety for all students.
howTo: Establish predictable routines, a calm tone, and clear expectations so students know the room is a stable, safe space regardless of what happens outside it.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: Creating a Safe Classroom Environment for Your Students
example: At the start of the year, the teacher posts a visual daily schedule on the board and follows the same opening routine every day — warm-up, agenda review, and a two-minute check-in — so students always know what to expect the moment they walk in. When conflicts happen outside class, the teacher keeps their tone even and predictable rather than escalating, so the room stays a stable space regardless of what happened in the hallway. Students know where to sit, what materials to have out, and what the first five minutes of class will look like every single day.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is smoother, more predictable routines and a calmer overall classroom tone.

title: Data-Based, Differentiated Core Instruction
description: Plan and deliver instruction based on current student data, tailored to readiness, interests, strengths, and preferences.
howTo: Review recent screening or formative data before planning the week's lessons, and adjust groupings or task options based on what the data shows.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: How Can Student Data Differentiate Instruction?
example: Before planning the week's fraction lessons, the teacher reviews the class's most recent exit-ticket data and notices a third of students are still struggling with finding common denominators. The teacher adjusts the week's plan to regroup those students for a short reteach session using fraction bars, while students who mastered the skill move to a word-problem extension task. The groupings shift again the following week based on the next round of formative data.
weeklyProduct: No new student artifact — the visible result is a lesson plan and groupings adjusted based on this week's data review.

title: Small-Group Instruction
description: Incorporate small groups into core instruction as a way to differentiate the learning experience.
howTo: Pull a small group with similar needs for a few minutes of targeted teaching while the rest of the class works independently or in centers.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: Jennifer Serravallo Teaches a Small Group Strategy Lesson
example: During independent reading workshop, the teacher pulls a group of four students who all struggled with identifying the main idea on the last comprehension check to a kidney table for eight minutes of targeted instruction using a short nonfiction passage about sharks. The rest of the class works at literacy centers or reads independently during this time. The teacher rotates through two more small groups with different focus skills before the workshop period ends.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is a small group of similar-need students receiving a few minutes of targeted reteaching.

title: Varied Learning Activities
description: Offer different types of learning activities to reach students' readiness levels, interests, and preferences.
howTo: Design a lesson with at least two ways to engage with the content (e.g. a visual task and a discussion task) so students can access the material through more than one channel.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: Classroom Activities For Differentiated Instruction
example: For a lesson on the water cycle, the teacher offers a visual task where students label a diagram of evaporation, condensation, and precipitation, alongside a discussion task where partners explain the cycle to each other using the diagram as a prop. A third option lets students act out the water cycle as a short skit moving between stations representing each stage. Students can choose which format helps them access the content, and all three groups reconvene for the same exit-ticket question.
weeklyProduct: No single artifact — the visible result is students engaging with the same content through at least two different activity types.

title: Student Choice of Activities
description: Offer choices among activities that still align to the same learning standard.
howTo: Start small — offer two options for a single task, such as writing an essay or recording a short video response — and expand choice as students respond well.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: Teacher Tips | Differentiation and Student Choice
example: For a unit on To Kill a Mockingbird, students can either write a traditional five-paragraph essay analyzing Atticus's closing argument or record a two-minute video response making the same argument on camera, with both options assessed against the same rubric for the standard on analyzing rhetorical choices. The teacher starts by offering just these two options rather than a longer menu. Based on how well the essay-versus-video choice goes, the teacher plans to add a podcast-style option for the next unit.
weeklyProduct: A student-selected product — either a written essay or a recorded video response — demonstrating the same standard.

title: Choice of Seats or Groups
description: Let students choose their seats or learning groups when appropriate, building autonomy.
howTo: Offer flexible seating zones or let students pick a partner for a specific activity, while retaining the ability to adjust if a choice isn't working.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: A Versatile Seating Arrangement That Really Works
example: For a group project analyzing persuasive techniques in advertisements, the teacher lets students choose their own partner for the activity rather than assigning pairs, while reserving the right to move anyone whose pairing isn't producing focused work. During independent reading time, students can also choose between a standing desk zone, a carpet corner, or their regular seat. The teacher checks in after ten minutes to make sure the choices are actually helping students focus rather than becoming a distraction.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is students seated or grouped by their own choice for the activity.

title: Build Trusting Student-Teacher Relationships
description: Establish trust by saying what you mean, meaning what you say, and staying calm when communicating expectations.
howTo: Be consistent between what you promise and what you deliver, and address concerns directly and respectfully instead of letting frustration show.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: 3 Ways to Build Trust with Your Students
example: When a student asks the teacher for an extra day on a lab report, the teacher agrees and then actually follows through by not marking it late, so the student learns the teacher's word is reliable. When the teacher is frustrated that half the class forgot homework again, they name the frustration calmly ("I'm annoyed, and here's why it matters") instead of raising their voice or going silent. Over time, students start bringing the teacher problems early, like a group project falling apart, because they trust the response will be direct rather than punitive.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is consistent follow-through on stated expectations that students can point to.

title: Greet Every Student by Name Daily
description: A simple daily habit that builds relationship and trust with every student.
howTo: Stand at the door and greet each student by name as they enter, using a brief personal comment or check-in when possible.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: Making Connections With Greetings at the Door
example: Every morning the teacher stands at the classroom door and greets each student by name as they walk in, mixing in a quick personal note like "How did the soccer game go last night?" for students they know play a sport. For a new student who just transferred in, the teacher makes a point of learning and using their name correctly on day one rather than waiting. This two-minute routine happens before every single class period, not just on days when things feel calm.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is every student greeted by name with a brief personal check-in at the door daily.

title: Honor Students' Talents and Interests
description: Recognize and respect individual student strengths in classroom interactions and instruction.
howTo: Learn one interest or strength per student early in the year and look for ways to reference or connect it to instruction throughout the semester.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: Celebrating and Honoring Students of All Backgrounds in ...
example: Early in the year, the teacher learns that one student is passionate about skateboarding and later designs a physics warm-up question about the forces involved in an ollie, referencing the student by name when introducing it. Another student who loves drawing is invited to illustrate the vocabulary wall for the unit on cell biology. The teacher keeps a running list of one interest per student from the first two weeks of school and refers back to it when planning examples all semester.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is a lesson moment that explicitly references a specific student's known interest or strength.

title: Universal Tier 1 Instruction on Grade-Level Standards
description: Provide curriculum, instruction, and assessment to all students in a grade level, focused on grade-level standards.
howTo: Keep the core lesson anchored to the grade-level standard for all students, using universal screening data to check whether the instruction is working.
sourceName: Renaissance
videoTitle: Improving Tier One Instruction with The New Classroom ...
example: For the whole ninth-grade Algebra I course, every teacher anchors the week's lesson to the same grade-level standard on solving systems of equations, regardless of which sections have historically struggled more. After a schoolwide screening shows one class average trailing the standard, the team doesn't pull those students into intervention yet — they first review whether the core lesson itself needs stronger modeling or examples. Only after strengthening the shared Tier 1 lesson do they revisit which individual students might still need extra support.
weeklyProduct: No new artifact — the visible result is screening data showing whether grade-level core instruction is working for the whole class.

title: Academic Praise and Feedback (3:1 Ratio)
description: Balance corrective feedback with specific praise, aiming for roughly three positive comments for every correction.
howTo: Track your own ratio for a class period. When you notice you're mostly correcting, intentionally add specific praise tied to academic effort or behavior.
sourceName: Renaissance
videoTitle: Dr. Randy Sprick Explains the 3:1 Ratio of Student-Teacher ...
example: During a 45-minute algebra class, the teacher jots a quick tally on a sticky note each time they give a correction versus a specific praise statement, and notices by the midpoint they're at four corrections to one praise. For the second half of class, the teacher intentionally adds specific praise like "You correctly isolated the variable on that last step" to rebalance toward three positive comments for every correction. By the end of the period the tally is closer to the 3:1 target.
weeklyProduct: A tally sheet showing your praise-to-correction ratio for one class period, used to rebalance toward more specific praise.

title: Use Shaping Procedures
description: Recognize and reinforce progress through the small stages of learning a new skill, rather than waiting for full mastery.
howTo: Break a skill into visible sub-steps and give specific acknowledgment each time a student or the class hits a sub-step, not just at final mastery.
sourceName: Renaissance
videoTitle: Shaping Procedures in ABA Explained
example: While teaching a student to write in cursive, the teacher doesn't wait until the whole alphabet is mastered to give feedback — they specifically acknowledge when the student successfully connects just the letters "a" and "n" for the first time. Each small milestone, like correctly forming a lowercase loop or keeping letters on the baseline, gets a specific comment ("Your loops are staying on the line now") before the student has mastered full words. The teacher tracks these sub-steps on a simple checklist taped to the student's desk.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is specific verbal acknowledgment given each time a student hits a visible sub-step.

title: Share Praise and Feedback with Families
description: Communicate students' academic successes to caregivers to build a positive home-school connection.
howTo: Send a quick positive note, call, or message home when a student makes progress, not only when there's a problem to report.
sourceName: Renaissance
videoTitle: Engaging Families With Social and Emotional Learning
example: After a student who has struggled with reading fluency finally reads a full paragraph aloud without stumbling, the teacher sends a two-line message home that same day: "Jordan read the whole passage about sharks fluently today — first time this year. Really proud of the growth." The teacher makes a habit of sending at least one positive note home per week rather than only calling when there's a discipline issue. Over the semester, several families mention this is the first positive contact they've had from a teacher in years.
weeklyProduct: A quick note, call, or message sent home documenting one specific piece of student progress this week.

title: Frequent Academic Response Opportunities
description: Give students frequent chances to apply what they've learned in new situations and demonstrate understanding.
howTo: Circulate during work time, check student work in real time, and call on a wide range of students rather than the same few volunteers.
sourceName: Renaissance
videoTitle: Increasing Instruction through Active Student Responding
example: During a lesson on identifying the theme of a short story, the teacher circulates every few minutes to check individual students' annotations instead of only calling on the same three raised hands. Using a randomized name-picker, the teacher calls on a quiet student who rarely volunteers to share their theme statement, then follows up with a struggling student to check their evidence. By the end of the period, every student has had at least one individual response opportunity, not just the confident regulars.
weeklyProduct: No single written artifact — the visible result is real-time checked work from a wider range of students, not just regular volunteers.

title: Student-Led Discussions
description: When students disengage, hand over most of the discussion to them to assess and rebuild understanding.
howTo: Pose a question and step back, letting students carry the conversation and build on each other's ideas while you listen for gaps in understanding.
sourceName: Renaissance
videoTitle: Using Discussions to Inspire Active Participation in Learning
example: Partway through a Socratic seminar on The Crucible, the teacher notices students have gone quiet and are just waiting to be called on, so instead of jumping back in, the teacher poses one open question — "Who in this play do you actually blame for what happens to Tituba?" — and steps back from the circle entirely. Students pick up the thread themselves, building on and challenging each other's claims for the next ten minutes while the teacher only takes notes on gaps in reasoning. The teacher waits until the conversation stalls again before re-entering with a targeted follow-up question.
weeklyProduct: A recorded discussion where students carry the conversation and build on each other's ideas after your opening question.

title: Repeated Major Concept Summaries
description: Repeatedly summarize important concepts, skills, and key points throughout the year to build a scaffold of information.
howTo: End each lesson or unit with a brief recap of the two or three most important ideas, and revisit those same ideas again in later units.
sourceName: Renaissance
videoTitle: Five Ways to Teach Summarizing
example: At the end of a lesson on photosynthesis, the teacher has the class state the two or three most important ideas out loud — that plants convert light energy to chemical energy and that this releases oxygen as a byproduct. Three weeks later, when starting a unit on cellular respiration, the teacher opens by having students recall those same photosynthesis ideas before introducing how respiration is essentially the reverse process. This same brief recap-and-connect routine happens at the start of most units throughout the year.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is students able to restate the two or three most important ideas from the lesson.

title: Use a Research-Based Curriculum
description: Anchor core instruction in a well-researched, standards-based curriculum selected at the school or district level.
howTo: Follow the adopted curriculum's scope and sequence closely for Tier 1 instruction, using it as the foundation before layering in supplemental strategies.
sourceName: Third Space Learning
videoTitle: Using a Research-Based Curriculum Development Process
example: For sixth-grade math, the department adopts a vetted, standards-aligned curriculum with a defined scope and sequence for teaching ratios and proportional relationships, and teachers follow its unit order and pacing rather than assembling their own worksheets from scattered sources. When a teacher wants to add a supplemental ratio activity involving recipe scaling, they layer it on top of the adopted sequence rather than replacing the core lesson. The whole team uses the curriculum's built-in unit assessments as the primary measure of whether Tier 1 instruction is working.
weeklyProduct: No new artifact — the visible result is this week's lessons following the adopted curriculum's scope and sequence closely.

title: Flexible Seating and Learning Environment
description: Adjust the physical classroom environment, such as seating, to help students access instruction.
howTo: Offer a mix of seating types (standing desk, cushioned floor spot, traditional desk) and let students self-select where they focus best.
sourceName: Third Space Learning
videoTitle: Flexible Seating supports Learning First
example: During independent writing time, the classroom offers a standing desk near the window, a cushioned floor spot with clipboards, and traditional desks, and students choose the spot where they draft best for that day's persuasive essay. A student who struggles to sit still all period chooses the standing desk and is noticeably more focused during that block. The teacher tracks briefly whether specific students are actually producing more focused work in their chosen spot and adjusts options if a choice isn't working.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is students self-selecting a seating type that helps them focus.

title: Math Tools and Manipulatives
description: Provide hands-on tools like fraction tiles, pattern blocks, or Cuisenaire rods so students can visualize math concepts.
howTo: Keep a variety of manipulatives accessible and let students choose which one helps them see the problem; draw the same visual on a whiteboard if physical tools aren't available.
sourceName: Third Space Learning
videoTitle: Our Favorite Math Manipulatives (and ideas for how to use them!)
example: When introducing adding fractions with unlike denominators, the teacher keeps a bin of fraction tiles on each table and lets students physically line up thirds and fourths to see why they need a common denominator before ever writing the algorithm. A student who prefers pattern blocks uses those instead to build the same equivalence visually. When physical tiles aren't available for a quick check, the teacher draws the same fraction bars on the whiteboard so every student still sees the visual model.
weeklyProduct: A completed math problem where the student used a chosen manipulative or whiteboard drawing to visualize their solution.

title: Scaffolded Math Problems
description: Adapt math problems to fit students' current level while keeping them connected to grade-level content.
howTo: Provide a simplified numeric version or a partially worked example of a grade-level problem so struggling students can still access the core concept.
sourceName: Third Space Learning
videoTitle: Classroom Strategies to Scaffold Math Learning
example: For a grade-level problem asking students to solve a two-step equation like 3x + 5 = 20, the teacher gives a struggling student a partially worked version showing the first step (3x = 15) already completed, so they only have to solve the final division step. Another student who needs more support gets a simplified version with smaller numbers, like 2x + 1 = 7, that uses the identical two-step structure. Both versions target the same underlying skill as the grade-level problem the rest of the class solves.
weeklyProduct: A completed simplified or partially worked version of the grade-level math problem, showing the student's own steps.

title: Student Goal Setting in Math
description: Set math goals collaboratively with students and have them track and reflect on their own progress.
howTo: Have each student set one specific, measurable math goal for the unit and check in on it weekly, noting what's working and what needs adjusting.
sourceName: Third Space Learning
videoTitle: Setting Goals for Students
example: At the start of a unit on solving multi-step equations, each student sets one specific goal, such as "get at least 4 out of 5 correct on distributing before combining like terms," and records it on a tracking sheet. Every Friday, the teacher gives students five minutes to check their recent quiz or homework against that goal and note whether they're on track or need to adjust their study approach. A student who isn't improving revises the goal to something more specific, like practicing ten extra distribution problems for homework.
weeklyProduct: A written, specific math goal with a weekly progress note on what's working and what needs adjusting.

title: Explicit Behavioral Expectations
description: Clearly and directly teach what appropriate behavior looks like in the specific classroom context.
howTo: Model and practice the expected behavior for transitions, group work, and independent work, rather than assuming students already know it.
sourceName: Third Space Learning
videoTitle: Setting behaviour expectations: Classroom management practice
example: Before the first small-group activity of the year, the teacher doesn't just tell students to "work well together" — they model what an effective group discussion sounds and looks like, then have two students demonstrate a poor example (everyone talking over each other) followed by a good example (one speaker, others listening). Students then practice the expected behavior in their own small groups for two minutes before starting the actual academic task. The same explicit modeling happens again before independent work time and before line-up transitions.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is students correctly demonstrating the modeled behavior during a transition or group task.

title: Clear Classroom Routines and Transitions
description: Establish predictable routines and efficient transitions between activities as a Tier 1 foundation.
howTo: Teach and practice specific transition procedures (e.g. how to move from whole-group to small-group work) until they run smoothly with minimal instruction.
sourceName: Third Space Learning
videoTitle: Classroom Transitions: Classroom Management Strategies
example: At the start of the year, the teacher teaches the exact steps for moving from whole-group instruction to small-group stations — pushing in chairs quietly, grabbing station folders in a specific order, and settling within 60 seconds — and has students practice the transition three times in a row until it runs smoothly. By October, the same transition takes under a minute with zero verbal reminders needed. The teacher re-teaches the routine briefly whenever it starts to slip, rather than assuming it will hold forever.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is a specific transition running smoothly and quickly with minimal verbal instruction.

title: Model Positive Social-Emotional-Behavioral Skills
description: Model the social, emotional, and behavioral skills the school wants students to demonstrate.
howTo: Narrate your own regulation in the moment — for example, naming that you're taking a breath before responding — so students see the skill in action.
sourceName: PBIS.org
videoTitle: Practical Strategies for Teaching Social Emotional Skills
example: When a lesson plan falls apart because the projector stops working mid-class, the teacher says out loud, "I'm frustrated, so I'm going to take a breath and figure out plan B," narrating the exact regulation skill they want students to use. Later, when a student's answer is wrong in front of the class, the teacher responds calmly and says, "That's a great try — let's see what we can learn from it," modeling the reaction they want students to have toward their own mistakes. Students see these regulation skills in action multiple times a week, not just hear about them in a lesson.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is students observing you narrate your own regulation strategy in a real moment.

title: Define and Teach Positively Stated Expectations
description: Identify 3-5 positively stated, memorable expectations and explicitly teach what they look like in action.
howTo: Post a short list of positive expectations (e.g. 'Be Respectful, Be Responsible, Be Ready'), and have students demonstrate examples in different classroom contexts.
sourceName: PBIS.org
videoTitle: Creating Positively Stated Behavior Expectations
example: The school adopts three short, positively stated expectations — "Be Respectful, Be Responsible, Be Ready" — and posts them in every classroom and hallway. In each classroom, the teacher has students demonstrate what "Be Ready" looks like specifically during a lab versus during a test, since the behavior looks different in each context. Students practice showing the expectation in both settings rather than just hearing the phrase read aloud once.
weeklyProduct: A posted list of 3-5 positively stated expectations with students demonstrating what each looks like in context.

title: Acknowledge Expected Behavior
description: Use a consistent system to positively recognize students when they demonstrate expected behavior.
howTo: Give specific, immediate praise tied to the exact behavior you want repeated ('Thank you for starting your warm-up right away') rather than generic praise.
sourceName: PBIS.org
videoTitle: Acknowledgement and praise: Classroom management skill
example: When a student who usually struggles to start work independently opens their notebook and begins the warm-up the moment the bell rings, the teacher says specifically, "Thank you for starting your warm-up right away, Marcus," rather than a generic "good job." The teacher uses this same specific, immediate phrasing consistently across the room so students know exactly which behavior is being reinforced. Over several weeks, more students start work immediately once they see this behavior getting noticed.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is specific, immediate verbal praise tied to the exact expected behavior observed.

title: Respond Instructionally to Unwanted Behavior
description: Address unwanted behavior by re-teaching the expectation rather than relying only on discipline.
howTo: When a behavior misstep happens, briefly re-teach or restate the expectation and give the student a chance to demonstrate it correctly before applying a consequence.
sourceName: PBIS.org
videoTitle: Classroom Strategy: Redirecting Misbehavior
example: When a student blurts out an answer without raising a hand during a math lesson, the teacher briefly restates the expectation — "We raise hands so everyone gets a turn to think" — and then gives the student a chance to redo it correctly by raising their hand for the next question before any consequence is applied. If the same student misses a group-work transition step, the teacher walks them through the correct steps once more rather than issuing a discipline referral immediately. Only if the behavior continues after re-teaching does the teacher escalate to a stronger consequence.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is a student correctly redemonstrating the re-taught expectation after a misstep.

title: Intervene Early on Behavior
description: Provide support the moment early signs of disengagement or misbehavior appear, before they escalate.
howTo: Watch for early signals like off-task fidgeting or withdrawn posture, and use a quiet proximity check-in or redirection before the behavior grows.
sourceName: PBIS.org
videoTitle: Video #7: A Classroom Intervention - Teacher Example
example: During independent work time, the teacher notices a student who is normally engaged has started tapping their pencil repeatedly and staring out the window instead of writing. Rather than waiting for the behavior to become disruptive, the teacher quietly walks over, crouches beside the desk, and asks a low-key redirecting question like "Which problem are you stuck on?" This proximity check-in happens the moment the early signal appears, before the student's frustration turns into refusing the work outright.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is a quiet redirection that stops early disengagement before it escalates.

title: Graphic Organizers
description: Use a visual structure to help students organize new information when reading complex text.
howTo: Give students a partially filled organizer (e.g. cause-and-effect chart, sequence chain) to complete as they read, so the structure of the text becomes visible.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: Using Graphic Organizers in Writing (Second-Grade Class)
example: While reading a nonfiction article about the causes and effects of the Dust Bowl, students fill in a partially completed cause-and-effect chart as they read, with a few boxes already filled in as models and others left blank for them to complete. The visible structure of the chart mirrors the text's organization, making it easier for students to track how drought led to soil erosion which led to mass migration. The teacher collects the completed charts as a quick check of comprehension before the class discussion.
weeklyProduct: A completed graphic organizer, like a cause-and-effect chart or sequence chain, filled in as each student reads the text.

title: Pair Text with Graphic Formats
description: Present written information together with a graphic representation to make a lesson accessible to more students.
howTo: Whenever you introduce a written passage on a complex idea, add a diagram, chart, or graphic organizer showing the same information visually.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: English Learners in STEM: Interactive Graphic Organizer and Text
example: When introducing a dense passage on the structure of the human respiratory system, the teacher pairs the written text with a labeled diagram showing the path of air from the nose through the lungs, so students can match each sentence in the passage to a specific part of the image. A student who struggles with the vocabulary-heavy paragraph can trace the airflow visually while still following along with the text. This same text-plus-diagram pairing is used again later in the unit for the circulatory system.
weeklyProduct: A paired handout showing the same written passage alongside a diagram or chart representing the same information visually.

title: Compare-and-Contrast Venn Diagrams
description: Break down and classify differences between two items, ideas, or concepts visually.
howTo: Have students fill in a Venn diagram comparing two characters, events, or concepts before writing a comparison paragraph or having a discussion about it.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: Using a Venn Diagram to Compare and Contrast Books
example: Studying the American and French Revolutions, students draw a Venn diagram with one circle for each revolution and an overlapping middle for shared causes like Enlightenment ideas about natural rights. They fill in details unique to each — the American colonists' tax grievances versus the French Estates system — before writing a short paragraph comparing the two uprisings' causes.
weeklyProduct: A filled-in Venn diagram plus a short comparison paragraph or discussion showing how each student sorted the similarities and differences.

title: Provide Background Knowledge Before Reading
description: Fill in missing background knowledge before teaching a text that assumes prior context students may not have.
howTo: Spend five minutes before a reading assignment giving students the historical, cultural, or scientific context the text assumes they already know.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: 4 Activities to Build Background Knowledge
example: Before reading excerpts from Anne Frank's diary, the teacher spends five minutes explaining the German occupation of the Netherlands, what going into hiding meant for Jewish families, and basic Holocaust-era vocabulary like "annex" and "deportation." Students then read the diary entries with enough context to understand what Anne is describing rather than getting lost in unfamiliar history.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is students entering the reading with the context they need instead of getting lost.

title: Activate Prior Knowledge
description: Connect the day's topic to knowledge students already possess before they read, so they can link old and new ideas.
howTo: Open with a quick brainstorm or turn-and-talk: 'What do you already know about X?' before introducing new text or content on that topic.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: Leveraging Prior Knowledge to Build Understanding
example: Before starting a unit on ecosystems, the teacher opens with a turn-and-talk: "What do you already know about food chains from earlier grades?" Students share what they remember about predators and prey, and the teacher uses their answers to bridge into new vocabulary like "decomposer" and "trophic level."
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is a quick brainstorm or turn-and-talk showing what students already know before reading.

title: Active Reading and Annotation
description: Have students interact directly with a text while reading rather than reading passively.
howTo: Teach a simple annotation code (underline main idea, circle unfamiliar words, star a key detail) and require students to mark up the text as they read.
sourceName: Branching Minds
videoTitle: How I teach annotations to my middle schoolers with FREEBIE
example: Reading "The Tell-Tale Heart," students use a simple code — underline the main idea of each paragraph, circle unfamiliar words like "sagacity," and star the moment the narrator first mentions the old man's eye. Their annotations then anchor a class discussion about how Poe builds suspense sentence by sentence.
weeklyProduct: A marked-up text with underlines, circles, and stars showing each student's main idea, unfamiliar words, and key details.

title: Flexible, Skill-Based Grouping
description: Form groups based on students' shared skill needs using data, and revisit those groups regularly.
howTo: Use recent screening or formative data to group students with similar needs, then review and reshuffle groups roughly every two weeks as skills change.
sourceName: Iowa Reading Research Center
videoTitle: How to Group Students by Skill (Not Reading Level) Using Flexible Grouping
example: After a fractions screener, a fourth-grade teacher groups students who all struggled with common denominators into one small group and students who are ready for mixed-number operations into another. Two weeks later, after new formative data on decimals comes in, she reshuffles the groups so students move based on their current need rather than staying in a fixed group all year.
weeklyProduct: No written student artifact — the visible result is a data-based grouping roster the teacher uses to place students by current skill need.

title: Use Universal Screening Data to Form Groups
description: Use screening results to identify students with similar performance and create initial instructional groups.
howTo: Review whole-class screening results; if most students score similarly, teach the skill whole-group instead of over-splitting into unnecessary small groups.
sourceName: Iowa Reading Research Center
videoTitle: How to Use Universal Screening Data to Form Effective Groups
example: After a beginning-of-year reading screener, a teacher finds that most of her class scored similarly low on inferencing, so instead of splitting into five small groups she teaches an inferencing mini-lesson to the whole class using a shared short story. She reserves small-group time for the handful of students whose screening scores flagged a different, more specific need in decoding.
weeklyProduct: No written student artifact — the visible result is a screening-data summary showing whether the class needs whole-group or split instruction.

title: Practice-Only Centers During Small Groups
description: While the teacher works with a small group, the rest of the class practices skills they've already mastered at centers.
howTo: Stock centers only with tasks students can already do accurately — never a brand-new skill — so independent time stays productive without teacher support.
sourceName: Iowa Reading Research Center
videoTitle: How To Teach Small Groups In Upper Elementary
example: While the teacher pulls a small group to reteach two-digit subtraction with regrouping, the rest of the class rotates through centers practicing skills they've already mastered: a fluency card game, a math journal prompt, and an independent worksheet reviewing place value. None of the centers introduce new content, so the teacher's full attention stays with the group that needs it.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact from this move itself — the visible result is independent centers running productively while the teacher works with a small group.

title: Start with Targeted Small Groups, Not Whole Group First
description: Use pre-lesson data to identify varied needs and deliver Tier 1 instruction in differentiated small groups from the start.
howTo: Before teaching a new concept, preassess understanding, then plan small groups with different entry points instead of defaulting to one whole-group lesson for everyone.
sourceName: Edutopia
videoTitle: Getting Started with Small Group Instruction
example: Instead of teaching a whole-class lesson on solving two-step equations to everyone first, a middle school math teacher starts the period by pulling the group of students who bombed yesterday's exit ticket for a targeted mini-lesson on isolating variables. The rest of the class works independently on an extension problem set while she reteaches the specific gap that group showed.
weeklyProduct: No single written artifact — the visible result is a preassessment-based small-group plan with different entry points for each group.

title: Use Preassessment to Plan Instruction
description: Preassess students before teaching a concept to determine understanding and plan grouping, rigor, and support accordingly.
howTo: Give a short, low-stakes preassessment a day or two before a new unit and use the results to decide how to group students and how much scaffolding each group needs.
sourceName: Edutopia
videoTitle: Using Pre-assessment Data to Design More Effectively
example: Before starting a unit on the Civil War, a teacher gives a short preassessment asking students to explain what they already know about slavery, states' rights, and Lincoln's role. She uses the results to decide that most students need more background on the economic causes before they're ready to analyze primary source letters from soldiers.
weeklyProduct: A short, low-stakes preassessment with student responses that the teacher uses to decide grouping and scaffolding for the unit.

title: Adjust Rigor and Complexity by Group
description: Modify the level of rigor in examples, practice, and tasks so instruction matches each group's readiness.
howTo: Prepare tiered versions of the same task — one with more scaffolding, one at grade level, one with an extension — and assign based on current data.
sourceName: Edutopia
videoTitle: Rigor by Design, Not Chance: Five Essential Teacher Moves
example: During a unit on persuasive essays, a teacher gives her stronger writers a prompt requiring a counterargument and rebuttal, while a group still building basic claim-evidence structure gets a prompt with a sentence frame and a shorter required length. Both groups are practicing the same core skill, but the complexity of the task matches what each group is ready for.
weeklyProduct: Three tiered versions of the same task (scaffolded, grade-level, extension) assigned to students based on current data.

title: Station Rotation Model
description: Rotate students through a teacher-led station, an online station, and an offline station.
howTo: Design three short stations for a lesson block; meet with each small group at the teacher-led station while others work independently online or offline, then rotate.
sourceName: Edutopia
videoTitle: What is the Station Rotation Model?
example: In a lesson on multiplication facts, students rotate through four stations over thirty minutes: a teacher-led small group, a digital fact-fluency app, a partner flashcard drill, and an independent worksheet. Each rotation lasts about seven minutes, and the teacher uses her station to give direct feedback to the group in front of her while the others work independently.
weeklyProduct: No single written artifact — the visible result is completed work samples from three stations (teacher-led, online, offline) after students rotate through.

title: Choose Evidence-Based Instructional Practices
description: Select and implement strategies supported by research and appropriate to the specific instructional goal.
howTo: Before adopting a new strategy, check whether it has strong, moderate, or promising research evidence for the specific goal (academic, behavioral, or social-emotional) you're targeting.
sourceName: Third Space Learning
videoTitle: Evidence-Based Teaching: Unlocking Effective Strategies for ...
example: When deciding how to teach long division to a class that's struggled with it for two years running, a school's math lead pulls research showing that explicit, systematic instruction with worked examples outperforms discovery-based approaches for this skill, and adopts a structured sequence of teacher modeling followed by guided and independent practice. The team checks their new lesson plans against that evidence rather than choosing an activity just because it looks engaging.
weeklyProduct: No student artifact — the visible result is a documented decision record showing which research-backed strategy was chosen and why.

title: The Turner Engagement Cycle
description: A six-phase instructional arc (Notice, Read, Talk, Solve, Defend, Revise) that underlies every lesson and ensures every student thinks rather than just receives content, which is the core mechanism the book credits for closing the achievement gap between producing an answer and being able to defend it.
howTo:
Notice: Open with something real (a source, graph, line, or phenomenon) and have students observe it before judging it, using background knowledge and vocabulary to make the noticing meaningful.
Read: Have students interrogate the text of the discipline (document, problem, passage, or data) closely before drawing a conclusion.
Talk: Have students rehearse their thinking with a partner so every student, including quiet ones, has said their idea once before the whole class hears it.
Solve: Ask students to build a claim, a solution, or an interpretation from the evidence.
Defend: Require students to put their answer in writing with the evidence named, making the thinking visible enough to coach.
Revise: Test the claim against a second source, value, or passage and change it when the evidence pushes back.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
example: For a unit on the water cycle, a teacher has students notice a foggy window (Notice), read a short diagram-based text on condensation (Read), turn-and-talk to predict what happens next (Talk), write a one-sentence claim about why the window fogged (Solve), defend it in writing citing the diagram (Defend), and revise the claim after comparing it to a classmate's (Revise). The six-phase arc stays the same lesson to lesson even though the content changes every day.
weeklyProduct: A written claim with named evidence, answering a higher-order 'why' question, revised after checking it against a second source.

title: Teaching, Engagement, and Learning (TEL)
description: A planning and look-for lens that separates what the teacher does (Teaching), what students actively do with content (Engagement), and the lasting change in what students understand and can do independently (Learning), so teachers and coaches don't mistake a busy activity or quiet compliance for actual learning.
howTo:
For each phase of a lesson, name the teaching move: set a clear purpose, model and explain, provide scaffolds, or give practice and feedback.
Check that students are engaging: noticing, reading, talking, solving, defending, and revising in ways that make their thinking visible.
Look for real learning evidence rather than activity: can students retrieve and explain without copying, apply and transfer understanding, correct misconceptions, and work with increasing independence.
Use the phase-by-phase map (Notice through Revise) to match each teaching move to the specific learning evidence it should produce, and treat a completed activity or correct answer under heavy prompting as not yet evidence of learning.
During a walkthrough, record what you see as evidence of instruction and engagement; rely on student work collected over time as the stronger evidence of learning.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
example: During a persuasive-writing unit, a coach doing a walkthrough notes that the teacher modeled a claim-evidence paragraph (Teaching) and students were annotating and drafting their own paragraphs (Engagement), but the real test of Learning comes a week later when students write a new persuasive paragraph on a different topic without the sentence frame and the coach checks whether they can still structure the argument independently. A lesson full of busy annotation is not counted as learning until that independent transfer shows up in student work.
weeklyProduct: No single student artifact — the visible result is a teacher's walkthrough notes distinguishing real learning evidence from busy activity or compliance.

title: Front-Loading Knowledge Before a Demanding Text
description: A boundary-setting technique for directly teaching the context, concepts, vocabulary, and background knowledge students need before they read a demanding text, which builds the comprehension floor without giving away the thinking students must still do themselves.
howTo:
Identify the two or three essential concepts or background facts the text turns on before assigning it.
Directly teach that context using a focused explanation, map, timeline, diagram, demonstration, short video, or worked example.
Stop short of pre-answering the purpose question, supplying the interpretation, announcing the conclusion, or completing the reasoning students are expected to build from the evidence themselves.
Use the appropriate-vs-over-scaffolding contrast as a check: explain what something was and when/where it happened, preteach key concepts, or review needed prior knowledge — but do not paraphrase every hard sentence, announce conclusions before students examine evidence, or hand students the 'correct' interpretation.
Pair this with the expectation that students read content-rich, course-aligned text tied to the current unit at least three times a week, so the front-loading always serves a real text students are about to read.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Activating Prior Knowledge/Predicting (REL West)
example: Before assigning a primary-source excerpt about the Berlin Airlift, a teacher spends five minutes explaining the basic post-WWII division of Germany and pointing to a map of Berlin's sectors, without telling students what conclusion the excerpt supports. Students then read the source themselves and have to determine, from the text, whether the airlift was primarily a humanitarian or a political move.
weeklyProduct: No written student artifact — the visible result is students entering a demanding text already knowing the two or three concepts it depends on.

title: Gradual Release of Responsibility
description: A four-phase framework (focused instruction, guided instruction, collaborative learning, independent learning) for shifting responsibility for thinking from the teacher to the student in increasingly precise, temporary steps, connecting directly to the Turner Engagement Cycle by explaining how that thinking moves from teacher modeling toward independent student performance.
howTo:
Focused instruction: establish the purpose, model disciplinary thinking, and make your process visible while students observe, notice, connect to prior knowledge, and track the model.
Guided instruction: prompt, cue, question, scaffold, and check understanding while students attempt the move with support and explain their emerging thinking.
Collaborative learning: structure accountable interaction and monitor the quality of reasoning while students rehearse, question, coach, challenge, and improve ideas with peers.
Independent learning: reduce support and collect individual evidence of learning while students read, solve, defend, apply, and revise with increasing independence.
Revisit or combine phases as needed rather than treating them as a rigid script, and remember that collaboration is a supported phase, not the endpoint — every student must still produce individual evidence of learning.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Gradual Release of Responsibility in Action: Classroom Video
example: In a lesson on balancing chemical equations, the teacher first models balancing one equation on the board while narrating her thinking (focused instruction), then coaches student pairs through a second equation with prompting questions (guided instruction), has small groups tackle a third equation together while she circulates (collaborative learning), and finally has each student balance a fourth equation alone as an exit ticket (independent learning).
weeklyProduct: Individual student work samples from the independent-learning phase showing each student reading, solving, or defending on their own.

title: PIES: The Cooperative-Learning Standard
description: PIES is a four-part checklist (Positive interdependence, Individual accountability, Equal participation, Simultaneous interaction) that turns simple group work into true structured cooperative learning. It matters for achievement because it guarantees every student thinks, produces, and can be held accountable individually rather than letting group consensus substitute for evidence of learning.
howTo:
Design a shared task where students genuinely need one another to complete or improve the work (positive interdependence).
Build in a requirement that every student must think, write, explain, or be ready to respond (individual accountability).
Structure turns, roles, or contributions so no single student can dominate (equal participation).
Arrange the task so many students are thinking and interacting at once, not one performing for the room (simultaneous interaction).
End every cooperative routine with an individual written artifact or individual response — group consensus never replaces it.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Structures Include PIES
example: For a lab on plant growth variables, a teacher checks her group task against all four letters: students need each other because each person collects a different data set (positive interdependence), every student must record their own data table (individual accountability), rotating recorder and reporter roles prevent one student from taking over (equal participation), and all four lab groups measure their plants at the same time (simultaneous interaction). Each student still turns in an individual lab write-up so group consensus never substitutes for the individual evidence.
weeklyProduct: An individual written response or explanation from every student at the end of a cooperative task, not just a group consensus.

title: Numbered Heads Together: Source Interrogation
description: A cooperative structure where teams jointly interrogate a source but only one randomly-numbered student answers for the team, so every member must be ready to explain who created a source, what it claims, and the evidence line. It builds accountable talk while keeping individual accountability intact.
howTo:
Give students 2 minutes to silently mark the source alone.
Have teams discuss for 3 minutes: every person must be able to explain creator, claim, and supporting evidence.
Give 1 minute for each student to individually record their answer.
Call a random number; that student responds for the team and names the evidence.
Fix domination by requiring the silent first write and round-robin evidence sharing before open discussion.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Kagan Cooperative Learning - Numbered Heads Together
example: Using the Dawes Act text, the teacher tells teams: "Read independently first. Then put your heads together. Every person must be able to explain who created the source, what it claims, and the exact line that supports the answer." After two minutes of silent source-marking and three minutes of team discussion, students each complete a sourcing box on creator, audience, purpose, claim, and evidence, and a randomly called number answers for the team, naming the evidence.
weeklyProduct: Each student's individually recorded written answer naming a source's creator, claim, and evidence before one number is called to report.

title: Timed PairShare: Claim Rehearsal
description: A tightly timed partner protocol that gives every student protected rehearsal of their claim before whole-group argument, using named source language and a required paraphrase to make listening visible.
howTo:
Give 30 seconds of private planning time.
Partner A states their claim and names one source in 45 seconds.
Partner B summarizes the claim and asks one evidence question in 20 seconds, then switch roles.
Each student writes a revised claim sentence after speaking, using a frame such as "My claim is… Source ___ shows…".
Stop any turn that does not name a source to prevent opinion-trading.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Teacher Toolkit: Time Pair Share
example: While rehearsing claims about the Dawes Act, Partner A gets 45 seconds to state a claim and name one source, then Partner B has 20 seconds to summarize the claim and ask an evidence question before they switch. Each student then writes a revised "Historian's Sentence" using the frame "My claim is… Source ___ shows…," and the teacher stops any turn that skips naming a source.
weeklyProduct: A revised claim sentence from each student naming a specific source, written right after their timed partner exchange.

title: RoundTable: Evidence Collection
description: A rotating-paper cooperative structure where each student adds one unique, non-repeated piece of evidence to a shared team bank, then individually selects and cites one item — building a rich collective evidence pool while still forcing individual precision.
howTo:
Give teams 1 minute to review the source before starting.
Run four rounds where each student adds one new item (detail, sourcing observation, question, or cross-source connection) and passes the paper — no repeats allowed.
Have teams sort contributions into strongest evidence, complication, and unanswered question (2 minutes).
Require every contribution to include a source name, section, quote, or specific detail — no vague phrases.
Each student initials their unique contribution and individually selects and cites one item in an exit response.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: The Power of Student Engagement: Simultaneous Round Table
example: Working from the Dawes Act document set, a team of four passes one paper around, each student adding one new source detail, sourcing observation, or cross-source connection without repeating an earlier contribution. After four rounds the team sorts its bank into strongest evidence, complication, and unanswered question, and each student initials their unique entry before citing one item in an individual exit response.
weeklyProduct: A shared team evidence sheet with each student's initialed, unique contribution plus an individually cited item in an exit response.

title: Quiz-Quiz-Trade: Vocabulary and Source Review
description: A mix-and-mingle vocabulary drill where students repeatedly quiz and coach partners using flashcards, then trade cards and rotate, building rapid retrieval of discipline vocabulary and immediate application to the day's source.
howTo:
Partner A quizzes for 45 seconds while Partner B answers and gets coached from the back of the card, then switch roles.
Trade cards, find a new partner, and repeat with at least three different partners.
Finish with 2 minutes of written application using one of the terms in relation to today's source.
Put an application prompt on every card (e.g., "How would this term change the way we read today's source?") so cards aren't just definition trivia.
For access, include a visual, example, and non-example on each card and allow preview time.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Teacher Toolkit: Quiz, Quiz, Trade
example: With vocabulary cards for terms like sovereignty, allotment, primary source, and corroboration tied to the Dawes Act unit, Partner A quizzes Partner B for 45 seconds and coaches from the back of the card, they switch roles, then trade cards and find a new partner, repeating with three different partners. Students finish with two minutes writing an application of one term to the day's source.
weeklyProduct: A short written response from each student applying one vocabulary term to today's source after several rounds of flashcard quizzing.

title: Frayer Model for Vocabulary
description: A four-quadrant vocabulary tool (definition, characteristics, examples, non-examples) used to pre-teach the one or two terms a unit's method turns on, with special weight on the non-example because that's where student misconceptions live.
howTo:
Choose only the term(s) the method actually turns on (e.g., "primary source") rather than every unfamiliar word.
Write a definition in student-usable words.
List defining characteristics that distinguish the term.
Give a real example drawn from the current inquiry.
Write a non-example that names the specific confusion students actually hold (e.g., mistaking a textbook summary for a primary source).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: A Before Instruction Vocabulary Strategy: Frayer Model
example: For the term primary source in the Dawes Act unit, the teacher builds a Frayer model with a student-usable definition, characteristics, a real example from the document set, and a non-example that names the actual misconception students hold: a textbook mistaken for a primary source. The teacher tells students, "Show me the thing itself: the map, the law, the letter," to correct that specific confusion.
weeklyProduct: A completed four-quadrant chart per term showing definition, characteristics, an example, and a targeted non-example.

title: The Dissection Protocol
description: A four-pass procedure for tearing apart a single hard, dense sentence (like legal or formal historical prose) so students can find hidden actors, unfreeze abstract nouns into actions, catch fine print, and produce a plain-language translation. It builds the close-reading skill needed to argue from primary sources rather than just decode them.
howTo:
Pass 1 — Circle the actors: identify who acts or is acted on; if no actor is visible, write the hidden actor in the margin.
Pass 2 — Underline the actions: identify what is done, unfreezing any nominalizations back into verbs (e.g., allotment → someone allots).
Pass 3 — Bracket the fine print: mark conditions, exceptions, and scope language such as "provided that," "except," "shall not extend to."
Pass 4 — Translate to plain speech: write one sentence of 20 words or fewer that a sixth-grader could repeat; if you can't translate it, return to pass one.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
example: On the Dawes Act's opening sentence, the teacher circles the hidden actor (the government, since the law's passive voice hides who is acting), underlines the actions while unfreezing "allotment" into "someone allots," brackets fine print like "provided that" and "shall not extend to," and finally translates the sentence into twenty words a sixth-grader could repeat. The class works through all four passes together before trying the next sentence independently.
weeklyProduct: Each student's marked-up sentence plus a written plain-language translation of 20 words or fewer.

title: The Annotation System: Five Marks for Any Document
description: A five-code annotation system (A, X, ?, !, V) that gives students a consistent, purposeful way to mark up any document so their marks actually drive later discussion instead of being decorative highlighting.
howTo:
Teach one code at a time: A = author's intent word, X = exception or fine print, ? = a genuine question, ! = a contradiction with another source, V = a voice missing from the document.
Have students mark the document with the appropriate codes as they read.
Require the codes to drive the discussion that follows — question marks open partner talk, exclamation marks trigger corroboration tasks, V-marks send students hunting for missing testimony.
Check that every annotation used gets referenced later; an annotation nobody uses in the talk did no work.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: How to Teach Annotation Skills
example: Reading the Dawes Act, students mark A over words revealing the government's intent, X over exceptions like Section 8's exemption for the Five Tribes, ? over genuine confusions, ! where the text contradicts Chitto Harjo's testimony, and V beside passages where no Native voice appears. The teacher then runs discussion directly off the codes, having students explain their V-marks and argue from their !-marks rather than treating the annotations as decoration.
weeklyProduct: A document marked with the five annotation codes (A, X, ?, !, V) that visibly drives the discussion that follows.

title: Text Mapping
description: A mechanical, pre-thinking annotation step that gives the whole class a shared address system for a document — numbering paragraphs, circling key terms, and underlining claims — so discussion can reference exact locations instead of vague descriptions.
howTo:
Number every paragraph in the margin of the document.
Circle key terms, including Tier 3 vocabulary and intent-carrying words.
Underline the author's claims.
Mark first for structure, then apply the five annotation codes (A · X · ? · ! · V) for thinking — the marks locate, the codes interpret.
Use the paragraph numbers in discussion so students can point to exact locations (e.g., "paragraph 4, second sentence").
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Lesson # 2 Close Reading/Annotation
example: Before any interpretation, students number every paragraph of the Dawes Act in the margin, circle Tier 3 vocabulary like "severalty" and "allotment," and underline the law's claims about protecting Native land. Once every student's copy has the same paragraph numbers, the class can discuss "paragraph 4, second sentence" instead of vaguely gesturing at "that part near the end."
weeklyProduct: A numbered, marked-up document with circled key terms and underlined claims that students reference by exact location in discussion.

title: Margin Thinking
