description: A set of six named margin-writing moves (Visualize, Summarize, Clarify, Connect, Respond, Question) that students use to think in writing beside the text, going beyond mapping and codes into active interpretation.
howTo:
Teach the six moves one at a time: Visualize (sketch what's described), Summarize (ten words or fewer), Clarify (name and work at a confusion), Connect (link to another document, event, or the reader's world), Respond (an argued reaction), Question (a real question at a named Costa level).
Model what each move sounds like on a shared document.
Once students are automatic with each move individually, require two different moves per page.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Annotation Strategies: Reading
example: Reading the Dawes Act, students practice the six margin moves one at a time: they sketch what a described land parcel would look like (Visualize), summarize a dense clause in ten words (Summarize), name their confusion about what "severalty" means (Clarify), connect Section 8's exemption to Chitto Harjo's later testimony (Connect), argue a reaction to the law's claim of protection (Respond), and pose a Costa-level question about who wrote the fine print (Question). Once each move is automatic, the teacher requires two different moves per page.
weeklyProduct: A page of margin writing showing at least two of the six thinking moves, including a genuine question at a named level.

title: The Says/Does Chart
description: A two-column chart (what a section SAYS vs. what it DOES) that turns reading comprehension into sourcing by isolating a document's rhetorical moves — promising, defining, authorizing, excepting, selling — separately from its content.
howTo:
Divide the page into two columns per section: SAYS (content summary) and DOES (rhetorical move).
For each section or excerpt, write a brief content summary in the SAYS column.
In the DOES column, name the section's rhetorical function (e.g., "frames the law as benevolent," "authorizes conversion of communal title").
Use the DOES column as the entry point into sourcing discussion, since that's where authorial intent becomes visible.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
example: Charting the Dawes Act's title against its actual sections, students write in the SAYS column that the title promises to "extend the protection of the laws," then in the DOES column note that Section 1 actually authorizes dividing communal land into individual parcels. The gap between the two columns becomes the entry point for the class's sourcing discussion about the law's real intent.
weeklyProduct: A written two-column chart per section naming what the text says and what rhetorical move it does, launching sourcing discussion.

title: SOAPStone
description: A six-element source-analysis lens (Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone) that extends basic sourcing questions by adding Tone — the attitude carried by the language — as its own piece of evidence.
howTo:
Identify the Speaker: who created the source and what is their stake in it.
Identify the Occasion: when and in what context it was made.
Identify the Audience: for whom it was written.
Identify the Purpose: why it was made.
Identify the Subject and then the Tone — the attitude the language carries — and treat the tone itself as evidence of the author's intent.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: How To Use the SOAPSTone Strategy
example: Running SOAPStone on a settler-era land guide promoting Indian Territory allotment, students identify the Speaker (a land promoter), the Occasion (the years just after the Dawes Commission's work began), the Audience (prospective settlers), the Purpose (to sell land), and finally the Tone, noting that its breezy, inviting language is itself evidence that the pamphlet is promotional rather than neutral.
weeklyProduct: Each student's written breakdown of a source's speaker, occasion, audience, purpose, subject, and tone as evidence of intent.

title: Cornell Notes, Tuned for Documents
description: A one-page adaptation of the Cornell note-taking format where the cue column holds the source-interrogation questions, the notes column holds sourced evidence, and the bottom summary strip becomes the Historian's Sentence — written last, after corroboration.
howTo:
Use the cue column for the interrogation lens questions: who created it, when, for whom, why, whose voice is missing.
Use the notes column to record evidence, with each entry tagged to its source verb.
Leave the bottom summary strip blank until after corroboration.
Write the summary strip last as the Historian's Sentence: claim, named evidence, corroboration — never write it before the second source is checked.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: How to Use Cornell Notes
example: For the Dawes Act, students use the cue column to hold interrogation questions (who created it, when, for whom, whose voice is missing), the notes column to record evidence tagged with source verbs like "authorizes" or "exempts," and leave the bottom summary strip blank until after checking a second source. Only then do they write the Historian's Sentence in the strip: a claim, named evidence, and the corroboration that tested it.
weeklyProduct: A one-page Cornell sheet with interrogation questions, sourced evidence entries, and a final Historian's Sentence citing corroborated evidence.

title: Frames: The Sentence, Then the Paragraph
description: Scaffolded sentence and paragraph templates with the thinking left blank, used to build students up from a single claim sentence to a full argumentative paragraph before the frame is retired.
howTo:
Start with sentence-level frames (e.g., "The author claims ______, but ______ shows ______").
Once students fill sentence frames fluently, move to the paragraph frame: claim sentence → first evidence with source verb → corroborating evidence from a second source with its verb → a sentence naming convergence or conflict → a so-what.
Model a full paragraph built from the frame before releasing students to write independently.
Post the frame during initial use, then retire it once students no longer need the scaffold — the frame is a ramp, not a floor.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Writing with Paragraph Frames
example: Students first fill in the sentence frame "The author claims ______, but ______ shows ______" about the Dawes Act's promise of protection, then build up to the full paragraph frame: claim sentence, first evidence with its source verb, corroborating evidence from a second source, a sentence naming convergence or conflict, and a so-what. The teacher models a full paragraph this way — "The Dawes Act presented allotment as protection, but its own text undermines the claim..." — before posting the frame and eventually retiring it once students no longer need it.
weeklyProduct: A student-written paragraph following the claim-evidence-corroboration frame, citing two sources with named source verbs.

title: The Response Journal
description: A running two-column notebook (evidence on the left, thinking on the right) kept across an entire inquiry, used to build the habit of corroboration over time rather than as a one-off assignment.
howTo:
In the left column, have students record a quoted line or detail with its citation.
In the right column, have students write at least three sentences of reaction, question, or connection — no summary allowed.
Collect weekly and read for thinking, never grade for polish.
Encourage students to let later entries argue back against earlier ones, building corroboration as an ongoing habit.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Reading Response Journals Made Easy - www.lauracandler ...
example: Across the Dawes Act inquiry, students keep a two-column notebook where the left side holds a quoted line like "the parcels are to be selected by the heads of families" with its citation, and the right side holds at least three sentences reacting to it — questioning who is really doing the "selecting" once the enrollment cards show the Commission recording families by blood quantum. Collected weekly and read only for thinking, later entries end up arguing back against earlier ones as the corroboration habit builds.
weeklyProduct: A two-column journal entry with a quoted, cited line on one side and at least three sentences of student reaction on the other.

title: RAFT: Writing From Inside the History
description: A perspective-writing structure (Role, Audience, Format, Topic) where students write as a historical figure while staying bounded by what that role could plausibly know, combining empathy with an evidence requirement.
howTo:
Assign or let students choose the four elements: Role, Audience, Format, Topic.
Require the writer to use only what their role could plausibly know in that year.
Label every RAFT piece a "historically informed fictional exemplar" — built from documents but not itself a document.
Anchor every claim in the piece to evidence from the actual document set.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: R.A.F.T. Role Audience Format Topic
example: For the Dawes Act unit, a student writes as a Muscogee (Creek) citizen in 1899 addressing the Dawes Commission, using only what that role could plausibly know at the time and labeling the piece a historically informed fictional exemplar rather than a real document. Every claim in the letter is anchored to evidence from the actual document set, such as the Commission's enrollment procedures.
weeklyProduct: A perspective-writing piece where the student writes as a historical figure, with every claim anchored to a cited document.

title: The Three-Pass Peer Review
description: A structured peer-editing checklist that replaces vague 'I liked it' feedback with three separate, targeted passes over a partner's draft — claim, evidence, and warrant/whole-text test — each producing a specific written note.
howTo:
Pass 1 — Claim: underline the claim and judge whether it is arguable or actually plot summary in disguise.
Pass 2 — Evidence: check whether every quote is exact, cited by paragraph, and quoted rather than paraphrased.
Pass 3 — Warrant and whole-text test: check whether the writer explains why the quoted words mean that, and whether the claim has been tested against a passage that could complicate it.
Have the reviewer write one specific sentence of feedback per pass.
Require the writer to revise against all three passes before the teacher ever sees the draft.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: 60-Second Strategy: Peer Review
example: Reviewing a partner's paragraph on the Dawes Act, a student runs three passes: underlining the claim to check it's arguable rather than "a fact wearing a claim costume," numbering each piece of evidence to confirm it has a named source and source verb like "authorizes" or "testifies," and checking whether a second, corroborating source appears. The reviewer writes one specific sentence per pass, such as "Your Harjo quote is sourced perfectly; make the other one match it," and the writer revises against all three notes before the teacher ever sees the draft.
weeklyProduct: A partner's draft marked up with three separate written feedback notes on claim, cited evidence, and warrant, then revised.

title: Mystery Document
description: Students examine a visually rich source with its caption removed, building an evidence-based hypothesis about who made it, when, and why before the answer is revealed — lowering the risk of entering a lesson and rewarding observation over guessing.
howTo:
Strip a visually rich source (photo, map, ledger page, cartoon) of every caption, date, and credit.
Give students 2 minutes of silent noticing, listing only observations, not interpretations.
Have pairs merge lists and sort into observed vs. inferred (3 minutes).
Run rounds where each pair offers one observation and one inference tied to a visible detail (5 minutes); the class drafts source guesses tied to details (5 minutes).
Reveal the caption and compare, discussing which detail carried the most information (3 minutes).
Have each student write a three-line source hypothesis and reconcile it with the reveal.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Analyzing Primary and Secondary Sources in a Middle School Classroom
example: The teacher projects an allotment-era map with its caption stripped away and gives students two silent minutes to list only observations, such as a perfect numbered grid with handwritten names filling the squares. Pairs sort their observations into observed versus inferred, offer a source hypothesis tied to a specific detail, and only then does the teacher reveal that it is a Dawes-era allotment map, letting the class check how close their reasoning came.
weeklyProduct: A three-line written hypothesis answering who-made-it-and-why, citing observed details, reconciled against the revealed caption.

title: Evidence Sort
description: Teams sort short document excerpts into supports/refutes/irrelevant piles against a posted claim, with an honest "irrelevant" pile that reveals who actually read closely, then rewrite the claim to match what the evidence supports.
howTo:
Cut 10–12 short excerpts from the document set into strips, including 2–3 plausible-looking but genuinely irrelevant distractors, and post one claim.
Have teams of three sort strips into supports / refutes / irrelevant piles (8 minutes), requiring a source verb to justify every placement.
Have each team defend its two hardest calls to a neighboring team and re-sort if needed (5 minutes).
Discuss as a whole class any strips that landed in different piles across teams, sources named (5 minutes).
Have each student individually write the claim as it survives the sort (2 minutes).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Using Relevant Text Evidence Activity
example: For the claim "Allotment fulfilled the promise in the 1887 title," teams sort ten to twelve strips cut from the Dawes Act document set into supports, refutes, and irrelevant piles, including a few plausible-looking distractors about railroad routes that belong in the irrelevant pile. After defending their two hardest calls to a neighboring team, students individually rewrite the claim to match what the sorted evidence actually supports.
weeklyProduct: Each student's individually written claim, revised to match the evidence after sorting document excerpts by source and citing a source verb for each placement.

title: Four Corners
description: A movement-based activity where students physically commit to a position (agree/disagree/it's complicated/need more evidence) on a posted claim and can only switch corners by naming the source that moved them, making revision physical and visible.
howTo:
Post four corner labels (AGREE, DISAGREE, IT'S COMPLICATED, NEED MORE EVIDENCE) and a claim with real texture.
Give students a silent minute to write their corner choice and one named source before anyone moves.
Have students move to their corner, then merge evidence with corner-mates and choose their strongest single source (4 minutes).
Have each corner report one speaker, one source, one verb (5 minutes).
Allow students to switch corners only if they can name the source that moved them (2 minutes), then close with a sourced one-sentence exit line.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: The Four Corners Classroom Strategy
example: Posting the claim "Allotment's supporters believed they were helping," the teacher sends students to AGREE, DISAGREE, IT'S COMPLICATED, or NEED MORE EVIDENCE corners, but only after each has silently written their choice and one named source. Students may only switch corners if they can name the exact source that moved them, such as the Lake Mohonk proceedings versus the Dawes Commission's acreage records.
weeklyProduct: A written exit line from each student naming their final position and the specific source that shaped or moved it.

title: Structured Academic Controversy
description: Pairs argue an assigned side of a debate from documents, then switch and argue the reverse side without reusing arguments, before dropping roles to write a consensus claim that survives both cases — making disagreement the engine of deeper reading.
howTo:
Assign each pair a side to argue (not their own opinion) so students must read sources supporting a position they may not hold.
Give 8 minutes where every argument must carry a source, date, and verb — no unsourced argument counts.
Have pairs switch sides and argue the reverse without reusing their opponent's arguments, forcing a second pass through the document set.
Have pairs drop roles and write one consensus claim that survives everything argued, naming evidence on both sides and specifying "for whom" and "when" if the answer is "both".
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Steps of Structured Academic Controversy
example: Arguing the Dawes Act's effects, pairs are assigned a side to defend using the document set, then must switch and argue the reverse without reusing their opponent's points, hunting the sources a second time for what they missed. Finally the pair drops roles and writes one consensus claim — for example, that allotment could be both sincerely intended and destructive at once — naming evidence from both the Mohonk proceedings and Chitto Harjo's testimony.
weeklyProduct: A written consensus claim answering a complex 'for whom and when' question, citing sourced evidence from both debated sides.

title: Silent Written Conversation
description: Small groups respond to a shared source and to each other entirely in writing on a shared sheet — no talking — drawing arrows to show whose comment they're building on, before voices come on to report the strongest thread. It supports achievement by giving every student, including the quietest, a full and equal voice regardless of speed, volume, or confidence.
howTo:
Glue one source excerpt to the center of a large shared sheet per group; give every student a pen for the whole activity.
Run a silent period where students write responses to the document and to each other — questions, challenges, connections — drawing arrows to link comments.
After the silent period, have the group silently read the entire sheet.
Bring voices on: each group states the strongest thread on their sheet and where it should lead next.
Have each student turn the thread they contributed to into one individual sourced sentence.
Enforce a 'second lap' rule: after a student's first comment, every later comment must attach to someone else's, preventing four parallel monologues.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Chalk Talk
example: With one Dawes Act excerpt glued to the center of a large shared sheet, a group of four writes silent responses and questions to the document and to each other for eight minutes, drawing arrows to show whose comment they're building on. After a silent read of the whole sheet, the group reports its strongest thread aloud, and each student turns the thread they contributed to into one individual sourced sentence.
weeklyProduct: A shared sheet of written, linked comments citing the source, plus each student's individual sourced closing sentence.

title: You Be the Curator
description: A multi-day capstone project where students design a three-item museum exhibit arguing one interpretation of an event, including a claim-based title, sourced captions, and a dissent label acknowledging the strongest objection — combining synthesis, sourcing, and intellectual honesty.
howTo:
Have students (solo or pairs) choose three items from the document set that together argue one interpretation.
Write three caption cards (each with source, date, source verb, and one sentence of significance) and a claim-based exhibit title (not a topic).
Write a fourth label: the strongest sourced objection to their own exhibit (the dissent label).
Run a gallery walk with docent rotations: half present while half visit and ask two required questions, then swap.
Grade with the same rubric logic throughout: title = claim, captions = named evidence, dissent = corroboration.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Museum Project-Based Learning
videoChannel: David Lee | Learning in Perpetual Beta
example: As a capstone, students choose three items from the Dawes Act document set to build a museum exhibit, writing a claim-based title like "Protection on Paper" instead of a topic label, sourced caption cards for each artifact, and a fourth dissent label naming the strongest objection to their own exhibit. During a gallery walk, half the class presents while the other half visits and asks two required sourced questions before they swap.
weeklyProduct: A three-item exhibit with a claim-based title, sourced captions, and a written dissent label citing the strongest counter-evidence.

title: Document Speed-Rotation
description: Teams rotate through four source stations, each with one interrogation-lens question, leaving written observations for the next group to build on or dispute — creating a class-wide, collectively built sourcing record.
howTo:
Set up four stations, each with a different type of source and one interrogation-lens question (who created it? for whom? for what purpose? whose voice is missing?).
Have teams rotate every 4 minutes, answering the station's question on shared paper and responding to or disputing what previous teams wrote (16 minutes total).
Run a fifth rotation where teams return to their home station, read the full sheet, and circle the single best line (3 minutes).
Have each home team report the best line and why it earned the circle (6 minutes).
Seed each sheet with a deliberately arguable starter line to prevent teams from only writing the obvious.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Gallery Walk: Creating Space for Observation and Analytical Thinking
example: Four stations each hold a different Dawes Act-era source with one lens question, and teams rotate every few minutes, leaving a written observation at each stop for the next group to build on or dispute. When teams return to their home station, they read the full accumulated sheet and circle the single best line, then report why it earned the circle.
weeklyProduct: A shared station sheet with each team's written, cited observations built on or disputing what earlier teams wrote.

title: The Tribunal
description: A mock-trial structure that puts a policy (never a people) on trial, with advocates, witnesses presenting numbered exhibits, and jurors who must cite specific exhibits in their verdicts — turning corroboration into courtroom drama grounded strictly in the document set.
howTo:
Assign roles: advocates for the policy, advocates against, witnesses who present exhibits, and jurors with verdict forms; build cases from the document set only, with every argument keyed to an exhibit number (Day 1).
Run opening statements (2 minutes each).
Have witnesses present exhibits while the other side may cross-examine the sourcing — who made it, when, why (20 minutes).
Run closings (2 minutes each).
Have jurors deliberate aloud and deliver verdicts that cite the two exhibits that decided the case and name one complicating exhibit (10 minutes).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Making Arguments Based on Evidence: Mock Trials
example: The class puts the allotment policy itself on trial: advocates for the policy cite the Lake Mohonk proceedings and the Act's title, advocates against call the acreage records and Chitto Harjo's 1906 testimony as witnesses, and jurors deliver verdicts that must cite the two exhibits that decided the case plus one complicating exhibit. The teacher reminds the room, "You may attack an exhibit's sourcing, its context, or its scope. You may not attack a people, and you may not invent evidence."
weeklyProduct: A juror's verdict answering a why-guilty-or-not question, citing two specific numbered exhibits and one complicating exhibit.

title: Hot Seat / Press Conference
description: One student role-plays a historical figure using a document-based dossier while the class asks sourced questions; the figure may only answer what the documents support, revealing the limits of a historical perspective without lapsing into caricature.
howTo:
Build one-page dossiers for figures connected to the documents, listing only what each figure could plausibly know, want, and cite.
Have a volunteer (or the teacher, the first time) take the seat with 2 minutes of prep.
Have the class ask sourced questions that must cite something from the document set (10 minutes).
Require the seat to answer only what the dossier and documents support, allowing "my figure wouldn't know that" as a valid answer.
Debrief out of role on what the figure could not see from their position (5 minutes).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Hot Seating
example: One student takes the hot seat as a Dawes Commission enrollment clerk, working from a one-page dossier built only from the document set, while classmates ask sourced questions like "The acreage records document three million acres sold: how do you explain that?" The seat may only answer what the dossier supports, and "my figure wouldn't know that" is treated as a valid, instructive answer during the out-of-role debrief on what the clerk's position couldn't let him see.
weeklyProduct: A recorded exchange where classmates ask cited, evidence-based questions and the role-play figure answers only what the sourced dossier supports.

title: Living Timeline
description: Students holding event cards physically arrange themselves along a timeline and must argue placement and causation aloud, turning a sequence of dates into an argument about mechanism rather than a memorization exercise.
howTo:
Give each pair one event card and set up a long open line on a wall or hallway.
Have pairs read their card and place themselves on the line without talking to other pairs first (3 minutes).
Have pairs state their placement and one reason it belongs there relative to a neighbor (4 minutes).
Allow the class to propose moves, but only with a stated causal reason ("because...") (5 minutes).
Check placements against the record and have pairs write the one causal link their card carries (3 minutes).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
example: Each pair holds an event card — the 1887 Dawes Act, the 1893 Dawes Commission, the 1898 Curtis Act, 1907 statehood — and physically places themselves along a wall without talking to other pairs first. A move on the line requires a stated "because," such as arguing the Curtis Act belongs after the Commission because the Commission's stalled negotiations are why Congress forced allotment forward without tribal consent.
weeklyProduct: A written causal-link sentence from each pair explaining why their event belongs where they placed it on the timeline.

title: Philosophical Chairs
description: A structured debate where two facing rows argue a binary claim, speakers must paraphrase the previous speaker before responding, and students may change seats mid-debate as long as they can name the argument that moved them — making changing one's mind from evidence the explicit goal.
howTo:
Post one genuinely arguable binary claim and set up chairs in two facing rows (agree/disagree) with a small undecided section.
Have each student silently write their position and one named source before sitting (3 minutes).
Run alternating speakers, one at a time, requiring each speaker to paraphrase the previous speaker to their satisfaction before responding (12 minutes).
Allow students to change seats whenever a speaker moves them, as long as they can name the argument that moved them.
Require undecided students to choose a side by the close, then have all students write a closing statement naming their position, source, and the strongest argument against them.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Instructional Strategy: Philosophical Chairs
example: For the binary claim "The reformers' stated purpose deserves to be taken seriously," two facing rows of chairs argue agree versus disagree, and no student may respond until they paraphrase the previous speaker to that speaker's satisfaction. Students change seats mid-debate whenever an argument moves them, then write a closing statement naming their final position, their source, and the strongest argument raised against them.
weeklyProduct: A written closing statement answering why they hold their position, naming a cited source and the strongest counterargument.

title: Socratic Seminar
description: A full-period, text-anchored student-led discussion with an inner and outer circle, requiring a marked text and written questions as the entry ticket so preparation — not confidence — determines who can participate, ending with a written revision that cites a classmate's contribution.
howTo:
Require a marked text and three written questions (one at each Costa level) as the entry ticket; unprepared students join the outer circle as process observers.
Open with a student's Level 2 or 3 question, never the teacher's, and seat 12–15 students in an inner circle with an outer circle observing and coaching.
Let the inner circle discuss for about 25 minutes while the teacher sits outside the circle and only intervenes to re-anchor the talk to the text (paragraph and line).
Require posted talk moves: build on, respectfully disagree with evidence, invite a quiet voice in, and return to the text.
At halftime, swap the outer circle in after one minute of coaching from their partner (about 15 minutes).
Close with a written revision of each student's Reader's Sentence in light of the seminar, citing one classmate's point by name.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Adapting Socratic Seminars for Elementary Students
example: Running a seminar on Kate Chopin's "The Story of an Hour," the teacher opens with a student's Level 3 question about whether the story blames Louise for her joy, then sits outside the inner circle of 12-15 students while they discuss for 25 minutes, intervening only to ask them to return to a paragraph and line. After the outer circle swaps in, the class closes by revising their Reader's Sentence claim in writing, citing a classmate's point by name, as when one student credits a peer's question about why the narrator never judges Louise.
weeklyProduct: Each student's marked text, three written entry-ticket questions, and a revised Reader's Sentence citing a classmate's point by name.

title: RallyRobin: Possible Interpretations
description: A timed partner-turn-taking structure where students alternate text-based observations and interpretations before the class settles on a reading, so every voice generates possibilities before consensus narrows them. It builds engagement by lowering the risk of a first interpretive attempt and requiring every turn to point to specific textual evidence.
howTo:
Give students 45 seconds of silent annotation before talking.
Have partners alternate one observation or interpretation at a time for 2 minutes, with no repeats, and require every turn to point to a word, image, structural choice, or pattern in the text.
Give partners 1 minute to choose the interpretation worth testing further.
Have each student individually record two different interpretations and circle the one they will defend or revise.
If students retell plot instead of interpreting, require the sentence stem: 'The author's choice of ___ may suggest ___.'
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Rally Robin Kagan Example
example: Using "The Story of an Hour," partners alternate observations and interpretations for two minutes, each turn pointing to a specific word, image, or pattern, such as the repetition of "free" or the open window imagery. If a student starts retelling the plot instead of interpreting, the teacher requires the stem "The author's choice of ___ may suggest ___," and each student ends by recording two different interpretations and circling the one they will defend.
weeklyProduct: Each student's card with two written text-based interpretations, one circled, tied to a specific word or pattern in the text.

title: Timed PairShare: Golden Line and Warrant
description: A structured partner routine that rehearses quotation integration and warrant-building before students draft independently, so every student practices explaining how language supports a claim before writing it alone.
howTo:
Give students 1 minute to select and mark a golden line in the text.
Partner A reads the line, states a claim, and explains how the language supports it (60 seconds).
Partner B paraphrases the explanation and asks how that word or choice carries the claim (30 seconds), then switch roles.
Give each student 2 minutes to independently write a Claim–Quoted Evidence–Warrant response.
If students say 'this shows...' and just repeat the claim, require them to name what the language does: creates, contrasts, repeats, withholds, shifts, or complicates.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Instant Engagement Demo: Timed Pair Share
example: On the Chopin story, Partner A reads their chosen golden line, states a claim, and explains how the language supports it in 60 seconds, then Partner B paraphrases and asks how a specific word carries the claim before the two switch roles. If a student just repeats the claim with "this shows...," the teacher requires them to name what the language actually does, such as contrasting, withholding, or shifting, before writing an independent Claim-Evidence-Warrant response.
weeklyProduct: Each student's independently written Claim–Quoted Evidence–Warrant response built from a golden line they marked in the text.

title: Numbered Heads Together: Whole-Text Test
description: A cooperative-learning structure using random accountability to test an existing interpretation against a new passage that supports, complicates, or contradicts it, ensuring every team member can explain how the reading changed.
howTo:
Have students read the initial claim and a second passage independently for 2 minutes and mark it up.
Give teams 4 minutes to decide together what the second passage does to the claim.
Give each student 1 minute to write an individual revised claim.
Call a random number to explain how the second passage changed the reading, so every student must be ready.
If the group searches only for agreement, label the second passage the 'inconvenient passage' and require a more precise claim rather than a discarded one.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Kagan Cooperative Learning - Numbered Heads Together
example: After students claim that "The Story of an Hour" proves Louise never loved her husband, teams test that claim against paragraph 13's "And yet she had loved him — sometimes," deciding together whether the second passage supports, complicates, or contradicts the original reading. Each student writes an individual revised claim, and a randomly called number must explain how the passage changed the team's thinking, with the teacher labeling it the "inconvenient passage" if the group tries to simply agree it doesn't matter.
weeklyProduct: Each student's individually written revised claim showing how a second passage supported, complicated, or contradicted their first reading.

title: RoundTable: Author's Choices
description: A round-robin cooperative structure that builds a shared bank of authorial choices and their effects before students write independently, forcing each contribution to pair evidence with an explained effect rather than a bare label.
howTo:
Give students 1 minute to reread the text.
Go around the group with each student getting 30 seconds to add one author choice, quote or point to it, explain what it does, and pass — no repeating a choice already named.
Give the team 2 minutes to sort the contributions into pattern, contrast, shift, and structure categories.
Give each student 2 minutes to individually select one contribution and use it in an independent paragraph.
If students label devices without explaining their work, require the sentence: 'The author uses ___ to ___, which shapes the reader's understanding by ___.'
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Kagan. "Round Table Consensus". Cooperative Learning in Action
example: Going around the group on the Chopin text, each student adds one authorial choice in 30 seconds, such as the repetition of "free," the turn in the window paragraph, or the passive construction of the first sentence, quoting or pointing to it and explaining its effect without repeating a choice already named. The team then sorts the contributions into pattern, contrast, shift, and structure categories, and each student uses one in an independent paragraph using the frame "The author uses ___ to ___, which shapes the reader's understanding by ___."
weeklyProduct: Each student's independent paragraph naming an author's choice, quoting or pointing to it, and explaining its effect on the reader.

title: Frayer Model for Literary Terms
description: A four-quadrant vocabulary tool that defines a key literary term, lists its features, and — critically — names what it is not, because student misconceptions live in the confused non-example rather than the definition.
howTo:
Choose the one literary term the current reading actually turns on, rather than every vocabulary word in a unit.
Write a student-usable definition in one quadrant and its distinguishing characteristics in a second.
Fill a third quadrant with a real example drawn from the class text.
Fill the fourth quadrant with the specific wrong meaning students actually hold (the seductive confusion), not just an unrelated non-example.
Use the completed chart to let students test, challenge, or replace the example with a better-supported one.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: How to use the Frayer Model
example: For "The Story of an Hour," the class Frayers the term tone rather than every vocabulary word, since the story's final irony depends on it: one quadrant holds a student-usable definition, a second lists characteristics like being produced by specific diction and capable of shifting mid-text, and a third gives real examples such as the exultant tone of "free, free, free!" The fourth quadrant names the actual misconception students hold — confusing tone with mood, or mistaking a reader's "boring" reaction for the narrator's attitude — since that confused non-example is where the misunderstanding lives.
weeklyProduct: A completed four-quadrant chart defining the term, listing features, giving a text example, and naming the specific wrong meaning students hold.

title: Three Reads for Literature
description: A three-pass rereading routine in which each pass has one explicit job — plot, craft, then argument — so students learn that rereading is the method, not a punishment, and so summary can't impersonate analysis later.
howTo:
Read 1, for the story: have students follow the plot and state it in two sentences maximum, so comprehension is contained and can't later pass as analysis.
Read 2, for the craft: have students reread with a pencil, circling repeated words, marking turns, and noting who speaks — applying annotation codes and the Says/Does chart.
Read 3, for the argument: have students identify what the text is really about and which lines they'd have to stand on to say so.
Tell students that if no one could disagree with their answer, it is a summary, not a claim — naming this prevents book-report answers.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: 60-Second Strategy: 3-Read Protocol
example: On "The Story of an Hour," Read 1 has students state the plot in two sentences maximum — a woman hears her husband died and dies herself when he walks in alive — so comprehension can't later pass as analysis. Read 2 has them reread with a pencil circling repeated words like "free," "open," and "heart" and marking turns using the annotation codes, and Read 3 asks what the story is really about, with the teacher noting that if no one could disagree with the answer, it's a summary, not a claim.
weeklyProduct: A two-sentence plot summary plus craft annotations and a claim backed by specific lines, produced across three successive close readings.

title: Chunk & Check
description: An on-ramp for struggling readers that breaks a dense text into small movements with a single margin note each, turning an intimidating wall of prose into a short numbered sequence of manageable steps.
howTo:
Divide the text into its natural movements or sections.
Have students write one short margin note per movement before any interpreting begins (e.g., 'the news,' 'the weeping,' 'the room').
Use the resulting small set of notes as a scaffold that turns a dense page into a handful of accessible steps for the struggling reader.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Chunking- Reading Strategy
example: For a struggling reader working through "The Story of an Hour," the teacher divides the story into its natural movements and has the student write one short margin note per section before any interpreting begins: "the news," "the weeping," "the room," "the window," "the word," "the door," "the stairs," "the end." Eight small notes turn a wall of 1894 prose into eight manageable steps the student can navigate before tackling the story's meaning.
weeklyProduct: A page of short, numbered margin notes, one per text section, showing each student tracked the passage before interpreting it.

title: Cornell Notes for Literature
description: A one-page note-taking format adapted for literary analysis: the cue column holds interpretive questions, the notes column holds quoted and cited evidence, and the bottom summary strip is written last as the claim-evidence-warrant sentence.
howTo:
In the cue column, write interpretive questions: what pattern is building, whose eyes we're behind, what turned.
In the notes column, record evidence, with each entry quoted and cited by paragraph.
Write the summary strip at the bottom last, after testing the claim against a second passage — a claim written before the whole-text test is just a first impression.
Use the summary strip as the Reader's Sentence: claim, quoted evidence, warrant.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: How to Use Cornell Notes
example: Using "The Story of an Hour," the cue column holds interpretive questions like "whose eyes are we behind" and "what turned," while the notes column records quoted, paragraph-cited evidence such as Louise's whispered "free, free, free!" The summary strip at the bottom is written last, after testing the claim against paragraph 13's "she had loved him — sometimes," and becomes the Reader's Sentence: the story's last line indicts everyone who spoke for Louise, tested and surviving the complicating passage.
weeklyProduct: A one-page Cornell notes sheet with interpretive questions, quoted and cited evidence, and a final claim-evidence-warrant summary sentence.

title: Five-Mark Annotation Code (P·T·?·!·W)
description: A five-symbol annotation system (Pattern, Turn, Question, Collision, Whose-eyes) taught one mark at a time so that annotation actively feeds later discussion, writing, and revision instead of sitting unused on the page.
howTo:
Teach mark 'P' for a pattern: a repeated word, image, or move that will feed a claim.
Teach mark 'T' for a turn: where the tone or direction shifts, feeding the Says/Does chart.
Teach mark '?' for a genuine question the text won't explain, to open partner discussion.
Teach mark '!' for a collision: a line that contradicts an earlier one, feeding the whole-text test.
Teach mark 'W' for whose eyes: where the point of perception changes, feeding SOAPStone analysis of the narrator.
Introduce the marks one at a time and require their use in the work that follows so annotation is not merely decorative.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Annotating Text for Close Reading
example: Reading "The Story of an Hour," students mark a P beside the repeated words "free," "open," and "heart" since the repetition feeds a claim, and a T at the window paragraph where the tone shifts from grief to something else entirely. They mark a ! where paragraph 13's "she had loved him — sometimes" collides with the earlier "free, free, free," and a W where the narration moves from outside Louise to inside her perception and back out to the doctors.
weeklyProduct: A marked-up text showing each student's use of the five annotation symbols (pattern, turn, question, collision, whose-eyes) feeding later discussion and writing.

title: Sentence and Paragraph Frames (Claim–Evidence–Warrant)
description: A set of fill-in sentence stems that scaffold interpretive writing, progressing from single-sentence frames to a full Reader's Paragraph frame (claim, quoted evidence, warrant, tested passage, so-what), meant to be retired once fluent.
howTo:
Start with sentence-level frames such as 'The text claims ______, but the line "______" (para ___) suggests ______' or 'The word "______" matters because ______.'
Once students use the sentence frames fluently, assemble the Reader's Paragraph frame: claim, then quoted evidence with paragraph citation, then a warrant explaining why the words mean that, then a second passage tested against the claim, then a so-what.
Post the frame on the wall so students can reference it while writing.
Retire the frame later in the year once students can produce the moves without it — the frame is a ramp, not a floor.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Spark Engagement with Sentence Frames
example: Students start with a sentence frame like "The word 'free' matters because ______" on "The Story of an Hour," then assemble the full Reader's Paragraph frame: a claim that the story's final irony is that the men around Louise misread her, quoted evidence from paragraph 21's "of joy that kills," a warrant explaining why, and a test against paragraph 13's complicating line. The teacher posts the frame on the wall early in the year and plans to retire it by November once students can produce the moves without it.
weeklyProduct: A student paragraph built from the posted sentence frame, containing a claim, quoted and cited evidence, and a warrant.

title: The Dialectical Journal
description: A two-column response journal placing a quoted line from the text on the left and the student's argued thinking on the right, collected weekly and read for thinking rather than graded for polish.
howTo:
In the left column, have students record a quoted line with its paragraph citation.
In the right column, have students write what they make of it — a reaction argued, a question, or a connection to another passage, in at least three sentences, with no summary allowed.
Collect journals weekly and read them for thinking, not polish.
Encourage entries to argue with earlier entries over time so the habit of testing claims against new evidence builds across the unit.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Dialectical Journal Tutorial
example: In the left column, a student quotes paragraph 9 of "The Story of an Hour": "There was something coming to her and she was waiting for it, fearfully," and in the right column argues why it arrives fearfully rather than joyfully, connecting it to a W-mark showing the narrator sees the feeling before Louise does. Collected weekly and read for thinking rather than polish, later entries argue with earlier ones as the student's reading of the story develops.
weeklyProduct: A two-column journal entry with a quoted, cited line on the left and at least three sentences of argued thinking on the right.

title: Perspective Writing
description: A RAFT-style writing tool (Role, Audience, Format, Topic) in which students write as a character bounded strictly by what that role could plausibly know, producing a labeled fictional extension that argues a textual reading 'in costume.'
howTo:
Assign or have students choose a Role, Audience, Format, and Topic tied to the text.
Require that the writer use only what their role could plausibly know at that moment in the story.
Require every piece to be labeled a fictional extension built from textual evidence, not free invention.
Require a defense sheet that cites the specific textual evidence each choice traces back to.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: R.A.F.T. Role Audience Format Topic
example: A student writes as Josephine in her diary the night of "The Story of an Hour," using only what Josephine could plausibly know — the begging at the locked door, the "feverish triumph" in Louise's eyes she witnessed on the stairs — rather than inventing new plot. The piece is labeled a fictional extension built from textual evidence, and the student's defense sheet cites the specific lines each detail traces back to, such as "Open the door — you will make yourself ill."
weeklyProduct: A labeled fictional extension written in a character's voice plus a defense sheet citing the specific textual evidence behind each choice.

title: Structured Partner Talk (A/B Roles)
description: A set of printable partner-talk protocols with assigned A/B roles and an 'add or challenge' rule, giving every student rehearsal time and requiring real listening rather than waiting to speak.
howTo:
Assign Partner A and Partner B roles using something visible in the room (e.g., 'the partner closer to the window is A') to avoid wasting time.
Have Partner A speak first (e.g., name the most important repeated word and where it appears).
Require Partner B to add an occurrence A missed or challenge the choice, rather than simply agreeing.
For claim rehearsal, have the partner ask the discipline's question, 'Where does it say so?', which the speaker must answer with a specific line before writing.
For revision, have partners trade the line they are standing on and find the passage that most complicates (not disproves) it, then decide together whether the claim survives, bends, or breaks.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Talking to a Partner (Interactive Modeling)
example: Assigned by proximity to the window, Partner A tells Partner B the most important repeated word in "The Story of an Hour" and where it appears, and Partner B must add an occurrence A missed or challenge the choice rather than just agreeing. Later, for revision, partners trade the line they're standing on and find the passage that most complicates — not disproves — it, such as testing a "bad marriage" claim against "she had loved him — sometimes," then decide together whether the claim survives, bends, or breaks.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact by default — the visible result is each student verbally citing a specific line before writing begins.

title: Exit Ticket with Quoted Evidence
description: A three-minute daily closing routine that requires every student — not just volunteers — to state a claim about the text with a quoted, cited line and a reason, sorted into three quick piles to plan the next lesson.
howTo:
At the end of every reading day, ask: 'What is this text really about, and what line makes you say so? Claim, quote with its paragraph, and one sentence of why.'
Do not grade the ticket that night; read only the quote line.
Sort papers into three piles in about fifteen seconds each: no quote = Not Yet; a quote with no why = Almost; quote, cite, and a why = Got It.
Open the next lesson by naming the most common gap found, without naming individual students.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: What is an Exit Ticket?: Using Exit Tickets in the Classroom
example: At the end of a reading day on "The Story of an Hour," every student answers: "What is this text really about, and what line makes you say so?" with a claim, a quoted and cited line, and one sentence of why. The teacher doesn't grade it that night but sorts papers into three piles in about fifteen seconds each — no quote is Not Yet, a quote with no why is Almost, and quote-cite-and-why is Got It — then opens the next lesson by naming the most common gap without naming students.
weeklyProduct: A stack of three-minute exit tickets, each with a claim, a quoted and cited line, and one sentence of reasoning, sorted into three piles.

title: Mystery Text
description: An entry-point activity that strips a passage of title, author, and context so students notice and hypothesize before interpreting, making the interpretive question arrive before the plot and lowering the risk of a first guess.
howTo:
Choose a short passage and strip everything around it: title, author, date, even the course.
Give students 2 minutes of silent noticing to list what the sentence does — who speaks, what's strange, what's missing.
Give pairs 4 minutes to merge lists and draft hypotheses about what kind of story or text this must be from.
In rounds, have each pair offer one hypothesis tied to one specific word in the line (5 minutes).
Reveal the title and first sentence only, and have students revise their hypotheses in writing (4 minutes) before reading the full text.
If students guess with no textual anchor, enforce the one-word rule: every hypothesis must name the word it stands on, or it waits.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
example: The teacher projects only the final line of "The Story of an Hour" — "When the doctors came they said she had died of heart disease — of joy that kills" — with no title, author, or story attached. Students spend two minutes silently noticing what the sentence does, then pairs draft hypotheses about what kind of story ends this way, tying each guess to one specific word like "they said," before the title is revealed and they revise their hypotheses in writing.
weeklyProduct: Each student's written, revised hypothesis about a stripped passage, anchored to one specific word from the text.

title: Golden Line
description: A quick activity converting a vague 'I liked it' into the smallest complete act of literary argument: every student picks one line the text cannot lose and defends what would be lost if it were cut.
howTo:
Give students 3 minutes to choose their golden line and write why it does something no other line does.
Have students stand and share around the room: the line, its paragraph number, and one sentence of why, with no repeats unless a new reason is added (5 minutes).
Cluster the picks on the board and discuss where the room converged and what that reveals about the story (4 minutes).
If everyone picks the famous last line, retire it after three picks and require students to find another load-bearing line.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Using Golden Lines When Reading
example: After reading "The Story of an Hour," a student picks "she had loved him — sometimes" (paragraph 13) as their golden line, writing that without it Louise becomes "easy — either a victim or a villain," since that one word forces the reader to hold two true things at once. Students share their lines and paragraph numbers around the room with no repeats unless a new reason is added, and the teacher retires the famous last line after three picks so students find other load-bearing lines.
weeklyProduct: Each student's written golden-line pick with its paragraph number and one sentence defending why the line can't be cut.

title: Say It Two Ways
description: A performance-based activity converting tone from a matter of taste into an evidence-based argument by having pairs perform a loaded line two plausible ways, then use surrounding text to rule one reading out.
howTo:
Choose lines whose meaning depends heavily on tone and give one line per pair.
Give pairs 3 minutes to rehearse the line in two different, both-plausible tones.
Have pairs perform both versions for another pair (3 minutes).
Have pairs find the surrounding words in the text that rule one version out and argue which reading the text actually supports (4 minutes).
Have students write an exit sentence: 'Our line means ___ because the text around it says "___".'
If students treat tone as pure taste, enforce the surrounding-words rule: a tone claim must cite the words that produce it.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
example: A pair rehearses Josephine's line "you will make yourself ill" from "The Story of an Hour" two ways — once sounding genuinely worried, once sounding controlling — then performs both versions for another pair. They argue that the surrounding words, where Josephine is "imploring for admission" while Louise is "drinking in a very elixir of life," support the controlling reading, and write the exit sentence naming the tone and the words that produced it.
weeklyProduct: Each pair's written exit sentence naming which of two performed tones the text supports, citing the surrounding words that prove it.

title: Two Claims and a Stretch
description: An activity where students write two text-supportable claims and one plausible-but-unsupportable 'stretch,' then a partner must catch and disprove the stretch with specific textual evidence, requiring close reading to write a convincing near-claim.
howTo:
Model one round first: two claims the text can support, plus one plausible-sounding stretch the text cannot carry.
Give students 4 minutes to write two supportable claims and one stretch about the text.
Have students swap papers with a partner, who must catch the stretch and convict it with specific missing support or a contradicting passage (5 minutes).
Share the best stretches on the board and discuss what made them almost supportable (3 minutes).
If stretches are silly and disconnected from the text, enforce the one-inch rule: a stretch must be built from real textual material, only slightly overstated.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
example: A student writes two supportable claims about "The Story of an Hour" — that the story links freedom to the natural world, and that every named character misreads Louise — plus a stretch claiming Louise never loved her husband. A partner catches the stretch and convicts it with paragraph 13's "she had loved him — sometimes," explaining that the stretch erased the story's hardest, most uncomfortable word.
weeklyProduct: Each student's written pair of supportable claims plus one stretch claim, and a partner's written rebuttal citing the missing or contradicting evidence.

title: Gallery of Readings
description: A gallery-walk activity displaying several genuinely different anonymous student readings so students can compare what evidence each reading stands on, transferring ownership of interpretation beyond the original writer.
howTo:
While students draft, circulate and select three or four genuinely different defensible readings; ask permission and post them numbered with names removed.
Give students 3 minutes for a silent gallery read of all the readings.
In pairs, have students discuss what evidence each reading stands on and where two readings use the same line differently (5 minutes).
As a class, discuss which reading would be hardest to defend against a complicating passage and which reading generalizes the furthest (5 minutes).
Have students write an exit sentence naming a reading they didn't write that they now understand, with its best evidence.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Gallery Walk - Classroom Strategy
example: While students draft Reader's Paragraphs on "The Story of an Hour," the teacher posts three anonymous, genuinely different readings — the marriage-indictment reading, the sympathetic-Josephine reading, and the irony-of-medicine reading. Pairs discuss what evidence each reading stands on, noting how two readings can use the same last line, "of joy that kills," differently, and each student writes an exit sentence naming a reading they didn't write but now understand.
weeklyProduct: Each student's written exit sentence naming a classmate's posted reading and its best supporting evidence from the gallery walk.

title: The Editor's Cut
description: An activity framing students as anthology editors who must nominate a paragraph to cut and defend or rescue that decision, teaching structural reading by forcing students to name exactly what a paragraph is doing.
howTo:
Present the premise: an anthology editor demands the story lose one paragraph, and the class must decide which cut does least damage.
Give pairs 5 minutes to nominate the most cuttable paragraph and write a defense of what the story loses and why it survives.
Post nominations on the board; for each, have one pair argue for the cut and another argue for the rescue, naming what the cutters missed (6 minutes).
Discuss the likely finding that nothing cuts cleanly, and name why: in compressed fiction, every paragraph is load-bearing (2 minutes).
Have students write an exit sentence naming the paragraph they'd fight hardest to keep and why.
If students argue for cutting based on boredom, enforce the damage rule: a cut must be argued by what remains, not by what feels slow.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
example: Framed as anthology editors, pairs nominate the most cuttable paragraph of "The Story of an Hour" and defend the cut, and another pair argues to rescue it — for instance, arguing that cutting the weeping paragraph would make Louise look heartless since her grief has to be real for her later freedom to feel complicated. The class usually finds nothing cuts cleanly, naming that in compressed fiction every paragraph is load-bearing, and each student writes which paragraph they'd fight hardest to keep.
weeklyProduct: Each pair's written defense of which paragraph to cut or keep, plus each student's exit sentence naming the paragraph they'd fight hardest to keep.

title: The Critical Introduction
description: A multi-day capstone writing project in which students write the introduction that will be printed for next year's students, requiring a claim, cited evidence with warrants, an honestly presented counter-reading, and leveled discussion questions for a real intended audience.
howTo:
Frame the task: the class is writing the introduction that will be printed with the text for next year's students.
Have students draft an arguable claim about the text and gather two quoted-and-cited pieces of evidence with warrants (period 1).
Have students write the introduction using the template, including one honestly presented counter-reading a smart reader could actually hold, at full strength (period 1–2).
Run a Three-Pass Peer Review and have students revise (period 2).
Read introductions aloud in small groups, and forward one from each group to a real audience — the department's anthology binder or next year's course folder (period 3).
Grade with the chapter rubric: claim must be arguable, evidence quoted and cited, warrant explains why, counter-reading passes the whole-text test.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
example: Framed as writing the introduction that will be printed for next year's students, a class drafts a claim about "The Story of an Hour" — that the most important word in the story is "sometimes" — gathers two quoted, cited pieces of evidence with warrants, and writes an honestly presented counter-reading that the story mourns the marriage rather than indicts it. After a Three-Pass Peer Review and revision, the strongest introductions are forwarded to the department's anthology binder for next year's actual class to read.
weeklyProduct: A multi-day drafted and peer-reviewed introduction with an arguable claim, quoted and cited evidence, warrants, and a written counter-reading.

title: RallyCoach: Data Analysis
description: A paired cooperative structure where one partner analyzes a row, graph segment, or calculation aloud while the other coaches without taking over, making data interpretation visible and building individual analytical skill.
howTo:
Give partners 30 seconds of private, silent look at the data.
Partner A analyzes one row, graph segment, or calculation aloud for 90 seconds while Partner B checks units and asks one reasoning question, coaching but never taking the pencil.
Switch roles for the next data item.
Give students 2 minutes to individually write a pattern statement with values and units.
Enforce the rule: coaches may ask, point, or prompt, but never perform the step for their partner.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Rally Coach: How to use this Collaborative Structure
example: Analyzing the ice-cube melting data table, Partner A reads the row showing the metal block reached 95% melted at minute 4 while Partner B checks the units and asks a reasoning question, coaching without taking the pencil, then the pair switches roles for the foam block's row. Each student finishes by individually writing a pattern statement with values and units, such as noting the metal curve is "fast, then flat at 5 minutes" compared to the foam's slow, steady climb.
weeklyProduct: Each student's individually written pattern statement with specific values and units, built from coached partner data analysis.

title: Numbered Heads Together: Scientific Explanation
description: A team-accountability structure in which every student drafts a claim-evidence-reasoning explanation individually before comparing with teammates, keeping every student responsible for the full explanation since any number can be called to answer.
howTo:
Give students 3 minutes to individually draft a claim, evidence, and reasoning plus an independent test.
Give teams 4 minutes to build the strongest team explanation together.
Give students 1 minute to individually revise their own response.
Call a random number to have that student explain the evidence, mechanism, and competing explanation still needing testing.
Require every claim to include measured values and units before team discussion begins.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Kagan Cooperative Learning - Numbered Heads Together
example: On the ice-melting phenomenon, each student first drafts an individual claim, evidence, and reasoning explanation with measured values and units before the team builds its strongest joint explanation naming conduction as the mechanism. A randomly called number must explain the evidence, the mechanism, and the still-untested competing explanation, such as whether the metal block simply started warmer.
weeklyProduct: Each student's individually drafted and revised claim-evidence-reasoning explanation with measured values and units.

title: RoundTable: Variables, Confounds, and Safety
description: A round-robin planning structure that requires each team member to add a distinct contribution to an investigation design, strengthening the design by forcing distributed, accountable thinking about variables and safety.
howTo:
Give students 1 minute to read the investigation scenario.
Go around the team for six rounds, with each student adding one item (independent variable, dependent variable, control, possible confound, safety consideration, or independent test) and explaining why it matters, 30 seconds per turn.
Give the team 3 minutes to review for missing or contradictory items.
Have each student initial their unique contribution and complete an individual investigation map using the team's strongest ideas.
When students list uncontrollable 'controls,' ask whether the factor can actually be kept constant, measured, or accounted for, and revise.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Kagan. "Round Table Consensus". Cooperative Learning in ...
example: Planning the ice-block investigation, the team goes around six rounds with each student adding one item — the independent variable (block material), the dependent variable (percent melted), a possible confound (uneven starting ice mass), or a safety consideration — and explaining why it matters. When a student lists an uncontrollable factor as a "control," the teacher asks whether it can actually be held constant, measured, or accounted for, prompting a revision.
weeklyProduct: Each student's individual investigation map with an initialed, unique contribution on variables, confounds, or safety.

title: Quiz-Quiz-Trade: Vocabulary in Context
description: A mingling vocabulary-retrieval structure that has students quiz each other with scenario-based questions rather than bare definitions, building the ability to apply scientific terms rather than just recall them.
howTo:
Give each student a card with a scenario question tied to today's investigation.
Partner A asks the scenario question, listens to Partner B's answer, and coaches from the card if needed (45 seconds).
Switch roles, then trade cards and move to a new partner; repeat with three total partners.
Have each student answer orally each time and require they explain why, not just name the term.
Finish with 2 minutes of individual written application: classifying observation/inference, variable type, confound, or independent test for today's investigation.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Teacher Toolkit: Quiz, Quiz, Trade
example: Using scenario cards tied to the ice-cube investigation, Partner A asks "Which variable changed?" or "What confound could explain this result?" rather than a bare definition question, and Partner B must explain why, not just name the term, before the pair trades cards and moves to a new partner. Students finish by individually classifying an observation, inference, variable type, or confound from today's investigation in writing.
weeklyProduct: Each student's short written application classifying observation/inference, variable type, confound, or independent test after mingling oral quizzing.

title: Frayer Model for Scientific Vocabulary
description: A four-cell vocabulary tool (definition, characteristics, examples, non-examples) used to teach the one term a unit's reasoning depends on, deliberately targeting the specific misconception students hold rather than just defining the word.
howTo:
Choose the single term the unit's reasoning turns on (e.g., variable), not every vocabulary word.
Write a student-usable definition and list distinguishing characteristics.
Provide real examples of the term drawn from the current investigation.
Write a non-example that names the specific wrong meaning students actually hold, not merely an unrelated item.
Discuss the non-example explicitly, since that is where the misconception lives and gets corrected.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: A Before Instruction Vocabulary Strategy: Frayer Model
example: The class Frayers the term variable rather than every vocabulary word, since the unit's reasoning depends on it: the definition names the independent variable as the one deliberately changed and the dependent as the one measured, with characteristics noting that controlled variables are held steady on purpose. Real examples come from the ice-block investigation — block material as independent, percent melted as dependent — while the non-example targets the specific misconception that a scientific control means "being in charge" rather than a factor held constant.
weeklyProduct: A completed four-cell chart with a definition, characteristics, real examples, and the specific misconception students hold about the term.

title: The Dissection Protocol (Four-Pass Data Table Read)
description: A repeatable four-pass routine for reading a data table that separates measurement, pattern, inference, and follow-up testing, teaching students to treat data as a text with a story rather than a list of numbers to copy.
howTo:
Pass 1: Read the columns aloud — identify what was measured, in what units, and how often, naming the independent, dependent, and controlled variables precisely.
Pass 2: Find the shape — run a finger along each row to describe its trend in one phrase (e.g., 'fast then flat' vs. 'slow and steady').
Pass 3: Separate observation from inference — mark what the table actually states versus what students are tempted to add as a conclusion.
Pass 4: Ask what would test it — have a student propose a check, such as running it again or identifying another difference between conditions.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Help students Read and Interpret Data Tables in four simple steps
example: On the ice-melting data table, Pass 1 has students read the columns aloud, naming block material as the independent variable and percent melted as the dependent variable measured every minute. Pass 2 has them run a finger along each row to find the shape — metal is fast then flat by minute 5, foam is slow and steady until minute 9 — Pass 3 separates the measured fact that metal reached 100% from the inference that "metal is hotter," and Pass 4 has a student propose running the trial again to test it.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact by default — the visible result is students verbally naming a data table's variables, trend, and a proposed follow-up test.

title: Reading a Graph: Frame, Units, Shape, Landmarks
description: A four-question routine for slowing down graph reading so students interpret a figure's meaning rather than just its plotted values, building the transferable skill of reading any science graph.
howTo:
Ask 'Frame': what is on each axis, and what would a point mean?
Ask 'Units': what is being measured and at what interval?
Ask 'Shape': is the line rising, falling, leveling, or crossing?
Ask 'Landmarks': where does something change — a peak, plateau, or crossing point — and what does that change mean?
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: How to Read Graphs Like a Scientist
example: Reading the ice-melting graph, students first identify the Frame — time on one axis, percent melted on the other — then the Units, minutes and percent, then the Shape, noting the metal curve rises fast while the foam curve climbs slowly. Finally they identify the Landmark: the metal curve's plateau at 5 minutes, which means the ice is entirely gone rather than that melting slowed down.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact by default — the visible result is students verbally answering four framing questions about a graph's axes, units, shape, and landmarks.

title: Mapping the Procedure
description: A technical-reading routine for lab procedures that has students number steps and annotate the purpose of each, turning a recipe into something they can troubleshoot, modify, and defend.
howTo:
Number every step of the procedure.
Circle the measured quantity within each step.
Write the purpose of each step in the margin (e.g., why a variable is being controlled), not just what to do.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
example: Given the ice-block lab procedure, students number every step and circle the measured quantity in each, such as the starting mass of the ice cubes. In the margin next to "cover one block," instead of writing just what to do, they write the purpose — "to rule out room air as the cause" — so the procedure becomes something they can troubleshoot and defend rather than a recipe to follow blindly.
weeklyProduct: A numbered, annotated lab procedure with measured quantities circled and each step's purpose written in the margin.

title: Reading a Diagram: Label, Arrow, and What's Invisible
description: A close-reading routine for science diagrams that teaches students to treat labels as claims and arrows as processes, and to identify the most important element that often isn't drawn.
howTo:
Treat every label on the diagram as a claim, not just a caption.
Treat every arrow as representing a process or mechanism in motion.
Identify what is invisible or missing from the diagram (e.g., an unseen force or flow).
Have students annotate the diagram by adding arrows the textbook left out to make the hidden mechanism visible.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
example: Looking at a diagram of the metal and foam blocks with the ice cubes, students treat the label "conductor" on the metal block as a claim rather than a caption, and note that arrows would represent heat as a process in motion. They identify that the heat itself is invisible and not drawn, then annotate the diagram by adding three arrows — room to block to ice, thick for metal and thin for foam — to make the hidden mechanism visible.
weeklyProduct: An annotated diagram with student-added arrows making a previously hidden mechanism or force visible.

title: Cornell Notes for Investigations
description: An adaptation of Cornell notes for science that dedicates the cue column to investigation questions and the summary strip to a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning statement, packaging the whole method onto one page.
howTo:
In the cue column, record the investigation's guiding questions: what was changed, what was measured, what would test this.
In the notes column, record data and observations, each labeled with units.
Write the summary strip last, after any repeat or check, as a Scientist's Sentence: claim, evidence, reasoning.
Remind students that a conclusion written before the repeat trial is 'a hypothesis wearing a lab coat.'
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: How to take Cornell notes
example: For the ice-cube investigation, the cue column holds questions like "what did we change, what did we measure, what would test this," while the notes column records data such as "metal: 95% melted at minute 4; foam: 27% melted at minute 4," each labeled with units. The summary strip is written last, after a repeat trial, as the Scientist's Sentence: metal conducts heat faster than foam, explaining the melting-rate difference — since a conclusion written before the repeat is "a hypothesis wearing a lab coat."
weeklyProduct: A one-page Cornell notes sheet with guiding questions, unit-labeled data, and a final claim-evidence-reasoning summary sentence.

title: The Five-Mark Annotation System (O, I, V, ?, C)
description: A five-code annotation system for marking any science text or dataset — observation, inference, variable, question, and confound — that trains students to separate what is measured from what is assumed.
howTo:
Mark 'O' next to anything observed or measured.
Mark 'I' next to any inference — a conclusion added to an observation.
Mark 'V' next to any variable that is changed, measured, or held steady.
Mark '?' next to any genuine question the text does not answer, to seed partner discussion.
