Mark 'C' next to any possible confound — a competing explanation not yet ruled out.
Teach one code at a time and require the marks in all subsequent work so the annotation actually gets used.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
example: Reading the ice-block data and procedure, students mark an O beside the measured fact that the metal-block ice was gone at 5 minutes, and an I beside the inference that "the metal was colder," which the thermometer readings actually contradict. They mark a V next to the block material as the changed variable and a C beside the possible confound that the metal block might have started at a different temperature than the foam block, seeding the follow-up check.
weeklyProduct: A marked-up text or dataset showing each student's use of the five codes (observation, inference, variable, question, confound) feeding follow-up discussion.

title: The Science Quickwrite
description: A two-to-three minute ungraded timed writing burst used at key moments in a lesson to surface student thinking as it forms, giving the teacher a fast, honest read on the room's reasoning.
howTo:
Use before the phenomenon: have students commit a prediction and reason in writing.
Use mid-investigation at a moment of surprise: have students write about the contradiction they just observed.
Use after the data talk: have students write the one sentence they would defend tomorrow.
Keep it timed (2-3 minutes), pens moving, and never graded.
Model a ragged, thinking-in-progress example so students see this is exploratory, not polished, writing.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Teaching Technique 10: Quick Write
example: Before the ice-block phenomenon runs, students get two minutes to write which cube they predict will melt first and why, then mid-investigation, at the moment the metal block wins unexpectedly, they write about the contradiction: "this is backwards, metal feels cold so it should keep the ice frozen longer, but it melted first." The teacher never grades these bursts and models a ragged, thinking-in-progress example so students see the writing is exploratory rather than polished.
weeklyProduct: A short, ungraded timed writing burst where each student commits a prediction, reaction, or defendable sentence in their own words.

title: The Scientist's Sentence and Paragraph Frames
description: A set of sentence-level frames that scaffold scientific explanation writing, progressing from single sentences to a full paragraph structure of claim, evidence, reasoning, and independent test.
howTo:
Start with sentence-level frames such as 'I claim ___ because the data show ___' and 'This is caused by ___ rather than ___ because ___.'
Once students use sentence frames fluently, introduce the Scientist's Paragraph frame: claim, then evidence with numbers and units, then reasoning naming the science idea, then the independent test, then a so-what statement.
Post the frame in the room for reference.
Retire the frame later in the year (e.g., by November) once it has become a ramp rather than a permanent crutch.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: How to Scaffold Claim Evidence Reasoning (CER) Writing Claim Evidence Reasoning Step by Step
example: Students start with the sentence frame "I claim ___ because the data show ___" applied to the ice-block phenomenon, then build the full Scientist's Paragraph: a claim that the ice melted faster on metal, evidence that 95% had melted on metal by minute 4 versus 27% on foam, reasoning naming conduction as the mechanism, and an independent test such as a covered repeat trial. The teacher posts the frame early in the unit and plans to retire it by November once students no longer need it.
weeklyProduct: A student paragraph built from the posted frame, containing a claim, numbered/unit evidence, reasoning, and an independent test.

title: Science Lab Notebook
description: A two-column notebook where the left column records what happened — measurements and observations with units and times — and the right column records what the student makes of it, including inferences clearly labeled as such and possible confounds. It builds achievement by turning independent testing and the separation of observation from inference into an ordinary weekly habit rather than a one-off assignment.
howTo:
In the left column, record only what was measured or observed, with units and time points — no interpretation.
In the right column, write at least two sentences of thinking: a question, a clearly labeled inference, or a possible confound — never restating the left column.
Collect the notebook weekly and read it for thinking; never grade it for polish.
Encourage entries to argue with earlier entries across the week, so testing ideas becomes routine.
Write the summary/conclusion strip last, only after a check or repeat — a conclusion written before the repeat is 'a hypothesis wearing a lab coat.'
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Science Notebooking - How I Use My Science Notebook | California Academy of Sciences
example: In the left column of the ice-block lab notebook, a student records only measurements — "Minute 4: metal 95% melted, foam 27% melted, both cubes started at 15 g, room 21°C" — with no interpretation. In the right column, they write at least two sentences of thinking, flagging a possible confound with a C: "were both blocks really the same starting temperature? If the metal started warmer, that would also explain the gap," and propose measuring both block temperatures at minute zero on the next run.
weeklyProduct: A two-column notebook entry with unit-labeled measurements on the left and at least two sentences of labeled inference or confound on the right.

title: Explain to an Audience
description: A Role-Audience-Format-Topic perspective-writing tool that has students translate mathematics for a specific real reader, forcing them to convert symbols into consequences without losing the underlying truth.
howTo:
Assign a Role (e.g., consumer advisor, pricing analyst), an Audience (e.g., a customer who hates algebra, a manager who reads only bullet points), and a Format (e.g., recommendation memo, warning label).
Require the writer to use only mathematics the chosen audience could follow.
Have the student translate the mathematical claim, rule, and check into audience-appropriate language without losing the truth of the result.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: RAFT Writing - The Ultimate Planning Strategy
example: Writing as a science reporter for readers who never took physics, a student explains the ice-block phenomenon: setting an ice cube on a metal tray melts it faster than a foam pad, even though metal feels colder, because that same fast heat transfer pulls warmth from your hand and pulls room heat into the ice. The student is required to use only mechanisms the intended audience could follow without stating anything false to simplify the science.
weeklyProduct: A short memo or note written in an assigned role and audience's language, translating a math claim and check without losing its truth.

title: Notice & Wonder the Phenomenon
description: An entry routine that opens a unit with a stripped-down, unexplained phenomenon so every student can begin with low-risk observation before being asked to explain or defend anything.
howTo:
Show the real phenomenon live or on a short video with no labels, explanation, or vocabulary.
Give students 2 minutes to silently write only what they notice — observations, no explanations.
Give students 2 minutes to write what they wonder.
Harvest both lists verbatim on the board with no judgment (4 minutes).
Have the class choose the wonder worth chasing and post it as the unit's investigation question (2 minutes).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Notice and Wonder | Iowa Science Phenomena
example: The teacher sets two identical ice cubes on a metal block and a foam block at the same moment, with no labels or explanation, and gives students two minutes to silently write only what they notice, such as "the metal one melted faster" or "there's a puddle under the metal one first." After harvesting notices and wonders on the board verbatim, the class chooses the wonder worth chasing — "why does ice melt faster on the metal when metal feels colder?" — and posts it as the unit's investigation question.
weeklyProduct: Each student's separate written lists of what they noticed and what they wonder about an unexplained phenomenon.

title: Prediction Commit
description: A routine where every student writes a reasoned prediction in ink before seeing the result, so the eventual reveal tests an idea the student personally owns rather than delivering a fact from the teacher.
howTo:
Show the phenomenon set up but paused before the outcome, naming the one variable that differs.
Give students 3 minutes to write which outcome they predict and one sentence of reasoning why.
Take a quick poll and tally the reasons given, not just the predictions (2 minutes).
Run the phenomenon or reveal the data.
Have students write: 'I predicted ___ because ___; the data showed ___' (3 minutes).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Commit and Toss - LEARN Strategy
example: Before running the ice-block phenomenon, every student writes in ink which cube they predict will melt first and one reason why, such as "the foam block's ice will last longer because metal always feels colder." After the reveal shows the metal-block ice melting almost twice as fast, students write "I predicted ___ because ___; the data showed ___," confronting their own reasoning with the measured result.
weeklyProduct: Each student's written prediction with one sentence of reasoning, followed by a written comparison sentence against the actual data.

title: Observation / Inference Sort
description: A team card-sort activity using statement strips about a phenomenon that forces students to practice the core scientific distinction between what was directly observed and what was inferred from it.
howTo:
Prepare 10-12 statement strips mixing genuine observations and inferences, including some inferences that sound like facts.
Have teams of three sort every strip into 'observation' or 'inference' (6 minutes).
Have each team defend its two hardest calls to a neighboring team and re-sort if needed (5 minutes).
Discuss as a class which strips split the room and argue those cases (4 minutes).
Correct sorting by truth rather than by source: remind students a true inference is still an inference.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Reading Comprehension Strategy: Inferencing (REL West)
example: Teams sort statement strips about the ice-block phenomenon into observation or inference piles, including tricky ones like "the metal block felt colder to the touch" (a true observation) versus "the metal block was colder" (an inference the thermometer disproves, since both blocks read 21°C). Teams defend their two hardest calls to a neighboring team, and the class argues over strips that split the room, such as whether "the metal is a conductor" counts as an inference from the data.
weeklyProduct: No written individual artifact — the visible result is each team's sorted set of observation/inference statement strips and their defended hardest calls.

title: Data Talk (Numberless Graph)
description: A staged graph-reveal routine that shows axes, then shapes, then values in sequence, training students to read a graph's story and meaning before jumping to specific data points.
howTo:
Reveal only the axes and labels first; have pairs discuss what the graph could be about and what a point would mean (3 minutes).
Add the curves with no numbers and have pairs discuss which is faster and where something changes (5 minutes).
Add the numbers and have pairs write the one sentence the graph is arguing (4 minutes).
Discuss as a class the landmark feature (e.g., a plateau) and what it means (3 minutes).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Developing & nurturing data literacy using slow reveal graphs ...
example: The teacher reveals the ice-melting graph in stages: first just the axes, prompting pairs to guess what the graph could be about, then the two curves with no numbers so students discuss which line is faster and where something changes, then finally the numbers. Students end by writing the one sentence the graph argues and identifying the landmark feature — the metal curve's plateau at 5 minutes, meaning the ice is entirely gone rather than that melting slowed down.
weeklyProduct: Each pair's written one-sentence claim about what the graph argues, built up in stages from axes to shapes to numbers.

title: My Favorite Wrong Prediction
description: An anonymous error-analysis routine, adapted from 'My Favorite No,' that publicly celebrates the reasoning in an incorrect prediction before repairing the misconception, changing the room's relationship with being wrong.
howTo:
Collect anonymous prediction cards and select the incorrect prediction with the strongest scientific reasoning.
Rewrite the chosen prediction on the board, protecting the author's identity (1 minute).
Ask the class what the scientist got right in their reasoning and collect several answers (3 minutes).
Ask the class to find the precise point where the reasoning goes wrong and name the misconception (3 minutes).
Work together to repair the prediction into a correct mechanism (3 minutes).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: My Favorite No: Turning Student Mistakes into Powerful Learning
example: After collecting anonymous prediction cards from the ice-block Prediction Commit activity, the teacher selects the wrong prediction with the strongest reasoning, such as one claiming the foam ice would last longer because "metal is colder so it keeps ice frozen." The class first names what the student's reasoning got right, then finds precisely where it goes wrong (the block isn't actually colder — both measured 21°C) and works together to repair the prediction into a correct conduction-based explanation.
weeklyProduct: No individual written artifact — the visible result is a class-repaired prediction on the board with the misconception verbally named and corrected.

title: Four Corners (Science)
description: A physical-movement discussion structure where students stake a position on an arguable claim using evidence, with a private pre-write that protects thinking from social pressure before students move.
howTo:
Post four corner signs: AGREE, DISAGREE, IT DEPENDS, NEED MORE DATA, tied to an arguable claim.
Give students 2 minutes to silently write their corner choice and one piece of evidence before moving.
Have students move to their corner, then merge evidence in pairs to choose their strongest data point (4 minutes).
Have each corner report one speaker, one piece of evidence, and one reason (5 minutes).
Allow students to switch corners only if they can name the evidence that moved them, then close with an exit line: 'I stand at ___ because the data show ___.'
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Discourse Strategies for Inquiry Science: Four Corners
videoChannel: DIT Labs - Fairfax County Public Schools
example: Posting the claim "The metal block was colder than the foam block" for the ice-melting investigation, students privately write their corner choice and one piece of evidence before moving to AGREE, DISAGREE, IT DEPENDS, or NEED MORE DATA. In corners, students merge evidence and report one speaker, one piece of evidence, and one reason, with the strongest disagreeing groups citing the equal 21°C starting temperatures to show the claim confuses "felt colder" with "was colder."
weeklyProduct: Each student's private pre-write of their position plus a final exit line stating their stance and the data point that supports it.

title: Whiteboard Modeling
description: A vertical-surface, random-grouping activity (drawing on Liljedahl's thinking classrooms) where teams draw the invisible mechanism behind a phenomenon with one shared marker, making causal reasoning visible and public.
howTo:
Form random teams of three at vertical whiteboards or large paper, with only one marker per team.
Have teams draw a model of the mechanism — not a picture of the event — using arrows to show what moves and why (10 minutes).
Circulate and advance teams with questions rather than answers (e.g., 'Where does the heat come from? Draw that arrow.').
Run a gallery freeze where teams tour two neighboring boards and leave one written question each (5 minutes).
Have teams revise their model based on the best question they received (5 minutes).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Increasing Participation With Individual Whiteboards
example: Random teams of three at vertical whiteboards draw a model explaining the ice-block phenomenon rather than a picture of it, using one shared marker to show arrows for the invisible heat moving from the room into each block and into the ice. The teacher circulates asking "where does the heat come from — draw that arrow," and after a gallery-walk exchange of written questions between teams, each group revises its model, aiming for a thick arrow labeled conduction on the metal block and a thin one on the insulating foam block.
weeklyProduct: A team whiteboard drawing of the causal mechanism with labeled arrows, revised after receiving one written question from a neighboring team.

title: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning Gallery
description: A gallery-walk activity using anonymized, teacher-selected student conclusions of varying strengths, teaching students to diagnose specific weaknesses in claim, evidence, and reasoning rather than simply rank quality.
howTo:
While students draft, select 3-4 genuinely different anonymized conclusions (e.g., strong evidence/weak reasoning, strong reasoning/thin evidence, one with an unaddressed confound) and post them with permission.
Have students silently read all posted conclusions (3 minutes).
In pairs with the rubric, have students identify the strongest and weakest slot (claim, evidence, reasoning, test) in each (5 minutes).
Discuss as a class which conclusion would survive a skeptic's challenge (5 minutes).
Close with an exit sentence naming which conclusion taught them the most and why.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: How to Scaffold Claim Evidence Reasoning (CER) Writing ...
example: Using the running ice-cube phenomenon (identical cubes melting faster on a metal block than a foam one), the teacher circulates while students draft their Scientist's Paragraph and selects four anonymized conclusions: one with strong data but weak reasoning, one with strong reasoning but thin data, one complete response, and one with an unaddressed confound. Students do a silent gallery read, then in pairs use the rubric to diagnose which slot (claim, evidence, reasoning, test) is strongest and weakest in each posted conclusion. The class discusses which conclusion would survive a skeptic asking whether the metal block simply started warmer, then each student names in an exit sentence which conclusion taught them the most and why.
weeklyProduct: An exit sentence from each student naming which posted conclusion taught them the most and citing why.

title: Two Claims and a Confound
description: A writing-and-swap activity where students generate supportable claims plus a plausible confound about the data, then trade papers so a partner must identify the confound and design a test to rule it out.
howTo:
Model one round: write two claims the data can support and one plausible (not silly) confound.
Have each student write two supportable claims and one confound about the phenomenon (4 minutes).
Have students swap papers with a partner, who must identify the confound and name a test that would rule it out (5 minutes).
Share the best confounds with the class, discussing what makes each plausible and what single design change would eliminate it (3 minutes).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Module 4, Chapter 2: Defining Confounding Factors
example: After collecting data on the metal-block-versus-foam-block ice-melting phenomenon, the teacher models one round first: two claims the data can support plus one plausible confound, such as the metal block having started at a warmer temperature. Each student then writes two supportable claims and one confound of their own about the phenomenon, swaps papers with a partner, and the partner must identify the confound and name a test that would rule it out, such as measuring both blocks' temperatures at minute zero. The class shares its best confounds, discussing what makes each genuinely plausible and what single design change would eliminate it.
weeklyProduct: Each student's written claims citing the data, plus a partner's written identification of the confound and a test to rule it out.

title: Design an Investigation
description: A multi-day capstone task where student pairs design their own controlled investigation from a testable question, applying the full claim-evidence-reasoning-test cycle to content of their own choosing.
howTo:
Have pairs choose a testable question and identify the one variable to change while holding all other relevant conditions constant.
Have pairs build a numbered procedure, each step naming its purpose, with the measurement and interval specified.
Run the investigation (or run it as a designed proposal with predicted data) including a built-in repeat.
Have another pair peer-review the design, hunting for confounds or uncontrolled variables and signing off or flagging issues.
Present the strongest designs to the class or run them live for an authentic audience.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Inquiry-Based Learning in the Science Classroom
example: As a capstone, pairs choose a testable question extending the ice-melting phenomenon, such as whether a block's surface color changes how fast ice melts under a heat lamp, and identify the one variable to change (color) while holding block material, mass, size, and distance from the lamp constant. They build a numbered procedure specifying the measurement and interval, run the investigation with a built-in repeat of three trials, and a second pair peer-reviews the design hunting for confounds like an uncontrolled distance from the heat source. The strongest designs, such as one predicting the black block melts ice faster because darker surfaces absorb more radiant heat, are then presented to the class or actually run.
weeklyProduct: A written, peer-reviewed investigation procedure with predicted data, citing measured evidence and flagged confounds from the review pair.

title: Costa's Three Levels of Questioning (Science)
description: A three-tier questioning framework — gather, process, apply — that teachers use to move discussion beyond simple data recall into reasoning and transfer, ensuring a class visits all three levels rather than staying at Level 1.
howTo:
Ask Level 1 (Gather) questions answerable by looking at the data or text directly.
Ask Level 2 (Process) questions that require reasoning with the concept to explain why something works the way it does.
Ask Level 3 (Apply) questions asking where the idea matters beyond this case or how a related claim could be tested.
Write at least one question of each level before the lesson and open with a Level 2 or 3 question rather than Level 1.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Costa's Levels of Questioning
example: Using the ice-melting phenomenon, the teacher opens with a Level 2 question rather than Level 1: 'Why does the ice on the metal block melt faster even though the metal feels colder to the touch?' A Level 1 gather question follows, asking students to read the percent-melted values directly off the data table at four minutes. Then a Level 3 apply question pushes transfer: 'Where else does this same heat-transfer property matter — for example, why is a cooler made of foam instead of metal?' The teacher writes at least one question at each level before the lesson so the class visits reasoning and transfer, not just recall.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact — the visible result is verbal student answers to at least one Level 2 or Level 3 reasoning-and-transfer question opening the lesson.

title: Exit Ticket with Data (Daily CER Scan)
description: A three-minute daily exit ticket requiring a claim, one measurement with units, and one sentence of reasoning, quickly sorted into three piles so the teacher knows exactly what to teach next without full grading.
howTo:
At the close of every investigation day, ask: 'What causes this, and what data makes you say so?' requiring a claim, one measurement with units, and one sentence of reasoning.
Do not grade the ticket that night; instead scan only the data line.
Sort papers into three piles in about 15 seconds each: no data is 'Not Yet,' data without a named mechanism is 'Almost,' data plus a named mechanism is 'CER Ready.'
Open the next lesson by naming the most common gap found in the scan.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Exit Tickets: Checking for Understanding
example: At the close of an investigation day on the metal-versus-foam block phenomenon, the teacher asks: 'What causes this, and what data makes you say so? Claim, one measurement with units, and one sentence of reasoning.' That night the teacher doesn't grade the tickets but scans only the data line, sorting them in about fifteen seconds each into three piles: no data is 'Not Yet,' data without a named mechanism like conduction is 'Almost,' and data plus a named mechanism is 'CER Ready.' The next lesson opens by naming the most common gap found in the scan, such as students citing the 95%-versus-27% melt data but never naming conduction as the mechanism.
weeklyProduct: A stack of exit tickets, each with a written claim, one cited measurement with units, and one sentence of reasoning, sorted into three gap piles.

title: RallyCoach: Solve and Justify
description: A cooperative structure in which partners alternate solving one step at a time while the non-writing partner coaches and demands justification, keeping every mathematical step and its rule visible.
howTo:
Give partners 30 seconds to individually plan an approach.
Partner A completes one step and names the rule; Partner B checks the step, asks for justification, and coaches without taking the pencil.
Alternate roles after each step.
Finish with 2 minutes of independent written justification and check, using the Statement–Rule Applied–Independent Check format.
Provide a rule bank, a worked first example, and manipulatives/calculators as access support; if the stronger student takes over, enforce 'one step, one reason, switch' and require the coach to question rather than write.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Kagan Rally-Coach in Math- Nov 2017
example: Working a multi-step equation like the phone-plan break-even problem (30 + 20m = 10 + 22m), Partner A completes the first step — subtracting 20m from both sides — and names the rule being applied, while Partner B checks the step, asks Partner A to justify why that operation is valid, and coaches without touching the pencil. The partners alternate after each step until they reach m = 10, then each writes an independent Statement–Rule Applied–Check response. A rule bank and a worked first example are provided as access support, and if one partner starts dominating, the teacher enforces 'one step, one reason, switch.'
weeklyProduct: A written justification using Statement–Rule Applied–Independent Check for one problem, citing the mathematical rule applied at each step.

title: Numbered Heads Together: Multiple Solution Paths
description: A cooperative structure where teams compare different solution methods and any numbered member may be called to defend the team's chosen method, holding every student accountable for understanding, not just copying.
howTo:
Students solve independently for 3 minutes.
Teams compare methods for 5 minutes, choose one to present, name the rule behind it, and prepare a different check.
Students individually summarize the method for 2 minutes, recording their original method, the team-selected method, and an independent check or second representation.
Call a random number to present; that student must explain one decision point and one likely error to prevent copying without understanding.
Offer multiple representations, partially completed diagrams, and a vocabulary bank as access support.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Numbered Heads Learning Strategy (Unlocking Curiosity ...)
example: Given a system like the two-phone-plan break-even problem, each student solves independently for three minutes, arriving at an equation, a table, or a graph. Teams then compare their different methods for five minutes, choose one to present, name the rule behind it, and prepare a different check, such as verifying algebraically and then confirming graphically. Each student individually summarizes the method, recording their own original approach, the team-selected method, and an independent check, and the teacher calls a random team member to explain one decision point and one likely error so no one can coast on a teammate's work.
weeklyProduct: A written individual summary recording the student's own method, the team's chosen method, and an independent check or second representation.

title: RoundTable: Representations
description: A rotating cooperative structure that has students connect equations, tables, graphs, diagrams, and words as different representations of the same mathematical relationship, deepening flexible understanding.
howTo:
Give the team 1 minute to interpret the prompt.
Each student adds one new, non-repeated representation in 60-second rounds across five rounds, explaining the connection before passing.
Spend 3 minutes as a team comparing which representation reveals what.
Require a shared value, label, point, or equation that proves the representations match, to prevent disconnected representations.
Have each student write an individual comparison explaining what two representations make visible, using graph paper, manipulatives, digital graphing tools, or templates as needed.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: The Power of Student Engagement: Simultaneous Round Table
example: Starting from the two-phone-plan relationship, the team passes one sheet around and each member must add a new representation — an equation, a table, a graph, or a written statement — connecting it to the relationship without repeating a representation already on the page. Each student explains the connection before passing, such as showing that the table's row where costs match is the same point as the graph's intersection. After five rounds, the team spends three minutes comparing which representation reveals what, and each student writes an individual comparison explaining what two of the representations make visible that the others don't.
weeklyProduct: A written individual comparison explaining what two mathematical representations reveal, backed by a shared value proving they match.

title: Timed PairShare: Mathematical Defense
description: A timed partner-talk structure that has students rehearse a complete mathematical explanation, using a Statement–Rule–Check script, before sharing with the whole group or writing it up.
howTo:
Give students 45 seconds of private preparation.
Partner A speaks for 60 seconds using the frame: 'My statement is ___. The rule I applied was ___. I know the conclusion is reasonable because ___.'
Partner B asks one question about the rule or check for 30 seconds, then switch roles.
Each student writes a complete defense individually after speaking; the listener records the question asked.
Require a rule, property, definition, theorem, or relationship in every response to prevent students from narrating procedures without justifying them.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Instant Engagement Demo: Timed Pair Share
example: After solving the phone-plan break-even problem, Partner A gets 45 seconds to prepare, then delivers: 'My statement is Plan B is cheaper under ten months. The rule I applied was setting the two cost equations equal. I know the conclusion is reasonable because I checked it at five months and got $130 versus $120.' Partner B asks one question about the rule or the check, such as whether testing a value past ten months would strengthen the argument, and then the partners switch roles on a related claim. Each student finishes with two minutes of independent written revision incorporating the question they were asked.
weeklyProduct: A written individual defense citing a rule, property, definition, or theorem, plus a listener's recorded follow-up question.

title: Frayer Model for Math Vocabulary
description: A four-quadrant vocabulary tool (definition, characteristics, examples, non-examples) used to pre-teach the one or two words a problem depends on, with the non-examples deliberately targeting the specific misconception students hold.
howTo:
Choose only the term the day's problem turns on (e.g., 'rate'), not every vocabulary word.
Write a student-usable definition and list distinguishing characteristics.
Provide real examples from the current unit.
Write a non-example that names the specific wrong meaning students actually hold, not just an unrelated wrong answer.
Reinforce with morphology (word families) and repeated use across the week.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Helping Youth Learn Math Vocabulary: The Frayer Model
example: Before tackling the two-phone-plan word problem, the teacher Frayers the term 'rate' so students can actually read the problem: definition (a quantity measured per unit of another), characteristics (compares two quantities in different units; in a linear relationship it's the graph's slope, not its starting point), examples ($20 a month, 60 miles per hour, 3 eggs per batch), and — the part most teachers skip — non-examples, naming the $30 start-up fee as a one-time amount rather than a rate and a computed total like $230 as a result rather than a rate. That non-example is exactly the confusion that sinks the phone-plan problem if left unaddressed.
weeklyProduct: A completed four-quadrant vocabulary chart with a definition, characteristics, real examples, and a targeted non-example for one key term.

title: Reading a Graph as a Text
description: A four-step protocol (frame, units/scale, shape, landmarks) that teaches students to read a graph systematically instead of jumping straight to its numbers, building genuine graphical literacy.
howTo:
Frame: identify what is on each axis, saying it aloud in words before anything else.
Units & scale: determine what one gridline equals and whether the graph starts at zero.
Shape: describe the overall story at arm's length (rising, falling, straight, bending, crossing) with no numbers yet.
Landmarks: name the points that matter — intercepts, intersections, peaks — in words before translating them into sentences or computation.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Teaching Graphing & Data in First Grade, Literacy Curriculum ...
example: Given the graph of two crossing phone-plan cost lines, students work through four questions in order rather than jumping to numbers: Frame ('months across, dollars up'), Units & Scale (what one gridline equals, and whether the axis starts at zero), Shape (one line starts higher but climbs more slowly, so they must cross), and Landmarks (the exact intersection point, named in words as 'they cross at ten months' before any values are pulled from it). Only after narrating the shape and landmarks aloud do students move to pulling specific data points, which prevents the common error of reading isolated values with no sense of the overall story the graph is telling.
weeklyProduct: No written artifact by default — students verbally name a graph's frame, scale, shape, and landmarks before computing, answering guiding questions.

title: The Annotation System (K, H, R, Q, E)
description: A five-code margin-annotation system for word problems — Known, Hidden quantity, Relationship word, Question, and Estimate/forecast — that makes a student's problem-reading process visible and catches errors before solving.
howTo:
Mark K on every known quantity, circled with its units.
Mark H on the hidden quantity, naming and lettering it in the margin as the variable.
Mark R on each relationship word (per, plus, to start, at least) that feeds the equation.
Mark Q by bracketing the actual question to prevent answering the wrong one.
Mark E by writing a forecast of what a reasonable answer looks like before solving, then check the computed answer against it.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Mathematics Annotation Strategy
example: On the phone-plan word problem, students apply the five codes as they read: circling the K (known quantities like the $30 start-up fee and $20 monthly rate, with their units), naming the H (the hidden quantity — months, the variable no one stated), underlining the R (relationship words like 'per' and 'to start'), bracketing the Q (the actual question: which plan is better, not just where they're equal), and writing an E (a forecast of what a reasonable answer looks like before solving). A computed answer that violates its own E-mark — for instance landing on a negative number of months — sends the student back to check their work before the teacher ever sees it.
weeklyProduct: A word problem with each student's own written margin codes (K, H, R, Q, E) marking knowns, the hidden variable, relationships, and an estimate.

title: Cornell Notes for Math Problems
description: An adaptation of Cornell notes for mathematics where the cue column holds reading questions, the notes column holds worked steps with their reasons, and a bottom summary strip captures the final Statement–Rule Applied–Check justification.
howTo:
In the cue column, record reading questions: what is hidden, what rule applies, what the check will be.
In the notes column, record the worked steps along with their 'becauses.'
Write the summary strip at the bottom last, after the check is complete, using Statement, Rule Applied, Check in full sentences.
Keep the whole routine to one page so the method travels home in a binder.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: How to Take and Use Cornell Notes in Math
example: Working through the phone-plan problem, students keep the cue column for the reading questions (what's hidden, what rule applies, what the check will be), the notes column for the actual work with its 'because' reasoning, and write the summary strip last, after the check: 'Plan B is the better deal for anyone keeping the phone under ten months, because its $20 head start shrinks by $2 a month and runs out at m = 10, tested on both sides of the break-even.' Writing the summary strip only after the check, rather than before it, keeps a guess from being dressed up as a conclusion.
weeklyProduct: A one-page handwritten Cornell-notes sheet with cue-column questions, worked steps with their 'becauses,' and a bottom Statement–Rule–Check summary.

title: The Math Response Journal
description: A running two-column notebook where students record a line of mathematics on the left and their reaction, question, or connection on the right, building the habit of ongoing mathematical reflection.
howTo:
Have students write a line of mathematics (an equation, a graph reading, a computed value) in the left column.
In the right column, students write at least two sentences reacting, questioning, or connecting to earlier problems, with no restating of the left column allowed.
Collect weekly and read for thinking, never grading for polish.
Encourage entries to reference and interrogate earlier entries so the habit compounds over time.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: How To Use A Math Journal in your Classroom
example: On the phone-plan problem, a student's left column reads '30 + 20m = 10 + 22m → m = 10,' the raw line of mathematics. The right column adds at least two sentences of thinking without restating: 'Solving felt like the end, but the 10 is really a border. This is the same thing that happened on the gym-membership problem — the crossing point wasn't the answer there either, it split the answer into two cases. Question for tomorrow: does every pair of plans have to cross?' Collected weekly and read for thinking rather than graded for polish, the journal lets Tuesday's right column keep interrogating Thursday's left column.
weeklyProduct: A two-column journal entry with a line of math on the left and at least two written sentences of reaction or connection on the right.

title: Mathematical Proof & Justification (Statement–Rule Applied–Check)
description: A three-part justification frame — Statement, Rule Applied, Check — that requires students to state a claim, justify it with a mathematical rule and reason, and verify it a second, genuinely different way, making reasoning visible and testable rather than just an answer.
howTo:
Statement: write the claim in a full sentence that answers the actual question asked, not a bare value like 'x = 4.'
Rule Applied: state the mathematics that backs the claim, using the word 'because' to turn steps into reasoning.
Check: verify the claim a second way — with a different value, representation, method, counterexample, or piece of evidence; a check that just restates the answer does not count.
For claims that cover an interval or general rule, pair a single-value check with the Rule that explains why the conclusion holds throughout, since one example alone cannot prove a general claim.
Post the frame and require it consistently across exit tickets, journals, and formal write-ups until students can produce it independently.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Teaching Math with ADI | What is Justification in Math?
example: For the phone-plan problem, a student writes: Statement — 'Plan B is the better deal for a customer who keeps the phone fewer than ten months.' Rule Applied — 'I set 30 + 20m equal to 10 + 22m, because the better deal changes exactly where the two costs are equal, giving m = 10.' Check — 'At five months, Plan A costs $130 and Plan B costs $120, consistent with Plan B being cheaper before the break-even.' For maximum rigor, the student also shows the cost difference 20 − 2m is positive for any m under 10, proving the claim for every month in that range rather than just the one tested value.
weeklyProduct: A written Statement–Rule Applied–Check justification citing the specific mathematical rule that backs the claim and a second, independent check.

title: Notice & Wonder
description: An entry routine where students observe a stripped-down graph, table, or image and generate their own notices and wonders, letting the class author the day's mathematical question and lowering the risk of entering the discussion.
howTo:
Project a mathematical object (graph, table, or photo) with every question and label beyond axes stripped away.
Give students 1 minute of silent writing for notices (observations only), then 1 minute for wonders (questions the object raises).
Harvest every offer onto the board verbatim without judgment, notices then wonders (4 minutes).
Let the class pick the wonder worth chasing, steering only if the target doesn't surface (2 minutes).
Post the chosen wonder as the lesson's purpose question for the rest of the period; park any wonder the teacher is tempted to answer immediately instead of answering it on the spot.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Spark curiosity with a “Notice and Wonder” math routine
example: The teacher projects the stripped two-line phone-plan graph with no labels beyond the axes and no explanation. Students spend one minute writing only what they notice ("two lines," "they cross," "one starts higher") and one minute writing what they wonder ("why would anyone pick the plan that starts higher?" "where exactly do they cross?"), and every offer is harvested onto the board verbatim with no judgment. The class then picks the wonder worth chasing — usually something like "which plan is cheaper, and does it depend on how long you keep it?" — and that question, in the students' own words, becomes the posted purpose for the lesson.
weeklyProduct: A board full of student-written notices and wonders about a stripped-down graph, plus one chosen wonder posted as the day's purpose question.

title: Numberless Word Problem
description: A staged-reveal activity that strips all numbers from a word problem so students must reason about structure and identify the hidden quantity before any calculation is possible, resetting who counts as 'good at math.'
howTo:
Rewrite the day's word problem with every number removed, leaving only the structure.
Post the numberless version and have pairs discuss the situation, what matters, and what's hidden (4 minutes).
Harvest as a class: have students name the quantity that will decide the problem before any number exists (3 minutes).
Reveal the numbers and have pairs predict what kind of answer is coming (3 minutes).
Reveal the question last, compare it to predictions, then dissect and solve with the structure already understood (5 minutes).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Intro to Numberless Word Problems
example: The teacher strips all numbers from the phone-plan problem, posting only: 'A phone company offers two plans. One costs more to start but less each month. The other costs less to start but more each month.' Pairs discuss what matters and what's hidden before any calculation is possible, and the class names the hidden quantity — how long you keep the phone — before a single number exists. Only after that structural conversation does the teacher reveal the dollar amounts, then finally the question itself, and pairs compare their predicted answer shape ('a plan and a condition') against what they actually find.
weeklyProduct: No fixed written artifact — the visible result is students verbally naming the hidden quantity and predicting the answer type before any numbers appear.

title: Estimation Lineup
description: An estimation activity where students commit to a reasoned estimate, physically place themselves along a number line by value, defend the extremes, and reflect on their error, turning estimation into a structured error-analysis exercise.
howTo:
Pose one question with a defensible estimate and have every student write an estimate plus one sentence of reasoning (3 minutes).
Have students place themselves or sticky notes along a wall number line representing their estimate (2 minutes).
Interview the lowest and highest estimates to defend their reasoning while the middle asks each a question (4 minutes).
Solve or reveal the actual answer.
Have every student write an 'I was off by ___ because I didn't account for ___' reflection (3 minutes).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Estimating Numbers on a Number Line
example: The teacher poses: 'At six months, how far apart are the two phone plans' totals?' and every student commits a written estimate with one sentence of reasoning — no blank guesses allowed — before placing a sticky note along a number line taped to the wall. The lowest and highest estimates defend their reasoning aloud while the middle of the line asks each one a question, and after the real value is revealed, every student writes a sentence like 'I was off by $2 because I didn't account for the lead shrinking every month.' The off-by sentence turns an estimation game into a quick piece of error analysis.
weeklyProduct: Each student's written estimate with reasoning, followed by a written 'I was off by ___ because ___' error-analysis reflection.

title: My Favorite No
description: A routine using anonymous index-card responses where the teacher selects the wrong answer with the most right thinking in it, has the class identify what the student did correctly before analyzing the error, changing the classroom's relationship with mistakes.
howTo:
Have every student solve a short problem on an anonymous index card (3 minutes).
Sort cards into yes/no piles and select the 'favorite no' — the wrong answer containing the most correct thinking (1 minute).
Rewrite the selected response on the board, protecting the author's identity, and ask the class what the student got right, collecting several answers (3 minutes).
Ask the class to find the exact step where the reasoning breaks and name the fix (3 minutes).
Never skip the 'what's right' round, since it is the culture-building move that makes error analysis safe.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: My Favorite No: Turning Student Mistakes into Powerful ...
example: Students solve a short phone-plan-style problem anonymously on index cards, and the teacher sorts them fast into right and wrong piles, picking the 'favorite no' — the wrong answer containing the most correct thinking, such as one that sets up the equation 30 + 20m = 10 + 22m perfectly but then stops at m = 10 and answers 'ten months' instead of naming which plan is better. The teacher rewrites it on the board anonymously and first asks the class what the student got right (a clean, correctly set-up equation), then asks where exactly the reasoning breaks down. The class repairs the error together, naming precisely that ten is the dividing line, not the answer itself.
weeklyProduct: An anonymous index card with one worked solution, publicly analyzed for what was done right and where the exact reasoning error occurred.

title: Which One Doesn't Belong
description: A low-risk classification activity using a 2x2 grid of related items where every item can be defended as the outlier, shifting the challenge from choosing correctly to defending precisely with mathematical vocabulary.
howTo:
Present four related items (equations, graphs, or numbers) arranged so each one could defensibly be the outlier for a different reason.
Give students 1 minute of silent time to pick an outlier and write a reason.
Have students group by their choice and defend it using precise vocabulary such as slope, intercept, or constant (5 minutes).
Reveal that all choices are valid and shift the discussion to what distinguishes a strong defense; rank two defenses as a class (3 minutes).
Require at least one Tier 3 vocabulary word in any defense to count, preventing surface-level justifications.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Strengthen math thinking with a “Which One Doesn't Belong” routine
example: The teacher posts a 2x2 grid of four related linear equations — y = 20m + 30, y = 22m + 10, y = 20m − 5, y = 30 — built so every item can be defended as the outlier for a different reason. Students silently pick their outlier and write a reason, then defend their choice in corners using vocabulary like slope, intercept, and rate; the teacher reveals that every choice is defensible and pushes the class to rank two defenses by precision, since 'it looks different' scores lower than 'it's the only one with no rate term, so its graph is flat.' Students then upgrade their own written defense once, replacing a surface observation with a defense grounded in slope, intercept, and consequence.
weeklyProduct: A written one-sentence justification for an outlier choice, required to use precise math vocabulary like slope or intercept.

title: Convince a Skeptic
description: A paired role-play activity where a scripted Skeptic relentlessly challenges a Prover's mathematical claim, forcing the Prover to strengthen their justification until it survives cross-examination.
howTo:
Pair students as a Prover, who argues the day's claim, and a Skeptic, who uses a script card ('How do you know? Does that always work? Show me a case where it breaks. Convince me with a different method.').
Have the Prover argue the claim while the Skeptic runs the script for 4 minutes.
Swap roles on a related claim for another 4 minutes.
Require the skeptic to use at least two script lines before conceding, to prevent folding early.
Have pairs write the strongest version of the argument that survived, including the check that finally convinced the skeptic (4 minutes).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Building Argumentation Skills in Math
example: In pairs, one student is the Prover arguing a claim like 'Plan B is better for short-term customers' using the phone-plan data, while the other is the Skeptic working from a script card: 'How do you know? Does that always work? Show me a case where it breaks.' The Skeptic must run at least two script lines before conceding, pushing the Prover to test additional values on both sides of the ten-month break-even rather than stopping at one convincing example. Afterward, pairs write the strongest surviving version of the argument, including the specific check that finally convinced the skeptic, such as verifying the claim held at both four months and twelve months.
weeklyProduct: A written record of the strongest version of a mathematical argument, including the specific check that finally convinced a scripted skeptic.

title: Whiteboard Relay
description: A vertical, randomly-grouped team activity with one shared marker that rotates on the teacher's signal, forcing every student to explain reasoning aloud since only one person may write at a time, described as one of the most engagement-dense structures in the playbook.
howTo:
Form random teams of three at vertical whiteboards or large paper with one marker per team.
Give teams a problem sequence from easiest to hardest; only the marker-holder writes, rotating the marker every two minutes on the teacher's signal (10 minutes).
Circulate and advance stuck teams with questions ('What's hidden here?'), never answers.
Give teams that finish early an extension rather than the answer key (5 minutes).
Freeze work and have teams tour two neighboring boards, leaving one written question each about a gap in reasoning (5 minutes).
Rotate the marker on the teacher's clock, not the team's, and make clear that marker-holders may transcribe but not decide, to prevent one student from dominating.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: 60-Second Strategy: Whiteboard Relay
example: Random teams of three stand at vertical whiteboards with one marker each, working through a sequence of problems building toward the two-phone-plan break-even question, easiest to hardest. Only the marker-holder writes, and the teacher rotates who holds the marker every two minutes on a signal, forcing the team to talk through the hidden quantity and the equation-setup aloud rather than let one student silently compute. Teams that finish early tour two neighboring boards, leaving one written question each, such as asking where a missing subtraction step came from, and then revise their own board against the best question they received.
weeklyProduct: A team whiteboard showing a full problem sequence worked step by step, plus one written peer question flagging a gap in another team's reasoning.

title: Gallery of Methods
description: An activity where the teacher selects and sequences several genuinely different correct student solution methods for the class to compare, helping students find the same underlying mathematics across different representations.
howTo:
While students solve, circulate and select three or four genuinely different correct or instructive methods (graph, table, equation, estimate-and-adjust), sequencing them from concrete to abstract; ask student permission before posting.
Have students do a silent gallery read of all posted methods (3 minutes).
In pairs, have students identify what is the same underneath the differences and find one method hiding inside another (5 minutes).
Facilitate a class discussion on which method would break first with uglier numbers and which generalizes (5 minutes).
Close with an exit prompt: 'The method I didn't use that I now understand is ___, and it works because ___' (2 minutes).
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: A Gallery Walk to Inspire Student Collaboration (Early Math Collaborative)
example: While students solve the phone-plan break-even problem, the teacher selects three or four genuinely different correct methods — a graph, a table, an equation, and an estimate-and-adjust approach — sequencing them from concrete to abstract and posting them numbered. Pairs do a silent gallery read, then discuss what's the same underneath the different-looking methods, hunting for the table hiding inside the graph and the equation hiding inside the table. Each student closes with an exit sentence like 'the method I didn't use that I now understand is the table, because each row is just the equation evaluated at one month, and the break-even is where the columns swap order.'
weeklyProduct: A written exit prompt naming a method the student didn't originally use and explaining why it works, after comparing several posted solution methods.

title: Two Truths and a Lie
description: A graph- or data-reading activity where students write two true statements and one plausible lie about a display, and partners must catch the lie by proving it wrong with a mathematical check.
howTo:
Project the day's graph or data display and model one round with two truths and one plausible lie.
Have each student write two truths and one lie about the display, requiring the lie to be plausible rather than silly (4 minutes).
Have students swap with a partner, who must identify the lie and prove it with a check — a tested value, a read point, or a computed slope (5 minutes).
Share the best (most subtle) lies with the class and discuss what made them almost true (3 minutes).
Enforce the 'one-inch rule': lies must be about quantities or relationships from the graph, not silly or unrelated claims.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Two Truths and a Lie - Classroom Strategy
example: Projecting the two-phone-plan cost graph, the teacher models one round of two true statements and one plausible lie, such as 'the plans cost the same at nine months' (a lie that lives close to the truth since they actually tie at ten). Each student writes their own two truths and one plausible lie about the display, swaps with a partner, and the partner must catch the lie by proving it wrong with an actual check — computing that at nine months Plan A costs $210 and Plan B costs $208, close but not equal. The class shares its best near-truths, discussing what made each one almost believable.
weeklyProduct: Two written true statements and one lie citing values from a graph, plus a partner's written proof identifying and disproving the lie.

title: Design a Plan
description: A multi-day capstone project where student pairs author two competing, realistic pricing plans, build the full mathematical model, and defend recommendations to peer reviewers who stress-test their break-even claim.
howTo:
Have pairs invent two competing pricing plans for something students actually buy, requiring each plan to be the right choice for somebody (no strawman plans) (period 1).
Have pairs build the mathematics: two cost equations, a labeled graph, and the break-even point verified both algebraically and graphically (periods 1–2).
Have pairs write three customer recommendations (a light user, a heavy user, and a customer at exactly the break-even), each as a Statement–Rule–Check paragraph (period 2).
Run a market test where pairs swap products and reviewers attack the break-even with a value of their choosing, signing off or not (period 3).
Enforce a no-strawman rule and a context sign-up sheet so no two pairs use the same context and numbers, and present the strongest designs publicly.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: The Brand New Math Project Your Middle Schoolers Will Love!
example: As a capstone, pairs invent two competing pricing plans for something students actually buy, such as two streaming subscription options, with the requirement that each plan must genuinely win for somebody so neither is a strawman. They build the mathematics — two cost equations, a labeled graph, and a break-even point verified both algebraically and graphically — then write three Statement–Rule–Check recommendations for a light user, a heavy user, and a customer at exactly the break-even. A reviewing pair 'market tests' the plan by picking a value of their own and attacking the claimed break-even, signing off only if the design survives.
weeklyProduct: A multi-day written model citing computed break-even evidence, with two cost equations, a labeled graph, and three customer recommendation paragraphs.

title: The Unit-Coherence Conversation
description: A set of seven questions a department asks before any unit begins to make sure knowledge, texts, expectations, and evidence are aligned across classrooms and courses rather than left to individual guesswork. It raises achievement by ensuring students in every section build the same essential knowledge and hand it forward reliably to the next unit or course.
howTo:
Ask what knowledge students should already possess when the unit begins.
Ask what knowledge this unit will deliberately build.
Identify which texts, sources, problems, datasets, or phenomena will carry that knowledge.
Decide what must be explained or front-loaded before students read.
Determine what every student will produce independently.
Agree on how the department will know whether students learned it, and what knowledge/reasoning must be handed forward to the next unit or course.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
example: Before starting a shared unit on persuasive writing, the ninth-grade ELA team meets to walk through the seven coherence questions: which texts and vocabulary students already encountered in eighth grade, which reasoning moves (like sourcing a claim or checking a counterclaim) have already been taught, and what the visible handoff to tenth grade should look like. The department chair records the agreed knowledge sequence and disciplinary expectations so that a student moving from Ms. Rivera's section to Mr. Osei's section next semester isn't re-taught the same annotation codes from scratch or, worse, never taught them at all. The conversation ends with a written note of what each teacher owns delivering before the unit begins.
weeklyProduct: No student artifact — the visible result is a department's written answers to seven alignment questions about texts, expectations, and evidence for the coming unit.

title: The 30-Minute Department Protocol
description: A tightly timed five-step department or PLC meeting structure that moves a team from naming shared knowledge goals to reviewing common student work to agreeing on instructional responses and a handoff, turning common intention into common action. It builds coherence across classrooms so that misunderstandings get caught and addressed collectively instead of separately by each teacher.
howTo:
Knowledge (5 min): Name what students should know by the end of the unit and what may reasonably be assumed at the start.
Text and task (5 min): Choose what students will examine, read, discuss, solve, defend, and revise.
Student work (10 min): Review a common artifact to identify what students understand, what they misunderstand, and which reasoning move is missing.
Instructional response (5 min): Agree on what every teacher will reteach, reinforce, or revise before the next common check.
Handoff (5 min): Record what the next unit or course should be able to assume and where that knowledge will be checked.
Have the department chair or PLC lead maintain the shared knowledge map, facilitate the student-work review, record decisions, and verify the handoff actually occurred.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: How to Efficiently Run a Teacher PLC or Team Meeting
example: At a monthly math PLC meeting, the department chair runs the 30-minute protocol on the Algebra 1 team's shared exit-ticket data from a systems-of-equations unit: five minutes reviewing the common knowledge map, ten minutes examining a stack of real student work sorted by common error, ten minutes deciding on one common next instructional move (re-teaching the check step across all three sections), and five minutes confirming who owns following up and by when. The chair records the decision and checks at the next meeting whether the agreed handoff — flagging students who struggled to the intervention teacher — actually happened.
weeklyProduct: A recorded set of department decisions on reteaching priorities and a written handoff note naming what the next unit can assume.

title: Advisory Knowledge-Building Read-Aloud
description: A 15-minute advisory-period routine in which a teacher reads aloud from a content-rich text in a coherent multi-week sequence, giving all students access to ideas, vocabulary, and sentence structures above what they can currently decode independently. It prevents students with decoding difficulty from being cut off from the knowledge their peers are building while separate foundational-skills support is developed, without replacing independent content reading or targeted intervention.
howTo:
Orient and retrieve (2 min): State the multi-week knowledge topic, recap what was learned previously, and give students a specific listening focus.
Read aloud (8 min): Read an engaging, content-rich text, pausing selectively to define an essential word, clarify context, unpack a difficult sentence, or connect to prior knowledge.
Partner talk (3 min): Have students discuss what the reading added to what they already knew and which detail changed or complicated their understanding.
Capture (2 min): Students complete sentence starters such as "Today I learned…", "This connects to…", and "One word or idea I can now explain is…".
Sequence read-alouds in four- to six-week blocks that build one coherent body of knowledge (e.g., the Dust Bowl and migration) rather than unrelated inspirational passages.
Treat this as one of three complementary parts — teacher read-aloud, content-class disciplinary reading, and targeted decoding intervention — with none replacing the others.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Ramp Up Your Read Alouds to Build Knowledge and Boost ...
example: Over a five-week advisory sequence, the teacher reads aloud fifteen minutes a day from a coherent set of short nonfiction pieces on tribal sovereignty and Oklahoma history, letting students who struggle to decode complex text access the same vocabulary and ideas as their peers. Each session builds on the last rather than jumping between unrelated inspirational readings, so that by week five students can discuss the Dawes Act and its consequences with real background knowledge. This read-aloud time supplements, but never replaces, the independent content-area reading students do in their actual social studies class.
weeklyProduct: Each student's completed sentence starters ('Today I learned...', 'This connects to...') capturing one new idea from a read-aloud passage.

title: Summary vs. Analysis
description: This poster distinguishes retelling what a text says (summary) from arguing what it means with textual evidence (analysis), a mix-up the book calls the most common source of weak student writing. Naming the difference explicitly helps students stop submitting plot summaries when a defensible, arguable claim is what's actually required.
howTo:
Tell students plainly which register is being asked for: summary, argument, or craft writing, since much confusion is really not knowing which job they're doing.
Cap plot/content summary at one or two sentences early in the reading, then require the writing to move beyond it.
Teach students to test their own claim: if no reasonable reader could disagree with it, it is a summary wearing a claim's costume, not an analysis.
Use a two-column chart (what the text SAYS vs. what it DOES) so summary and interpretation are visibly separated on the page.
Score summary-only responses at the lowest rubric level so students know going in that summary cannot substitute for analysis.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Summary vs. Analysis
example: A student reading Kate Chopin's 'The Story of an Hour' first drafts a summary sentence — 'Louise Mallard hears her husband died, feels free, then he comes home alive and she dies' — and the teacher shows how this only retells events. The class then revises toward analysis: 'Chopin's repetition of "free, free, free" reveals that Louise's death comes not from joy but from the sudden loss of the independence she'd only just discovered,' a claim built on textual evidence rather than plot recap. Students practice sorting their own draft sentences into a two-column chart labeled Summary and Analysis to see which register they're actually writing in.
weeklyProduct: A two-column chart where each student separates what a text SAYS, citing its content, from what it DOES, forming an arguable claim.

title: The Quote Sandwich
description: This poster gives students a repeatable structure for integrating quoted evidence into writing: a claim, the exact quoted words with their citation, and a warrant explaining why those words mean what the writer says they mean. It helps achievement by making student thinking checkable — a stranger can see exactly which words support the claim and why.
howTo:
State the claim first, in a full sentence that takes a position.
Insert the text's exact words, quoted and cited (e.g., by paragraph number), never paraphrased into vagueness.
Write the warrant: explain specifically why those quoted words support the claim — name what the language does (creates, contrasts, repeats, shifts).
Test the claim against a second passage that could complicate it, and revise if the claim doesn't survive.
Use sentence frames (e.g., 'The text claims ___, but the line "___" (para ___) suggests ___') as a temporary ramp, then retire the frame once students are fluent.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: The Quote Sandwich (a way to deliver or package a quote)
example: Writing about the Gettysburg Address, a student is taught to build each paragraph as claim, quote, explanation: 'Lincoln reframes the war as a test of democracy itself. He argues the nation must ensure "government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth." By tying the Union's survival to democracy's survival everywhere, Lincoln elevates a local battle into a universal cause.' The teacher has students underline the claim, box the exact quoted words with their citation, and star the explanation sentence in a partner's draft to check no slice of the sandwich is missing.
weeklyProduct: A written paragraph with a claim, an exact quoted and cited line of text, and a warrant explaining why that quote supports the claim.

title: Counterclaim & Rebuttal
description: This poster asks students to state their own claim, then present the strongest opposing reading or argument at full strength before answering it — the book calls this 'steel-manning' the counter-position. It builds achievement by teaching intellectual honesty: a claim isn't finished until it can name and survive its best objection.
howTo:
Draft the main claim so it is arguable, not a summary or an undeniable fact in disguise.
Identify one honestly presented counter-reading or counterclaim — one a smart, informed reader could actually hold, stated at full strength, not a weak version.
Support the counterclaim with its own quoted or cited evidence so it isn't a strawman.
Write the rebuttal: explain why the original claim survives the counterclaim, or revise the claim if it doesn't.
Grade with a rubric that requires the counter-reading; an argument that can't state the other side isn't finished.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Writing a Counterclaim with a Rebuttal
example: Arguing whether the Dawes Act's allotment policy helped or harmed Native nations, a student states a claim — that allotment caused dispossession — then must present the strongest opposing case at full strength: reformers at the 1885 Lake Mohonk Conference sincerely believed individual land ownership would bring citizenship and protection. Only after presenting that counterclaim fairly does the student answer it, citing the Dawes Commission's acreage records showing millions of tribal acres lost within a generation despite the stated intent. The teacher checks that the counterclaim isn't a strawman by requiring it to be one a genuinely informed person could hold.
weeklyProduct: A written argument with a main claim, a fully stated counterclaim backed by its own cited evidence, and a rebuttal defending the claim.

title: Synthesis Across Multiple Sources
description: This poster requires a claim to be tested against an independent second source, and pushes students to notice where multiple sources converge or conflict rather than accepting one source alone. It raises achievement because corroboration across different kinds of evidence — not repeating one voice — is what separates a real argument from an assertion.
howTo:
Assemble a set of sources of genuinely different types (e.g., a law, a record, a testimony, a map) so students corroborate across kinds of evidence, not within one.
State a claim from the first source, naming its evidence and source verb.
Check the claim against a second, independent source; independent sources that converge strengthen the claim, sources that conflict require it to become more precise.
Write a sentence explicitly naming where the sources converge or conflict.
Watch for false corroboration — two sources that are really one voice (e.g., two reports from the same institution) — and require true independence.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Learning to Synthesize Through a Hands-On Activity
example: Researching the allotment era, a student must test a claim about the Dawes Act against at least one independent second source, such as corroborating the Lake Mohonk reformers' stated intentions with Chitto Harjo's 1906 Senate testimony describing the policy's actual effects on his community. Where the sources converge, the student's claim gets stronger; where they conflict, the claim must become more precise, for instance narrowing from 'allotment helped Native people' to 'allotment's designers believed it would help, but its administration dispossessed the people it claimed to protect.' The final paragraph names both sources by type and shows exactly where they agree and diverge.
weeklyProduct: A written claim tested against a second, independent cited source, with one sentence naming exactly where the sources converge or conflict.

title: Structured Academic Controversy → Consensus
description: In this structure, pairs argue an assigned side from the documents, then switch and argue the reverse side, then drop roles entirely to write a consensus claim that has to survive both cases. It drives achievement by making disagreement the engine of evidence-based thinking rather than opinion.
howTo:
Assign pairs a side of a genuinely arguable question and require them to argue it using only the document set, citing exhibits or sources.
Have pairs switch and argue the opposite side from the same evidence, so no one is allowed to stay 'their' side's advocate.
Drop roles: partners write a single consensus claim that has to hold up against both cases they just argued.
Require the consensus claim to name the evidence that decided it, and name one piece of evidence that complicated it.
Debrief on how the switch changed anyone's thinking, crediting genuine revision over 'winning.'
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Structured Academic Controversy
example: On the question of whether the Dawes Act's allotment policy delivered what it promised, Pairs A are assigned to argue that supporters delivered on their promise, citing the Lake Mohonk proceedings and the Act's own title, while Pairs B argue the record contradicts it, citing the Dawes Commission's acreage data and Chitto Harjo's testimony — each argument requiring a named source, date, and verb. After eight minutes, pairs switch sides and must argue the reverse without reusing their opponents' points, forcing a second pass through the document set. Finally, pairs drop their assigned roles and write one consensus claim that survives both cases, such as 'the policy could be sincerely intended as protection and still function as dispossession, and the sources show it being both.'
weeklyProduct: A written consensus claim, built after arguing both sides of a document set, naming the cited evidence that decided it.

title: Socratic Seminar → Written Reflection
description: A student-led, text-anchored discussion where a marked/annotated text is the ticket to speak, every claim must return to a specific paragraph, and the seminar closes with each student revising their written claim to cite a classmate's point by name. It boosts achievement by converting talk visibly into writing, proving discussion changed thinking rather than just filled time.
howTo:
Require a marked, annotated text as the entry ticket; unprepared students observe from an outer circle until ready.
Have each student bring written questions at multiple levels of depth (e.g., Costa's three levels) and open with a student's question, not the teacher's.
Run the inner-circle discussion with every claim anchored back to the text by paragraph or line number; the teacher tracks talk but intervenes only to re-anchor to the text.
Require talk moves such as building on, respectfully disagreeing with evidence, and inviting quieter voices in.
Close with a written revision of each student's claim that explicitly cites a classmate's point by name, showing the discussion changed the writing.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Scaffolding Discussion Skills With a Socratic Circle
example: Before a seminar on Kate Chopin's 'The Story of an Hour,' each student marks up the text and brings three written questions, one at each Costa level, since the marked text is the ticket to sit in the inner circle.
