A student opens with a Level 2 question about why the narrator never judges Louise Mallard, and the discussion runs student-to-student with every claim anchored to a paragraph number, the teacher intervening only to redirect back to the text. Afterward, each student revises their own written interpretation and must cite a specific classmate's point: for example, crediting a peer named Marcus whose question about the narrator's refusal to condemn Louise changed their reading of the ending.
weeklyProduct: A revised written claim, anchored to a specific paragraph or line and explicitly citing a classmate's point by name from the seminar discussion.

title: Mathematical Proof & Justification
description: This poster gives students a fixed frame — Statement, Rule Applied, Check — for justifying a mathematical claim in full sentences, then verifying it a second way with a different value, method, or representation. It raises achievement because it forces students to state a claim, back it with reasoning that includes the word 'because,' and prove the check isn't just circular.
howTo:
Write the Statement: the claim in a full sentence that answers the actual question asked, not just a numeric answer.
Write the Rule Applied: the mathematics that backs the claim, in words and symbols together, using 'because' to turn steps into reasoning.
Perform the Check: verify the claim a second way — a different value, representation, method, or counterexample; plugging the same value back in doesn't count as a check.
Note that a single numerical check is 'consistent with' a claim but is not a proof for every value — reach for algebra or a general argument when the claim covers a whole interval.
Apply the same three-part frame across course types (algebra, geometry, trigonometry, statistics), since the form of evidence changes but the demand doesn't.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Teaching Math with ADI | What is Justification in Math?
example: Asked to find the exterior angle at vertex C of a triangle with interior angles of 50° and 60°, a student writes: Statement — 'The exterior angle at C measures 110°.' Rule Applied — 'By the Exterior Angle Theorem, an exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, so it's 50° + 60° = 110°.' Alternate-method check — 'The interior angle at C is 180° − 110° = 70°, and 50° + 60° + 70° = 180°, matching the triangle angle-sum rule, so the answer checks out a second way.'
weeklyProduct: A written Statement–Rule Applied–Check justification citing the specific mathematical rule and a genuinely different second check.

title: Feedback to Action
description: A structured three-pass peer review process where each pass has one specific job (claim, evidence, reasoning/warrant), reviewers write one targeted sentence per pass, and writers must revise against all three passes before the teacher ever sees the work. It improves achievement because specific, actionable feedback teaches more revision than a page of unfocused teacher comments — and teaches the reviewer as much as the writer.
howTo:
Structure peer review into three passes, each with a single job — for example: Pass 1 the claim, Pass 2 the evidence, Pass 3 the warrant/reasoning and a second, complicating test.
Have the reviewer initial a box for each pass and write exactly one targeted feedback sentence per pass, naming the specific gap rather than giving a vibe ('looks good').
Model what a precise, actionable feedback sentence sounds like (e.g., naming exactly what's missing and what move would fix it).
Require the writer to revise against all three pass-comments before the teacher ever reads the piece.
Reuse the identical pass structure across subjects so students transfer the revision habit rather than relearning a new checklist each time.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: How to Scaffold Claim Evidence Reasoning (CER) Writing ...
example: Reviewing a partner's science conclusion about the ice-melting phenomenon, a student runs the three-pass peer review: Pass 1 checks the claim (does it actually answer the question, or restate the procedure?), Pass 2 checks the evidence (is every number present with units and time-points?), and Pass 3 checks the reasoning and test (does the writer name the mechanism — conduction — and rule out a competing explanation, like the metal starting warmer?). The reviewer writes one targeted sentence per pass, such as 'you never ruled out that the metal started warmer; add the start-temperature check or a skeptic will sink your claim,' and the writer must revise against all three notes before the teacher ever sees the draft.
weeklyProduct: A student draft carrying three initialed peer-review passes, each with one written feedback sentence on claim, evidence, or reasoning, plus the writer's revision.

title: From Prompt to Defended Answer
description: This poster teaches students to unpack a task before answering it — surfacing hidden quantities or requirements, marking relationship language, bracketing the actual question being asked, and forecasting what shape a reasonable answer should take — before building a claim carried by evidence and verified a second way. It lifts achievement because most wrong answers are 'right answers to unasked questions,' and forecasting the answer's shape catches errors before any work is done.
howTo:
Pass 1 — identify the known quantities or given information, circling them with their units or context.
Pass 2 — mark the relationship words or structural cues that reveal how the pieces connect (e.g., 'per,' 'plus,' 'because').
Pass 3 — bracket the actual question being asked, since a computed answer to the wrong question is the most common failure.
Pass 4 — translate the task into a plain-language restatement and forecast what shape the final answer should take before solving.
Build the claim from evidence, then defend it in writing using the discipline's own sentence-shaped destination (claim, reasoning, and an independent check), per the book's 'one thinking standard, four disciplinary forms.'
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Close Reading in Math
example: Given the phone-plan word problem, a student runs the four-pass dissection protocol before computing anything: circling the known quantities with units ($30 start-up, $20 a month), naming the hidden quantity (months, the variable never explicitly named), bracketing the actual question (which plan is better, not just where they cross), and forecasting the answer's shape ('a plan and a condition, not just a number') before solving. Only after this unpacking does the student solve, then defend the answer with a Statement–Rule Applied–Check paragraph, catching early that a computed answer violating the forecast means a misread question.
weeklyProduct: A written claim built from marked-up task cues (knowns, relationships, bracketed question) and defended with cited evidence and an independent check.

title: Administrator Walkthrough Lens
description: A two-part coaching poster listing what an observer should see during a lesson (evidence of student reasoning, not compliance) and what to ask in an immediate five-minute follow-up. It supports achievement by keeping classroom walkthroughs focused on visible student thinking and non-evaluative coaching rather than teacher performance or scoring.
howTo:
During the walkthrough, look for instructional evidence: students working from an identifiable source, an explainable and posted question, and students talking or writing before the teacher supplies the interpretation.
Check that claims carry named evidence (a source, date, or verb) and that a second source is used to test a claim before it settles.
Confirm the teacher gathers a visible artifact of student thinking before students leave.
In the five-minute follow-up, ask reflective coaching questions such as 'What were students expected to produce?' and 'Show me the student work that informed that decision.'
Keep the visit strictly in the coaching lane — walkthrough notes are never evaluation evidence — to protect safe practice while still holding a clear instructional standard.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Evidence-Driven Classroom Walkthroughs: 7 Keys to Sustainable Impact
example: During a walkthrough of a science classroom running the ice-melting investigation, the coach looks for whether students are explaining the phenomenon rather than reciting a definition off a slide, whether claims carry measured data such as the 95%-versus-27% melt figures, and whether the teacher gathers a visible artifact like an exit ticket before students leave. Afterward, the coach asks five-minute follow-up questions such as 'what were students expected to produce today, and can I see a few?' and 'which student's explanation surprised you, and what did you do with it?' The visit stays coaching, not evaluation, and never converts into a score.
weeklyProduct: No teacher-facing written product — the visible result is a collected classroom artifact of student thinking plus notes from a five-minute non-evaluative coaching follow-up.

title: Student Evidence Progress Form
description: A simple recurring tracking form that counts, for a given class and document/task, how many students named a source, used an accurate source verb, and corroborated with an independent source — plus one instructional adjustment for the next lesson. It raises achievement by turning vague impressions of a lesson into a visible trend line the teacher and PLC can act on.
howTo:
Record the teacher/course, date, class size, and the document or task used.
Count and record how many students named a source, used an accurate source verb, and corroborated with an independent source.
Capture one specific piece of evidence from student discussion or work.
Record one concrete instructional adjustment planned for the next lesson.
Keep three or more dated copies side by side per class period so growth becomes a visible trend line rather than a single snapshot.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: PLCs at Work: Analyzing and Using Formative Assessment Data
example: A social studies teacher running the allotment-era inquiry unit tracks, across three dated uses of the Historian's Sentence, how many of her 28 students named a source, used an accurate source verb (like 'the pamphlet promotes' versus 'the records document'), and corroborated their claim against a second independent source. On the first use, only 9 students corroborated their claim; by the third use, after she modeled the move explicitly, 22 did, and she brings that rising count — not just an impression — to her next PLC meeting to decide what to model next.
weeklyProduct: A dated tracking form recording how many students named a source, used an accurate source verb, and corroborated with an independent source.

title: Build Your Own Strategy
description: A lesson-design tool that takes each strategy a teacher just watched modeled on the book's own example and asks the teacher to rebuild it, blank by blank, on their own content — naming the two or three decisions that make a good version and the common way it goes wrong. It matters for achievement because a move a teacher has only watched is a demonstration, while a move built from scratch on real content is one the teacher actually owns and can teach well.
howTo:
Take a strategy already modeled in the book on its worked example, and identify the two or three decisions that make a strong version of it.
Fill in a blank template on your own unit content, mirroring exactly what the modeled example did (e.g., the arguable question, the source, the levels of questions).
Compare your draft against the 'Watch for' common failure listed for that strategy, and revise so your version avoids it.
Do this once with a colleague so the move is checked before it's run with students.
Repeat across a few strategies rather than many — the book advises mastering a handful deeply instead of collecting many shallowly.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Learning Strategies: Model the Strategy
example: Having watched the Two Claims and a Confound activity demonstrated on the ice-melting phenomenon, a biology teacher fills in the blank card to rebuild the same move for a photosynthesis unit: she picks her own phenomenon (why aquatic plants release more oxygen bubbles under a bright lamp than a dim one), drafts the model round of two claims and one confound (light intensity versus water temperature rising near the lamp), and runs it with a colleague before trying it live. Doing this once from scratch on her own content, rather than only ever running the book's ice-cube version, is what turns the activity from a demonstration she watched into a move she owns and can vary for the next unit on cellular respiration.
weeklyProduct: A teacher-built version of a modeled strategy, filled in on the teacher's own content and checked against a colleague before running it with students.

title: Sort the Stack: What Does the Student Need Next?
description: A fast, ungraded formative routine where the teacher scans a stack of short student responses (like exit tickets) and sorts them into simple piles — such as Got It / Almost / Not Yet — in seconds per paper, then opens the next lesson by naming the most common gap. It drives achievement because it turns everyday student work into an immediate, low-effort instructional decision instead of a grading burden.
howTo:
Add one low-stakes exit-ticket question that requires evidence in the answer (e.g., a claim that must name its source or line).
Do not grade the responses individually.
Quickly sort the stack into a small number of piles, such as Got It / Almost / Not Yet, spending only seconds per paper.
Identify the single most common gap across the 'Not Yet' and 'Almost' piles.
Open the next lesson by directly naming and addressing that most common gap before moving on.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Assessment Practices: Exit Tickets
example: After collecting a stack of exit tickets from a lesson on the phone-plan break-even problem, the teacher scans just the data line of each response in about fifteen seconds per paper, sorting them into three piles: no equation or check is 'Not Yet,' a correct equation without a named rule is 'Almost,' and a full Statement–Rule Applied–Check response is 'Ready.' Seeing that half the stack landed in 'Almost' because students never explained why they set the two costs equal, the teacher opens the next class by re-modeling exactly that missing rule rather than moving on to a new topic.
weeklyProduct: A stack of written tickets, each citing a source for its claim, sorted fast into Got It / Almost / Not Yet piles.

title: The Quickwrite
description: A short, ungraded burst of continuous writing (2–4 minutes) used at key moments of a lesson to let students think in writing before polish is demanded, building the fluency graded writing will later need. In math classrooms, use the same technique before, mid-solve, or after a problem to let students draft rough thinking that becomes a polished justification.
howTo:
Give a 2–4 minute timed prompt where pens must keep moving and nothing is collected for a grade.
Use it before the read to surface prior belief (e.g., "Write what you already believe about...").
Use it mid-read at a friction point when the text contradicts an earlier claim.
Use it after discussion to capture the one sentence students would defend tomorrow.
Expect rough, half-formed writing — it becomes the rough draft of a later claim.
In math: use before the problem to activate prior knowledge, mid-solve at a point of friction, or after discussion to commit to a defensible claim — never collect it for a grade.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner
videoTitle: Teaching Technique 10: Quick Write
example: Mid-way through solving the phone-plan problem, the teacher stops the class at a friction point: 'Your equation says ten months, but your gut said Plan B always wins. Write about the disagreement for two minutes.' A student's ragged, ungraded response reads, 'm = 10 came out of the algebra but I don't know what it IS yet. Maybe it's where the plans tie? If they tie there, then before it one is winning and after it the other is. So the answer isn't 10 — 10 is where the answer changes.' That half-formed insight, captured in the quickwrite, becomes the seed of the student's polished Statement by the end of the week.
weeklyProduct: A short, ungraded burst of rough continuous writing capturing one belief, friction point, or defensible claim from the lesson.

title: Sentence Combining
description: A technique where students combine several short, simple sentences into one longer, more sophisticated sentence — building syntactic control and sentence variety instead of relying on one flat sentence pattern.
howTo:
Give students 2-4 short, related sentences on the same topic.
Ask them to combine the sentences into one using conjunctions, subordination, or appositives.
Have students share multiple valid combinations with a partner or the class.
Discuss how each version changes the emphasis or flow of the sentence.
sourceName: Research School Network (EEF)
videoTitle: The ART of Sentence Combining
example: In a unit on the Dust Bowl, students receive three short sentences: "The wind blew for days. Topsoil disappeared. Farmers lost their crops." They combine them into one sentence such as "As the wind blew for days, disappearing topsoil left farmers without crops," then compare their combination to a partner's and discuss which version reads more smoothly.
weeklyProduct: A student-authored combined sentence (or short paragraph of combined sentences) showing control over conjunctions, subordination, and varied sentence structure.

title: Wait Time After Questioning
description: Deliberately pausing 3-5 seconds after asking a question — and again after a student responds — before calling on anyone, giving every student time to think instead of rewarding the fastest hand.
howTo:
Ask the question, then silently count to at least 3-5 seconds before calling on a student.
Resist the urge to fill the silence, rephrase, or call on the first raised hand.
After a student answers, pause again before responding or calling on another student.
Watch for more hands (and more varied hands) rising as the pause continues.
sourceName: Kent State Center for Teaching and Learning
videoTitle: Targeted Questioning + Wait Time
example: After asking "Why did the author choose to end the chapter here?" the teacher counts silently to five, watching more hands slowly rise across the room instead of calling on the first hand up, then calls on a student who was not among the first to raise a hand.
weeklyProduct: More, and more varied, student responses to the same question — a visible increase in hands raised and unique answers compared to a no-wait-time baseline.

title: Cold-Call: Equitable Participation System
description: A daily routine where the teacher calls on students at random — using sticks, cards, or a name-picker — rather than only on volunteers, so every student stays accountable for being ready to answer.
howTo:
Build a random-call system: popsicle sticks, numbered cards, or a digital randomizer.
Ask the question first, give thinking/wait time, then draw a name.
Return each name to the pool after it's drawn so students know they could be called again at any point.
Keep the tone warm and low-stakes — frame it as "everyone thinks, then I'll pick," not a gotcha.
sourceName: teacherhead.com (Teach Like a Champion)
videoTitle: What is Cold-Calling? | with Doug Lemov
example: Before discussing the causes of WWI, the teacher asks a question, waits five seconds, then draws a name from a cup of popsicle sticks. Every stick returns to the cup after being drawn, so students know they could be called again at any point and stay prepared throughout the lesson.
weeklyProduct: A discussion record showing a wide, evenly distributed spread of student names called — not just the same 4-5 volunteers.

title: Jigsaw Method
description: Each student in a group becomes the sole expert on one sub-topic, studies it (often with an "expert group" from other teams), then teaches it back to their home team — so the group only gets the full picture if every member teaches their piece.
howTo:
Split the content into 3-5 distinct sub-topics.
Assign one sub-topic to each student in a home group.
Let students with the same sub-topic meet in an "expert group" to build understanding together.
Send students back to their home groups to teach their piece.
Hold every student accountable with a task requiring information from all sub-topics.
sourceName: Hattie / Visible Learning
videoTitle: The Jigsaw Method
example: For a unit on the branches of government, each home group of three splits into Legislative, Executive, and Judicial experts. Experts from every group meet together to build a one-page summary of their branch, then return to teach it to their home group using their summary. The home group then completes a task requiring information from all three branches.
weeklyProduct: A completed team task or product (poster, quiz, graphic organizer) that could only be finished correctly if every group member taught their piece.

title: Explicit, Systematic Phonics and Decoding Instruction
description: Direct, sequential teaching of sound-symbol relationships and decoding rules — rather than relying on context or memorization — so students can sound out unfamiliar words systematically.
howTo:
Teach one phonics pattern or decoding rule at a time in a planned sequence.
Model sounding out words using the pattern explicitly, out loud.
Give students immediate guided practice reading words, then short connected text, containing the pattern.
Progress to the next pattern only after most students demonstrate mastery on a quick check.
sourceName: Hattie / Visible Learning; NWEA
videoTitle: Explicit Phonics Instruction Using the 6 Step Method
example: Before reading a passage, the teacher explicitly teaches the "silent e" pattern (cap → cape), models sounding out five example words on the board, then has students read a list of new words using the same pattern before applying it in the connected passage.
weeklyProduct: A quick decoding check or running record showing accuracy on words using the taught pattern.

title: Whole-Class Real-Time Checking-for-Understanding Signals
description: A quick, universal-response routine — individual whiteboards, thumbs up/down/sideways, "fist to five," or digital polling — where every student shows an answer or confidence level at the same moment so the teacher can scan the whole room instantly.
howTo:
Ask a question with a short, showable answer.
Have every student write it on a whiteboard, or show a hand signal (fist to five for confidence, thumbs for agree/disagree).
Say "show me" and have all students reveal at the same time.
Scan the room and adjust instruction immediately based on the spread of responses.
sourceName: Edutopia
example: Mid-lesson on solving one-step equations, the teacher asks a quick problem, and on "show me" every student holds up their whiteboard answer at once. Seeing several students with the same error, the teacher reteaches that step on the spot before moving on.
weeklyProduct: A real-time, whole-class snapshot of understanding the teacher can act on immediately, without waiting to grade papers.

title: Spaced, Cumulative Retrieval Practice
description: Short, low-stakes quizzes or recall tasks that deliberately revisit content from previous days, weeks, or units — not just the current lesson — so students practice retrieving older material before it fades.
howTo:
Keep a running log of key content from past weeks.
Open class 2-3 times a week with a 3-5 question, no-grade retrieval quiz mixing today's content with content from 2-4 weeks ago.
Review correct answers immediately as a class.
Rotate older content back in on a spaced schedule rather than testing it once and moving on.
sourceName: retrievalpractice.org
videoTitle: Spacing and Retrieval | Alfred Deakin High School
example: Every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, students spend the first five minutes answering three questions: one from today's lesson, one from two weeks ago, and one from the start of the unit. The teacher quickly reviews correct answers aloud before starting new instruction.
weeklyProduct: A short, dated retrieval log showing which older content is being revisited and how accuracy on it changes over time.

title: Student Self-Assessment Against Rubrics
description: Students rate their own work or predicted performance against explicit criteria or a rubric before receiving teacher feedback — building an accurate internal sense of their own progress rather than relying only on outside judgment.
howTo:
Share the rubric or success criteria before the task begins.
After completing a draft or practice set, have students score their own work against each criterion.
Have students briefly justify each score in writing.
Compare student self-scores to teacher scores on a sample and discuss any gaps.
sourceName: Hattie / Visible Learning
videoTitle: What Happens When Students Grade Themselves?
example: Before turning in a persuasive essay, each student uses the same 4-point rubric the teacher will use to score their own claim, evidence, and organization, writing one sentence justifying each score. The teacher then scores the same essay and briefly conferences with students whose self-score differs by more than one point from the teacher's.
weeklyProduct: A student-completed self-assessment rubric or prediction sheet, submitted alongside the work it evaluates.

title: Number Talks
description: A short daily routine where students mentally solve a problem, then share and compare multiple valid strategies for solving it — building number sense and flexible mental math rather than a single memorized procedure.
howTo:
Pose a single problem designed for mental math — no paper or pencil.
Give quiet think time; students show a thumbs-up when ready.
Collect 2-4 different student strategies on the board, in the student's own words.
Ask the class to compare strategies — which was fastest, which makes the most sense, are they all valid?
Keep it short (5-10 minutes) and low-stakes; no grades.
sourceName: NAESP
videoTitle: Using Math Number Talks to Develop Mental Math
example: The teacher writes "29 + 47" on the board. After a minute of silent thinking, three students share different strategies: rounding 29 up to 30 and adjusting, breaking both numbers into tens and ones, and counting up from 47. The class briefly compares which strategy felt fastest and why all three land on the same answer.
weeklyProduct: A running class anchor chart of student-generated mental-math strategies, added to after each number talk.

title: Interleaved, Mixed Practice Sets in Math
description: Practice sets that deliberately mix several previously-learned problem types together — instead of a block of problems using a single skill in a row — forcing students to first identify which strategy a problem calls for.
howTo:
After introducing a new skill, build practice sets that mix the new skill with 2-3 previously taught skills in random order.
Have students name which strategy or concept each problem requires before solving it.
Avoid blocking practice by type; mix problem types within the same set.
Revisit and re-mix older skills into practice sets throughout the unit and beyond.
sourceName: Mathematics Hub (Australia)
example: Instead of 15 straight problems on solving two-step equations, the teacher builds a 12-problem set mixing two-step equations, one-step equations, and simplifying expressions in random order. Before solving, students first label each problem with which skill it requires.
weeklyProduct: A completed mixed practice set showing which skill students identified for each problem alongside their solution.

title: Growth-Mindset Instructional Routines
description: Deliberately embedding process-praise and "yet" language into daily feedback — praising strategy, effort, and progress rather than fixed ability — so students build a mindset that ability grows with effort and better strategies.
howTo:
Replace ability-praise ("you're so smart") with process-praise naming the specific strategy or effort ("that re-reading strategy really paid off").
Add "yet" to statements about struggle ("I don't understand this yet").
Publicly normalize mistakes as part of learning.
Share a brief story of your own struggle-then-improvement when relevant.
sourceName: American Psychological Association
videoTitle: Developing a Growth Mindset with Carol Dweck
example: When a student says "I can't do fractions," the teacher responds, "You can't do it yet — let's look at which step is tripping you up," then later names the specific strategy the student used to fix the error, rather than praising the student generally.
weeklyProduct: A visible shift in classroom language — teacher and peer feedback naming specific strategies and effort rather than fixed traits, trackable through a quick self-audit of feedback given during a lesson.

title: Culturally Responsive Teaching Practices
description: An explicit instructional lens that intentionally connects content to students' cultural backgrounds, experiences, and identities, and applies culturally responsive approaches to classroom management — rather than treating "neutral" instruction as automatically equitable.
howTo:
Learn about students' cultural backgrounds and interests through surveys or conversations.
Intentionally choose examples, texts, and problem contexts that reflect that diversity.
Examine your own disciplinary patterns for bias (who gets referred, and for what).
Invite students to bring their own cultural knowledge into discussions as an asset, not a distraction.
sourceName: National Equity Project
videoTitle: Increasing Engagement by Using Culturally Responsive Curriculum
example: Before starting a unit on persuasive writing, the teacher surveys students about issues they care about in their own communities and builds the unit's mentor texts and example topics around those issues, then reviews the past month's discipline referrals with a colleague to check for patterns by student group.
weeklyProduct: A brief curriculum-connection note (how this week's content connected to students' backgrounds) or a discipline-pattern check.

title: Movement and Brain Breaks
description: A short, scheduled physical or cognitive reset (1-3 minutes) built into the lesson — not just transition time — to restore attention and energy before returning to instruction.
howTo:
Plan a brief break every 20-30 minutes during longer blocks — a 60-90 second stretch, a quick movement activity, or a brief mindfulness pause.
Announce it as a planned part of the lesson, not a reward or punishment.
Use a clear signal to start and end the break.
Return directly to instruction afterward exactly where the lesson left off.
sourceName: PMC (Impact of Brain Breaks)
example: Partway through a 90-minute block, the teacher pauses instruction for a 90-second stretch-and-breathe break, then signals with a countdown to return to seats and resume the lesson exactly where it left off.
weeklyProduct: A visible increase in sustained attention during the second half of longer class periods — fewer off-task redirections needed.

title: Independent Reading Time with Accountability
description: A scoped block of independent, self-selected reading paired with a brief written or verbal accountability response — not unstructured free reading — so silent reading time reliably builds both practice and evidence of engagement.
howTo:
Give students a set block of time (10-15 minutes) to read a self-selected, appropriately leveled text.
Require a short accountability response at the end — a one-sentence reaction, a logged page count and brief summary, or a quick conference.
Rotate through students for brief one-on-one check-in conferences over the week rather than trying to monitor everyone every day.
sourceName: VU Amsterdam (meta-analysis)
videoTitle: Master Independent Reading: Accountability Made Easy
example: During the last 12 minutes of class, students read a book of their choosing at their independent reading level, then write two sentences in their reading log about what happened and one line predicting what comes next. The teacher conferences with four students individually while the rest read silently.
weeklyProduct: A student reading log with dated entries — pages read, a brief response, and periodic conference notes — showing sustained engagement with self-selected text.

title: Making Your Classroom a No-Worksheet Space
description: Swap fill-in-the-blank worksheets for a blank page. Instead of completing a template someone else already organized, students build their own visual representation of their thinking — through sketchnoting or a thinking map — which forces them to decide what matters, not just where to write it.
howTo:
Give students a blank page instead of a worksheet. Ask them to represent the day's content visually as they listen or read — using headers, boxes, arrows, symbols, and quick sketches rather than sentences alone. Treat this as ideation, not an art assignment: a stick-figure diagram that shows real thinking beats a neat worksheet that shows none.
Model it first. Sketchnote on the board yourself before asking students to try it, narrating your choices out loud ("I'm drawing an arrow here because this step causes the next one").
For content with a clear structure (comparing, sequencing, cause-and-effect), teach a simple thinking map instead of a free sketch — students build the map themselves rather than filling in a pre-made organizer.
Let the drawing stay unfinished and evolving. Use it to prompt follow-up questions ("Why did this happen here and not earlier?") instead of treating it as a completed, gradable product.
sourceName: ASCD Educational Leadership — "Ditch the Worksheets!"
videoTitle: Sketchnotes for Classroom: Why, How, and Tips
example: Instead of handing out a worksheet listing each stage of cell mitosis, a teacher gives students a blank page and asks them to sketch the process as if drawing a comic strip — chromosomes become characters lining up, arrows loop back to show repeated steps, and captions record what the student thinks is happening. The drawing is left intentionally unfinished, and the teacher uses it to ask, "Why do the chromosomes split here but not earlier?" The visible gaps in a student's sketch tell the teacher more about their understanding than a completed answer key ever could.
weeklyProduct: A student-built sketchnote or thinking map of the day's content — not a filled-in template, but a page the student organized and drew themselves.

title: Counting Collections
description: A hands-on math routine where students count a real collection of objects — buttons, cubes, pom poms — in pairs, choose their own strategy for organizing and tracking the count, and record how they counted, replacing a worksheet of pre-set problems with a task that reveals a student's actual counting strategy and number sense.
howTo:
Prepare: bag sets of countable objects (buttons, cubes, counters, pom poms) in quantities matched to where each pair of students is developmentally — small counts for students still building one-to-one correspondence, larger or "messier" counts for students ready to group by tens.
Launch: model the routine once for the whole class before releasing pairs to work — show how to choose a bag, decide on a plan together, and use tools like ten-frames or cups to organize the count as you go, narrating your thinking out loud.
Work: release students in pairs to choose a bag, count together, and record their total using pictures, tally marks, numerals, or an equation, however makes sense to them. Circulate and ask questions rather than correcting: "How are you counting?" "Can you count it a different way?" "Would you get the same total?"
Wrap up: bring the class back together to share strategies, not just answers — ask which strategies were fastest, which were most accurate, and whether two different counting methods landed on the same total.
sourceName: Erikson Institute Early Math Collaborative — Counting Collections Builds Strong Counting Knowledge
videoTitle: Lakeridge Elementary School kindergarten teacher Stephanie Latimer uses the Counting Collections method to teach students mathematics
example: A pair of first graders chooses a bag labeled "C" holding 22 pom poms. Instead of a worksheet page of addition problems, they decide together to group the pom poms into piles of five using a muffin tray, then draw four full groups of five and two leftover circles on blank paper, writing "4 groups of 5 and 2 more = 22" underneath. When the teacher asks, "Would you get the same number if you counted them one at a time instead?", the pair recounts by ones to check, confirming their total and discovering their grouping method was faster but just as accurate.
weeklyProduct: A recorded page from each pair showing how they counted their collection — drawing, tally, or equation — kept as an ongoing record of a student's counting strategies over time.

title: The Document-Based Lesson
description: A three-part structure for teaching with primary sources — establish background knowledge, have students read and annotate a set of documents to answer guiding questions, then hold a whole-class discussion of a central historical question — replacing a single worksheet packet with a genuine investigation where students must weigh conflicting evidence before writing a defended answer.
howTo:
Establish background knowledge: before opening any documents, give students the minimum context they need through a short mini-lesson, video clip, or textbook excerpt, then post the central historical question the lesson will investigate (a question with a real, arguable answer — not a fact to look up).
Read and annotate primary source documents: give students two or more documents on the question, each excerpted and leveled for your class's reading range. As students read, they answer guiding questions about each document's source, context, and content, or complete a graphic organizer that has them note what each document claims and who is making the claim.
Discuss and write: hold a whole-class or small-group discussion where students use evidence from the documents — citing them by name — to support claims about the central question, including where documents agree or conflict. Close with a written, evidence-based answer to the central question, requiring students to cite at least two documents.
sourceName: Stanford Graduate School of Education — Reading Like a Historian
videoTitle: Reading Like a Historian Introduction
example: Studying the construction of the Great Pyramid at Giza, the teacher gives brief background on ancient Egypt, then posts the central question: "Did slaves build the Great Pyramid?" Students read five short, leveled excerpts — a letter from the ancient historian Herodotus, a 1959 textbook passage, a 2010 news article, a documentary transcript, and comments from an Egyptologist — noting each source's author and claim. In the closing discussion, students find that the Herodotus and 1959 textbook accounts agree slaves built it, while the modern archaeological sources disagree, pointing to worker housing and burial records. Each student then writes a paragraph answering the central question, citing evidence from at least two of the five documents.
weeklyProduct: A written, evidence-based answer to the day's central historical question, citing at least two of the assigned documents by name and noting where they agree or conflict.

title: The Science Observation Journal
description: A running notebook where young students stop, look closely at something real — a plant, the weather, a classroom animal — and record what they notice, wonder, and predict in words and pictures, then revisit old entries to spot changes over time, replacing a fill-in-the-blank science worksheet with a student-built record of their own observations.
howTo:
Choose something to observe repeatedly over days or weeks — the weather, a classroom plant, a pet, or shadows outside — rather than a one-time worksheet topic.
Model close observation before students write: think aloud using all the senses except taste ("I notice the leaves look a little different today — I wonder why"), then model recording that noticing as a quick drawing and a sentence.
Give students sentence starters ("I notice…", "I wonder…", "I think…") and let them choose to draw, write, or both — younger students often communicate an observation through a picture before they can write it.
Have students share their entry with a partner or the class after journaling, building vocabulary and letting the class compare what different students noticed about the same subject.
Periodically have students revisit older entries to name what has changed, turning the journal into evidence of a pattern over time rather than a single completed page.
sourceName: The Primary Planet — Observation Journals: How to Bring Real Science into Your Classroom
videoTitle: Be a Field Scientist! - #sciencegoals
example: A second-grade class keeps a running journal on a classroom bean plant. Each Monday, students draw the plant, measure its height with a ruler, and write a sentence such as "I notice the stem is taller and I wonder if the new leaf will unfold this week." After four weeks, a student flips back through her entries and notices her own drawings show the plant leaning toward the window, prompting the class to discuss why plants grow toward light.
weeklyProduct: A dated journal page, in words and/or drawings, recording what a student noticed, wondered, and predicted about an ongoing classroom observation.

title: Phonemic Awareness — Daily Oral Routine
description: A short daily oral routine that develops students' ability to hear, identify, and manipulate the individual sounds in spoken words. Phonemic awareness is the single strongest kindergarten predictor of later reading success — IES rates the evidence 'Strong' for developing awareness of the sounds in speech and how they link to letters.
howTo:
Warm-up with syllable and onset-rime blending and segmenting before moving to phoneme-level tasks.
Rotate the six phoneme skills across the week — isolation, blending, segmenting, addition, deletion, substitution.
Use say-it-then-tap-it: children push a chip for each sound heard, then map letters to chips.
Keep it oral first. Letters are added once children can hear and manipulate the sounds accurately.

Classroom example: During the first eight minutes of the K block, the teacher runs a Heggerty-style routine on the rug. Today's focus is initial sound isolation with CVC words. She says 'run' and children signal (thumb on chest) once they can name the first sound; on her cue the class chorally says /r/. She rotates through eight words, then moves to blending: she taps /s/ /a/ /t/ and the class blends 'sat'. Total time: 8 minutes, no worksheets, every child producing sound.
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Foundational Skills to Support Reading for Understanding in K–3rd Grade
videoTitle: How to Teach Phonemic Awareness in Kindergarten, 1st, & 2nd Grade

title: Systematic, Explicit Phonics
description: A planned, cumulative sequence for teaching students to decode words, analyze word parts, and write and recognize words. IES gives a Strong evidence rating to systematic phonics — meaning the sequence is planned in advance and every lesson builds on the last.
howTo:
Follow a six-step routine: introduce sound-symbol, blending drill, word chaining, decodable reading, encoding, and application.
New sound → model → blend in words → read in decodable text → dictate/encode the pattern.
Keep a visible scope-and-sequence in the room and mark today's target sound or pattern.
Reteach any pattern more than 20% of students missed on the weekly check. Encoding (spelling) is not extra — it's how phonics sticks.

Classroom example: Today's first-grade phonics block focuses on the digraph 'ck'. The teacher models /k/ at the end of one-syllable short-vowel words, blends 'kick, back, rock' with the class, then chains words: 'kick → sick → lick → lock → lock → sock'. Students read a decodable passage packed with -ck words in whisper voices, and end by dictating three -ck words and one sentence. Twenty-two minutes, every step visible on the pocket chart.
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Foundational Skills to Support Reading for Understanding in K–3rd Grade
videoTitle: Explicit Phonics Instruction Using the 6 Step Method

title: Decodable Text Reading
description: Novice readers practice the phonics patterns they have been taught by reading connected text intentionally written using those patterns. IES recommends daily connected-text reading tied to the phonics scope so students accumulate accurate practice with the code.
howTo:
Preview only the tricky heart words (irregular high-frequency words); never pre-teach the decodable ones.
First pass: whisper-read or partner-read while the teacher listens for accuracy and prompts by sound.
Second pass: reread for fluency and meaning.
End with two to three comprehension questions. Retire the decodable when 95%+ of students read it accurately.

Classroom example: A first-grade small group meets at the guided reading table with a short decodable focused on short-a CVC words plus the heart words 'the' and 'is'. The teacher previews the two heart words on the whiteboard, points to them in the text, then students whisper-read while she leans in to prompt: 'What sound? Slide it. Say the word.' Second pass is choral for fluency, and she ends with 'Where did the cat sit? Why?'
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Foundational Skills to Support Reading for Understanding in K–3rd Grade
videoTitle: Introducing Decodable Readers in 1st Grade

title: Fluency — Repeated and Performance Reading
description: Students reread the same grade-level passage across the week with modeling and feedback so that accuracy, rate, and prosody all improve. The National Reading Panel identified guided repeated oral reading as producing moderate-to-strong gains in fluency and comprehension.
howTo:
Choose a short (75–150 word) grade-level passage aligned to the current unit.
Model → echo → choral → partner → performance across the week.
Chart words correct per minute across the week; the goal is prosody, not race-reading.
End the week with readers' theater or a performance so fluency has a real audience.

Classroom example: A second-grade teacher picks a 120-word passage tied to the class's animal-habitats unit. Monday: she models expressive reading and the class echoes each sentence. Tuesday: choral reading. Wednesday and Thursday: partner reads with a fluency rubric. Friday: two volunteers perform for a first-grade buddy class. Weekly WCPM chart shows growth from 42 to 71.
videoTitle: Improving Fluency with Technology: Repeated and Performance Reading

title: Vocabulary Through Knowledge-Building Read-Alouds
description: A daily read-aloud built around a two-to-three-week topic set of books that build both vocabulary and background knowledge — the two biggest levers on later comprehension. IES gives this practice a Moderate evidence rating and it aligns to the vocabulary strand of the K–3 Foundational Skills guide.
howTo:
Choose a 2–3 week topic set of books that share a topic and vocabulary.
Pre-teach 3–5 tier-2 words per book with student-friendly definitions and examples/non-examples.
During reading, stop at each target word: define, connect to prior use, ask students to use it.
After reading: sketch, write, or discuss using the words. Add words to a visible topic wall.

Classroom example: Kindergarten is three weeks into a topic set on 'weather and seasons.' Today's book introduces 'howling, drift, blizzard.' The teacher shows a photo, gives kid-friendly definitions, and turns three times during the read-aloud: 'Where's the drift? Point.' 'When did the wind howl? Show me with your voice.' By Friday every child uses two of the words in a shared write about a storm.
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Foundational Skills to Support Reading for Understanding in K–3rd Grade
videoTitle: Read Aloud with Attention to Vocabulary — Dr. Tanya S. Wright

title: Dialogic Reading & Comprehension Talk
description: The teacher becomes the questioner and the child becomes the storyteller, using the PEER routine and CROWD prompts to build oral language and comprehension. WWC lists Dialogic Reading as an evidence-based practice with positive effects on oral language.
howTo:
Use the PEER routine: Prompt → Evaluate → Expand → Repeat.
Ask CROWD prompts: Completion, Recall, Open-ended, Wh-, Distancing.
Give at least one turn-and-talk per read-aloud; monitor and lift one exemplar.
For expository texts, add 'What did the author want us to learn?' to every closing.

Classroom example: During a K read-aloud of a picture book about firefighters, the teacher stops at page 6: 'Why do you think the firefighters slide down the pole instead of walking?' (Open-ended.) A student answers, she expands: 'Yes — to be faster, because seconds matter in an emergency,' and asks the class to repeat the expanded idea. She uses two more CROWD prompts before finishing the book.
sourceName: WWC — Dialogic Reading Intervention Report
videoTitle: Dialogic Reading With Expository Text (Video 3)

title: Number Talks — Daily Mental Math Routine
description: An 8-to-10-minute daily routine where students solve one problem mentally and share their strategies. It builds flexible thinking, mathematical language, and community — Hattie ranks classroom discussion at d ≈ 0.82 and this is the classroom home for it.
howTo:
Pose one problem. Silent think time — students signal (thumb on chest) when ready.
Collect all answers first with no reactions, then ask: 'How did you get it?'
Record 2–3 strategies on the board using students' names.
Close with: 'Which strategy is new to you? Which will you try next time?'

Classroom example: The teacher writes '29 + 47' on the board. After a minute of silent thinking, three students share different strategies: rounding 29 up to 30 and adjusting, breaking both numbers into tens and ones, and counting up from 47. The class briefly compares which strategy felt fastest and why all three land on the same answer.
sourceName: Inside Mathematics — Number Talks Library
videoTitle: Number Talks in Kindergarten, First, and Second Grade

title: Subitizing & Number Sense
description: Perceptual and conceptual subitizing — instantly recognizing small quantities without counting one-by-one — is the ground floor of number sense. IES gives 'building children's understanding of number' a Strong evidence rating in the Teaching Math to Young Children Practice Guide.
howTo:
Dot-card flash: show for 2 seconds, hide, ask 'How many? How did you see them?'
Vary arrangements (line, ten-frame, dice, random) so children don't memorize pictures.
Move from 1–5 to 6–10, then to two-part patterns (5 + 2, 4 + 3).
Ten-frames become the anchor for + and − work all year.

Classroom example: K children sit on the rug. The teacher flashes a ten-frame card with 7 dots (5 on top, 2 on bottom) for 2 seconds. Hands up: 'Seven.' 'How did you see it?' 'Five on top and two on the bottom.' 'Anyone see it differently?' A second child: 'I saw one missing on top and two.' Three cards, three ways of seeing, in five minutes.
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Teaching Math to Young Children
videoTitle: Subitizing for Kids — Learn Numbers Fast (Dot Cards 1–5)

title: Concrete → Representational → Abstract (CRA)
description: Students build a concept first with manipulatives, then draw it, then work symbolically. Students taught with CRA consistently outperform peers taught symbolically first. WWC lists visual representations as a top intervention practice in the 2021 Math Intervention Practice Guide.
howTo:
Concrete: cubes, counters, or base-10 blocks in every child's hands.
Representational: student draws what they built — quick sketches, ten-frames, bar models.
Abstract: only after C and R feel solid; connect back with 'Where do you see the ___ in the equation?'
For struggling students, drop back one stage — don't just re-explain the symbols.

Classroom example: Second grade is learning to subtract with regrouping. Students first build 32 with base-10 blocks and physically trade a ten-rod for ten ones to take away 15. Next they draw the same trade on a place-value mat. Only then does the teacher write the vertical algorithm alongside — and asks: 'Point to the ten in your drawing. Now point to it in the numbers.'
videoTitle: CRA — Concrete Representational Abstract

title: Cognitively Guided Instruction (CGI)
description: Problem-first teaching: instruction centers on students' own strategies for solving story problems, with teachers learning to interpret student thinking and select problem types deliberately. WWC evidence for problem-solving instruction is Positive; decades of Carpenter, Fennema, Franke, Levi, and Empson research back it.
howTo:
Give the story problem BEFORE teaching a procedure. Let students choose tools.
Circulate; select 2–3 student solutions to share (least → most sophisticated).
Name the strategies — 'direct modeling,' 'counting on,' 'derived facts.'
Vary problem type across the week (Join, Separate, Part-Part-Whole, Compare).

Classroom example: First grade: 'Maria had 8 stickers. She got some more. Now she has 14. How many did she get?' No procedure taught. Kids solve — some use counters, some count on from 8, one uses 8+6=14 as a known fact. The teacher selects three solutions to share in that order, then names each strategy on the anchor chart.
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Teaching Math to Young Children
videoTitle: CGI Math For Teachers

title: Math Language Routine — Convince Yourself, a Friend, a Skeptic
description: Structured discourse routines that give every child a turn — not just the volunteers — so explaining and justifying math builds both understanding and language. IES gives math discourse a Moderate evidence rating and Hattie ranks classroom discussion at d ≈ 0.82.
howTo:
Post sentence stems in the room: 'I know ___ because ___.' 'I disagree because ___.'
Turn-and-talk in every math block; teacher names one exemplar per lesson.
'Say it another way' — call on a second student to restate the first.
'Convince a skeptic' — teacher plays doubter to push justification.

Classroom example: During a place-value lesson, a third grader claims 340 > 304. The teacher says: 'Convince me. I'm the skeptic.' The student uses base-10 blocks to show three hundreds and four tens vs three hundreds and four ones. A second student is asked to restate: 'She's saying four tens is 40 and four ones is 4, so 340 is 36 more.'
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention (2021)
videoTitle: Bringing Number Talks to the Online Classroom (discourse moves)

title: Fact Fluency — Strategy First, Then Practice
description: Fluency isn't memorization; it's efficient, flexible use of known facts. Teach the strategies first (make ten, doubles, near doubles, decomposing), then practice inside games and short timed sets. IES gives fact-fluency instruction a Moderate evidence rating and Bay-Williams & Kling frame the developmental sequence.
howTo:
Teach one strategy per week; add it to a visible 'strategies we know' chart.
Practice with games (Roll & Cover, War, ten-frame flash) — not just worksheets.
Track progress against known-facts, not against speed alone.
Small-group re-teach for students still direct-modeling all facts by mid-year.

Classroom example: First grade's Week 6 fact-fluency focus is 'making ten' for addition. Monday: mini-lesson on 8+5 = 8+2+3. Tuesday-Thursday: ten-frame games in pairs. Friday: a 20-item known-facts quiz where students circle which strategy they used for the tricky ones. Anchor chart now has 'doubles,' 'near doubles,' and 'make ten.'
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention (2021)
videoTitle: Fact Fluency — Building Number Sense with Games (K-2)

title: Write Daily — Dedicated Time, Real Audiences
description: The IES Writing Practice Guide's Recommendation 1: provide daily time for students to write. Volume matters; without it, no strategy transfers. Graham & Perin meta-analysis: writing-for-learning effect sizes d ≈ 0.30–0.55 depending on subject.
howTo:
Protect the block — even 20 minutes daily beats 60 minutes twice a week.
Give real audiences and purposes: notes home, class books, letters, how-to guides.
Rotate a mini-lesson (5–8 min) → work time (18–22 min) → share (3–5 min).
Never grade every piece — publish some, respond to others.

Classroom example: A second-grade room protects 30 minutes right after lunch as writing time. Today's mini-lesson (7 min) is on strong endings. Work time (20 min) has students drafting a letter to a first-grade buddy about the school garden. Share (3 min) ends the block: two volunteers read their strong endings. Every child wrote for 20 straight minutes.
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Teaching Elementary Students to Be Effective Writers
videoTitle: How Short, Low-Stakes Writing Challenges Build More Confident Writers

title: Handwriting Instruction — Until It's Automatic
description: Handwriting fluency frees working memory for composition. Students who struggle to form letters can't hold onto the sentence they wanted to write. IES rates handwriting instruction in K–2 as having Strong evidence.
howTo:
Explicit letter formation — model, verbalize the path, students trace, then write.
Group by stroke family, not alphabet order (magic-c letters, tall letters, hook letters).
Distributed practice: 3–5 minutes of letter formation daily beats 30 minutes once a week.
Watch for grip and posture. Correct early — habits set fast.

Classroom example: K teacher works on the 'magic-c' stroke family: c, a, d, g, o, q. She models on the board, verbalizing 'around like a c, up like a stick, back down.' Students air-write, then trace, then form each letter on their paper. Total: 8 focused minutes, done again tomorrow with the same family.
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Teaching Elementary Students to Be Effective Writers
videoTitle: How to Teach Handwriting in Kindergarten and First Grade

title: Encoding & Spelling — Decoding in Reverse
description: Encoding practice reinforces the same phoneme–grapheme knowledge students use to read. Dictation of sounds → words → sentences is one of the highest-leverage ten minutes in the day. IES rates spelling instruction as having Strong evidence.
howTo:
Dictate: sound → letter, then word (using this week's pattern), then a sentence.
Elkonin boxes / sound boxes for tricky words — one box per phoneme.
Word chains: change one sound to make a new word (map → nap → nab → nag).
Weekly heart-word review — 'the tricky part is here.'

Classroom example: First grade — Wednesday encoding block. The teacher dictates six words with this week's -ck pattern (kick, pack, sock, luck, back, rock) and one sentence: 'The duck sat on a rock.' She circulates, checking for correct trap-word spellings. Total: 10 minutes.
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Teaching Elementary Students to Be Effective Writers
videoTitle: How to Teach Spelling & Handwriting in Kindergarten, 1st, and 2nd

title: Shared & Interactive Writing
description: Teacher and students co-compose a text on chart paper. The teacher shares the pen, thinking aloud about letters, words, punctuation, and word choice. It bridges emergent writing and independent writing. IES rates this practice as having Strong evidence in the 2018 Effective Writers guide.
howTo:
Set a real purpose — a class letter, a recap, a how-to.
Compose the sentence together; children help spell the parts they know.
Reread each new sentence with the class before moving on.
Post the finished chart; return to it as a mentor text.

Classroom example: K class writes a thank-you letter to the school custodian after a field trip. Teacher: 'How should we start?' Students dictate 'Dear Mr. Ramos.' She writes the capital D and asks: 'What sound does Ramos start with? Come put the R.' A student takes the marker. They reread each sentence together as it grows. Finished chart hangs by the door all week.
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Teaching Elementary Students to Be Effective Writers
videoTitle: Interactive Writing Instruction Online With Young Children

title: Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD)
description: The most-studied writing intervention in elementary school. Students learn a genre strategy, memorize it with a mnemonic, and self-monitor their use. WWC rates SRSD as producing Positive effects on writing quality; Graham & Harris meta-analyses show d ≈ 1.0+ across multiple studies.
howTo:
Develop background knowledge of the genre with mentor texts.
Introduce a mnemonic (e.g. POW+TIDE for opinion: Pick idea, Organize notes, Write; Topic sentence, Ideas, Details, Ending).
Model — think aloud writing a full piece using the strategy.
Memorize with the class, then guided practice with fading support, then independent use.

Classroom example: Third-grade opinion-writing unit, Week 2. The teacher introduces POW+TIDE and the class chants the mnemonic. She thinks aloud writing an opinion piece: 'Pick — I pick that recess should be longer. Organize — three reasons.' Students then plan their own with a POW+TIDE graphic organizer, referring back to the anchor chart. By Week 3, most students recite the mnemonic without prompting and produce a full piece.
sourceName: WWC Intervention Report — Self-Regulated Strategy Development
videoTitle: Inside the SRSD Writing Process for K–2 Classrooms

title: Morphology — Prefixes, Suffixes, Roots
description: Explicit instruction in morphemes (base words, prefixes, suffixes, Greek/Latin roots) accelerates word reading, spelling, and vocabulary — especially for older elementary readers hitting multisyllabic academic vocabulary.
howTo:
WEEKLY CYCLE:
• Monday: Introduce the target morpheme with meaning + 3–5 example words.
• Tuesday: Word matrix — combine base + affixes to build family.
• Wednesday: Peel-off routine — model reading an unknown word by removing prefix/suffix and blending base.
• Thursday: Encoding — dictate 6–8 morphologically related words.
• Friday: Application — find morpheme family in a science/social studies text and generate sentences.

Classroom example: 3rd–5th-grade cycle on the root <spect> ("look"): inspect, spectacle, spectator, retrospect, spectacular. Class builds a word web and uses two in exit-ticket sentences.
sourceName: Bowers, Kirby, & Deacon (2010) meta-analysis; Reed (2008) morphology review; Reading Rockets
videoTitle: Morphology in a K-2 Classroom — Science of Reading

title: Retrieval Practice — Brain Dumps, Mini-Quizzes, Cold Calls
description: Frequent low-stakes retrieval — asking students to pull knowledge from memory without notes — is one of the most robust findings in learning science. Meta-analytic effects hold up in elementary classrooms across subjects.
howTo:
DAILY BUILD-IN:
• Do Now: 3–4 questions from yesterday, last week, and last month (spaced).
• Brain Dump: 2 min silent write — 'everything you remember about X.'
• Two Things: name two things from today's lesson at the door on the way out.
• Weekly: a mixed 8-question quiz drawn from a running question bank.
• Feedback: correct answers made visible immediately — retrieval fails without corrective feedback.

Classroom example: 4th-grade science: Monday's Do Now asks about last Friday's rock-cycle vocabulary, last week's water-cycle stages, and last month's parts of a plant.
sourceName: Agarwal, Roediger et al. — Retrieval Practice Consistently Benefits Student Learning (Springer, 2021)
videoTitle: Making Retrieval Practice a Classroom Routine

title: Reciprocal Teaching — Predict, Question, Clarify, Summarize
description: A structured comprehension routine where students take turns leading a small group through four strategies: predicting, questioning, clarifying, and summarizing. WWC and multiple meta-analyses identify it as an evidence-based comprehension practice.
howTo:
BUILD IT IN 3 PHASES:
• Model — teacher does all four moves out loud for 2–3 lessons.
• Guide — hand off one role at a time; class fills the others.
• Release — students lead the routine in groups of 4 with role cards.
WEEKLY: One 20-minute session in a shared text; strategies posted in the room.

Classroom example: 5th-grade science: students read a chunk of a chapter on erosion. Predictor previews from headings, questioner poses two 'why' questions, clarifier flags 'sediment,' summarizer gives the 15-second version.
sourceName: WWC / IES Adolescent Literacy Review; Palincsar & Brown (1984)
videoTitle: Reciprocal Teaching: Helping Students Take Charge

title: Close Reading of Informational Text
description: Purposeful re-reading of a short, complex informational text focused on how the author's words, structure, and evidence build meaning. Anchors comprehension in text — not in memory or guesses.
howTo:
3-READ PROTOCOL:
• Read 1 (Gist): What is this text about? Students annotate main idea only.
• Read 2 (Craft): How does the author organize information? Circle text features, transitions, precise nouns/verbs.
• Read 3 (Meaning): Text-dependent question requiring evidence. Students cite lines.
Keep passages SHORT (300–600 words) and slightly above grade level.

Classroom example: 4th grade reads a 400-word passage on hurricanes. Read 3 question: 'Which two details best show why storm surge is more dangerous than wind?'
sourceName: Fisher & Frey — Close Reading of Informational Texts (Guilford); Massachusetts DESE Quick Reference Guide
videoTitle: Close Reading with Emerging Readers

title: Worked Examples — Show, Then Fade
description: Novice learners gain more from studying fully worked examples than from solving problems on their own. Alternating a worked example with a matched problem accelerates fluency while managing cognitive load.
howTo:
EXAMPLE–PROBLEM PAIRS:
• Present a fully worked example — read every step aloud, name the WHY of each step.
• Give a matched problem — students solve on their own.
• Alternate for 6–8 problems, then move to problems only.
• Include a completion example (last step missing) as a bridge.
• Never lecture through 5 problems in a row — the study effect requires the try step.

Classroom example: 3rd-grade long multiplication: teacher shows 24 × 6 fully worked with partial products labeled; students immediately solve 23 × 7 with the same layout.
sourceName: Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas — Cognitive Load Theory; Booth et al. (2015) worked examples
videoTitle: Cognitive Load Theory in Practice — Worked Examples

title: Interleaved Practice — Mixed Problem Sets
description: Instead of one operation per assignment, mix problem types together. Interleaved practice consistently outperforms blocked practice on delayed tests — the harder in-the-moment practice produces the more durable learning.
howTo:
INTERLEAVE INSIDE THE HOMEWORK/EXIT SLIP:
• 8 problems: 2 today's, 2 last week's, 2 from two weeks ago, 2 from last month.
• Mix problem TYPES (perimeter, area, addition, subtraction) so students must first decide which strategy applies.
• Expect lower in-class accuracy — that's the point.
• Use short cycles at first (2 topics) and grow to 4–5.

Classroom example: 5th-grade end-of-week practice mixes 3 fraction-multiplication, 2 fraction-addition, 2 volume, and 1 order-of-operations problem in one 8-question set.
sourceName: Rohrer, Dedrick & Stershic (2015) Interleaved Mathematics Practice, Journal of Educational Psychology
videoTitle: Interleaved Practice Improves Mathematics Learning — Rohrer

title: Productive Struggle — Support Without Rescuing
description: NCTM identifies supporting productive struggle as one of the eight Effective Mathematics Teaching Practices. Students learn most when they engage in tasks slightly beyond current understanding — and when teachers hold the space instead of taking over.
howTo:
TEACHER MOVES DURING STRUGGLE:
• Wait — count silently to 10 before intervening.
• Ask a smaller version: 'What's this problem asking?' 'What DO you know?'
• Redirect to a peer: 'Ana, can you share your first step?'
• Provide a strategy, not the answer: 'Try drawing what you know.'
• Normalize struggle publicly: 'Good — that's your brain building the connection.'
Debrief mistakes as valued data in whole-class discussion.

Classroom example: 4th grade tackles a non-routine problem before formal instruction on remainders. Teacher circulates, asks 'What have you tried?' and selects three student strategies to share — including the incomplete one.
sourceName: NCTM — Principles to Actions: Effective Mathematics Teaching Practices
videoTitle: Susie Katt — Productive Struggle

title: Partner (Paired) Reading for Fluency
description: Structured peer partnerships — stronger reader with developing reader — practicing repeated oral reading with a 4-step error-correction procedure. Documented gains in accuracy, fluency, and confidence.
howTo:
REL SOUTHEAST PROTOCOL:
• Pair a stronger reader (Coach) with a developing reader (Reader).
• Both read together for 30 seconds, then Reader takes over.
• Error correction: Coach says the word, Reader repeats, rereads the sentence.
• After 3–5 minutes, swap roles.
• End with each partner summarizing the passage in one sentence.
3× per week, 15 minutes.

Classroom example: 2nd–3rd grade uses paired reading with a 200-word decodable passage; teachers listen in on one pair per session for fluency data.
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Foundational Skills to Support Reading (K–3); Topping (2006) paired reading review
videoTitle: Partner Reading (Video 35, REL Southeast)

title: Opinion Writing with Reasons & Evidence (Grades 3–5)
description: By grade 5, students must state a claim, support it with reasons backed by facts and details, group ideas logically, and provide a conclusion. Teach the structure explicitly and revisit it across the year in multiple contexts.
howTo:
OREO PLUS FRAME (grade 3–5):
• Opinion: state clearly ('I believe...').
• Reason 1 + Evidence (text, statistic, quote).
• Reason 2 + Evidence.
• Opinion restated + call to action.
BUILD IT: mentor text → shared writing → guided writing → independent. Revisit each nine weeks with a new topic.

Classroom example: 4th grade reads two articles on school start times, then writes an opinion piece citing at least two pieces of text evidence from each source.
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Teaching Elementary Students to Be Effective Writers (Rec. 2); CCSS W.4.1 / W.5.1
videoTitle: Opinion Writing for Kids: What is it? (Reasons and Evidence) | Grades 3–5

title: Summarizing — Get-the-Gist / Somebody Wanted But So Then
description: Direct instruction in summarizing produces some of the largest comprehension effects in the research. Two research-backed frames: Get-the-Gist (informational) and Somebody Wanted But So Then (narrative).
howTo:
MODEL THE MOVES:
• Informational (Get-the-Gist): (1) name the WHO or WHAT, (2) name the most important thing about it, (3) write a sentence in ≤ 10 words.
• Narrative (SWBST): Somebody–Wanted–But–So–Then, one line each.
• Practice 5 in a row on short texts before applying to a chapter.
• Use as an exit ticket 2× per week.

Classroom example: 5th grade after reading a two-page passage on Rosa Parks: 'Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat, which sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott and helped launch the civil rights movement.'
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Improving Reading Comprehension in K–3 (Rec. 4); National Reading Panel
videoTitle: Somebody Wanted But So Then — 5th grade summarizing lesson

title: Sentence-Level Writing — Combining and Expanding
description: Sentence-combining is one of the highest-effect writing practices in the research. Students learn to expand kernel sentences with 'when? where? why? which one? what kind?' Graham & Perin (2007): sentence-combining effect size d ≈ 0.50; IES rates the practice Moderate.
howTo:
Give a kernel sentence: 'The dog ran.' Students expand: when, where, how, why.
Combine short choppy sentences into one strong one; compare versions.
Sentence-of-the-day: teacher displays a strong sentence; students identify the moves.
Add to writing checklist: 'Did I use at least one expanded sentence?'

Classroom example: Second-grade opener: 'The dog ran.' Teacher asks the class to expand it. One student: 'The muddy dog ran through the yard after dinner.' The class identifies what the writer added: a describing word (muddy), a where (through the yard), and a when (after dinner). Sentence goes on the wall as a mentor sentence for the week.
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Teaching Elementary Students to Be Effective Writers
videoTitle: Warming Up Cold Calling by Writing Ideas Down First

title: 5E Instructional Model (Engage → Explore → Explain → Elaborate → Evaluate)
description: A five-phase sequence that builds a NGSS-aligned science lesson around student sensemaking. Widely adopted for elementary science; a systematic review across K–12 settings found 5E lessons produce large gains in conceptual understanding and process skills compared with traditional instruction.
howTo:
Engage: pose a phenomenon, image, or discrepant event that surfaces prior ideas.
Explore: students investigate hands-on before any vocabulary or explanation.
Explain: introduce the science idea/vocabulary that names what they just experienced.
Elaborate: apply the idea to a new context, problem, or design task.
Evaluate: use a short performance task, exit ticket, or CER to check understanding.
Protect Explore before Explain — do not front-load the vocabulary.

Classroom example: For a 3rd-grade balancing forces lesson: Engage with a photo of a magician balancing chairs. Explore with tape, pennies, and cardboard 'balancers.' Explain center of mass. Elaborate by redesigning to balance heavier objects. Evaluate with a claim-evidence exit slip.

title: Anchoring Phenomenon Routine (NGSS Sensemaking)
description: Every unit opens with an observable, puzzling phenomenon students can't fully explain yet — then the whole unit becomes the effort to explain it. NextGenScience calls anchoring phenomena the driver of coherent NGSS units.
howTo:
Pick a phenomenon that is observable, culturally relevant, and requires the unit's DCIs to explain (not a single lesson's worth).
Day 1: show it, then run a Notice/Wonder to surface student questions.
Build a class 'Driving Questions Board' from those wonders — post it on the wall.
Begin every lesson by connecting the day's work back to the anchor.
End of unit: students explain the anchor using the science ideas they built.

Classroom example: K–2: 'Why did the puddle disappear?' anchors a states-of-matter unit. Grade 4: 'Why did the Oso landslide happen?' anchors an earth systems unit. Grade 5: 'Why did the raisins in the soda bottle bounce?' anchors a matter/forces unit.
Oklahoma standards this supports:
  • K.ESS2.1 — Use and share observations of local weather conditions to describe patterns over time
  • 2.ESS2.3 — Obtain information to identify where water is found on Earth and that it can be solid or liquid
  • 4.ESS2.1 — Plan and conduct an investigation to gather evidence on the effects of water, ice, wind, and vegetation on the rate of
  • 5.PS1.1 — Develop a model to describe that matter is made of particles too small to be seen

Puddle/water phenomenon anchors K.ESS2.1 (weather patterns), 2.ESS2.3 (water on Earth as solid/liquid), and 5.PS1.1 (matter made of particles). Landslide phenomenon anchors 4.ESS2.1 (effects of water and wind on land).

title: Claim–Evidence–Reasoning (CER) for Elementary Science
description: A three-part scaffold that turns an observation into a scientific explanation: a claim answering the question, evidence from data or observations, and reasoning connecting the two using a science idea. Research supports CER for building both content understanding and scientific argumentation in elementary classrooms.
howTo:
Post the frame: 'My claim is ___. My evidence is ___. My reasoning is ___ because ___.'
Start oral, then move to written CER once the routine is familiar.
Give the class a shared data set (chart, video, investigation) so evidence is grounded.
Model a strong CER, then a weak one — have students critique both.
Use the same frame across units so the reasoning muscle transfers.

Classroom example: After a plant-growth investigation, a 3rd grader writes: 'Claim — the plant in the sunny window grew taller. Evidence — the sunny plant grew 8 cm, the closet plant grew 2 cm. Reasoning — plants need light to make food, so more light means more growth.'

CER is the exact structure for OAS 'construct an argument with evidence' and 'support an argument with evidence' performance expectations across K–5.

title: Science Notebooks — Write to Learn
description: Each student keeps a running science notebook — questions, drawings, data tables, procedures, findings, and reflections. Research links regular notebook use to gains in elementary students' content understanding and academic writing.
howTo:
Set up sections: Questions, Investigations, Data & Diagrams, What I Learned.
Model labeled scientific drawings — labels beat pretty pictures.
Give 3–5 minutes of silent writing after every investigation before class talk.
Periodically pull a page for feedback — mark for evidence use, not spelling.
Use notebooks as the primary source of formative data on students' thinking.

Classroom example: After exploring magnets, 1st graders sketch which objects stuck and which didn't, then write one sentence: 'The paperclip stuck because it is made of metal.' Their teacher scans notebooks to spot the small misconception that all metals are magnetic.

Supports every 'make observations' and 'represent data in tables and graphical displays' PE — notebooks are the container for observational and data-representation evidence.

title: Productive Science Talk Moves
description: A small toolkit of teacher moves — revoicing, restating, adding on, pressing for reasoning, wait time — that turn science discussion from IRE recitation into collective sensemaking. Grounded in Michaels & O'Connor's Talk Science work.
howTo:
Wait time (3–5 seconds) after every question — hands down first.
Revoice: 'So you're saying the water changed to gas because ___?'
Say more: 'Can you say more about that?'
Add on: 'Who wants to build on what Aisha said?'
Press for reasoning: 'What makes you think that? What's your evidence?'
Post the moves on a wall chart so students start using them on each other.

Classroom example: During a 4th-grade weather discussion, the teacher hears 'The clouds get heavy.' She revoices ('Heavy with what?'), presses for reasoning ('What makes them heavy?'), and calls on a peer to add on — the class arrives at condensation together instead of the teacher stating it.

Talk moves support any PE requiring 'ask questions to determine cause and effect' or discussion around a shared observation.
