title: Argument-Driven Inquiry (ADI) — Lab Investigations
description: An 8-stage lab model that gives students a guiding question, tools, and time — then requires them to build and defend an argument from their own data. Widely used K–12 for building the NGSS science-and-engineering practices.
howTo:
Stage 1: Task + question posed by the teacher.
Stage 2: Small groups design a method with teacher check-in.
Stage 3: Investigate and collect data.
Stage 4: Groups build a tentative argument on a whiteboard (claim + evidence + rationale).
Stage 5: Argumentation session — groups rotate and critique each other.
Stages 6–8: Written report, peer review, revision.
Keep classroom norms visible: attack the idea, not the person.

Classroom example: 3rd graders investigate 'Which soil holds the most water?' Groups run their own tests, chart data, then defend their claim in a round-robin session before writing a lab report.
Oklahoma standards this supports:
  • 1.PS4.3 — Plan and conduct an investigation to determine the effect of placing objects made with different materials in the path of a beam
  • 2.LS2.1 — Plan and conduct an investigation to determine if plants need sunlight and water to grow
  • 3.PS2.1 — Plan and conduct investigations on the effects of balanced and unbalanced forces on the motion of an object
  • 4.PS3.3 — Ask questions and predict outcomes about the changes in energy that occur when objects collide
  • 5.PS1.4 — Conduct an investigation to determine whether the mixing of two or more substances results in new substances

Direct fit for any 'plan and conduct an investigation' PE grades 1–5.
sourceName: The ADI Model

title: Hands-On, Minds-On Investigation (Not Just Activity)
description: A commitment that every hands-on science experience is paired with sensemaking — a question, a prediction, data, and a class conversation. Prevents the common 'fun activity, no learning' failure mode in elementary science.
howTo:
Before the materials come out, post the driving question and take predictions in the notebook.
During: circulate with probing questions ('What are you noticing? What surprises you?').
After: mandatory 5-minute debrief — data on the board, patterns named, question answered (or refined).
No activity without an entry (prediction) and an exit (findings).
If you can't articulate the science idea it targets, redesign the activity.

Classroom example: A K/1 'sink or float' station becomes real science when the teacher first asks 'What do you predict about the crayon?' has students record, then ends with 'What did we learn about which objects float?' — not just 'that was fun.'

Structure for any investigation PE — supports every 'plan and conduct' and 'make observations and measurements' expectation.

title: Vocabulary After Experience (Not Before)
description: In elementary science, introduce the science term AFTER students have investigated the phenomenon, so the word names something they already understand. Aligns with NGSS 3D learning and cognitive-load research on meaningful vocabulary acquisition.
howTo:
Never open a unit with a vocab list.
Run the investigation or read-aloud first.
At the sensemaking discussion, when students describe the idea in their own words, introduce the formal term: 'Scientists call this ___.'
Add the word + a student-generated definition + a drawing to an anchor chart.
Use a Frayer or word-map only after the concept is in place.

Classroom example: Before saying 'evaporation,' 2nd graders leave wet paper towels in different spots for a day. When they notice some dried faster, the teacher says, 'That drying-up process has a name — evaporation.' The word sticks because it labels something they saw.

Applies to any concept-heavy PE — evaporation, life cycles, energy transfer, phase change — where a term names a phenomenon students first observed.

title: Model-Based Reasoning — Draw, Revise, Explain
description: Students draw and iteratively revise scientific models (systems diagrams, cause-and-effect chains) to explain phenomena. NGSS names 'developing and using models' as a core science practice; iterative modeling builds elementary students' explanatory reasoning.
howTo:
Introduce the phenomenon and ask each student to draw their initial model — arrows, labels, and a short caption.
Post several student models side by side.
After investigations or read-alouds, students revise their model in a new color.
End of unit: 'final model' that must include the science ideas learned.
Use the model progression as evidence of learning growth.

Classroom example: 3rd graders modeling a plant. Initial models show a stem, leaves, a sun. After weeks of investigation and reading, revised models add roots pulling water, arrows showing sunlight into leaves, and labels for 'plants make their own food.'

title: C3 Framework Inquiry Arc
description: The National Council for the Social Studies' four-step inquiry arc: develop questions → apply disciplinary concepts → evaluate sources & use evidence → communicate conclusions & take informed action. Adopted by dozens of states as the K–12 backbone for rigorous social studies.
howTo:
Step 1 — Compelling question: pose an authentic, debatable question ('Was our town's growth good for everyone?').
Step 2 — Supporting questions: break the compelling question into 3–4 kid-sized sub-questions.
Step 3 — Sources & evidence: students examine primary and secondary sources tied to each supporting question.
Step 4 — Communicate & act: produce an argument (writing, presentation, or community action).
Keep the compelling question posted for the entire unit.

Classroom example: 4th grade: 'Why did people move to Oklahoma?' Supporting questions look at land runs, sharecropping, and Dust Bowl migration. Students use photos, maps, and short readings to build an argument and share it as a class exhibit.

title: Primary Source Analysis (Library of Congress Routine)
description: A structured Observe → Reflect → Question protocol from the Library of Congress that helps K–5 students think like historians as they look at photographs, maps, letters, and artifacts. Scaffolds close looking before interpretation.
howTo:
Project one primary source (photo, map, artifact image) — no context yet.
Observe: 'What do you notice?' (2 minutes of quiet looking, then share).
Reflect: 'What do you think is going on? What time period? Whose perspective?'
Question: 'What questions do you have? What would help you find out?'
Reveal source information only after students have generated observations.
For older elementary, add a written analysis using the LOC Primary Source Analysis Tool.

title: Reading Like a Historian — Sourcing, Contextualizing, Corroborating
description: The Stanford History Education Group's approach: students read short primary sources and use three history habits — sourcing (who wrote it and why), contextualizing (what was happening at the time), and corroborating (what other sources say). Adapts well to grades 3–5 with excerpted documents.
howTo:
Choose 2–3 short (kid-length) primary sources on the same event or question.
Before reading, teach the Sourcing questions: 'Who wrote it? When? Why?'
During reading, model contextualizing: 'What was happening in this time and place?'
After reading, corroborate: 'Where do the sources agree? Where do they disagree? Which do you trust more, and why?'
End with a written or oral claim backed by cited sources.

Classroom example: 5th graders compare two short first-person accounts of the first Thanksgiving — one from a colonist, one from a Wampanoag perspective — then answer 'Whose story gets told, and why does that matter?' using sourcing and corroboration.

title: Structured Academic Controversy (SAC)
description: A cooperative discussion protocol where small groups examine two sides of an issue, then must reach consensus. Research shows SAC develops multi-perspective thinking, evidence use, and civic dispositions in social studies classrooms.
howTo:
Pose a debatable question with two defensible positions ('Should our town build a new park where the old warehouse is?').
Groups of 4 split into two pairs. Each pair receives sources for one side and must present that side's best case.
Rotate: each pair now presents the OTHER side (to force perspective-taking).
Pairs drop the assigned roles and, as a group of 4, must reach consensus (or clarify remaining disagreement).
Each group shares their conclusion and reasoning with the class.

Classroom example: 4th grade civics: 'Should recess be shortened to add more math time?' Groups build both cases, then negotiate consensus — surfacing real trade-offs about learning, health, and school priorities.

title: Map & Geography Skills Routine
description: A weekly routine that builds systematic map skills K–5 — cardinal directions, keys/legends, distance, and thematic map reading. A 21st-century skills geography map and multi-study review both call for regular, cumulative map work rather than isolated units.
howTo:
Once a week, project a map (physical, political, thematic, or historical) tied to current content.
Run a 5-question routine: 1) What kind of map is this? 2) What does the key tell us? 3) Find a specific feature. 4) Compare two places. 5) Draw a conclusion ('Why might people have settled here?').
Rotate map types monthly so students see many.
Have students sketch their own maps of familiar places (school, town) once a quarter.

Classroom example: During an Oklahoma history unit, the Friday map might be a historical Land Run map. Students identify the date, find their county, and infer why certain areas were settled first.

title: Take Informed Action — Civic Project
description: The fourth dimension of the C3 Framework: after inquiry, students apply their learning to a real civic action within their school or community. Builds civic dispositions and shows students social studies has consequences beyond the classroom.
howTo:
End each major unit with a small 'informed action' step — writing a letter, making a poster campaign, presenting to another class, proposing a policy to the principal.
Actions must be tied to unit evidence, not opinion alone.
Keep the scope realistic: one classroom, one hallway, one grade level.
Debrief after: 'What happened? What did we learn? What would we do differently?'
Document actions on a class 'Civic Action Board' across the year.

Classroom example: After a unit on rules and community, K/1 students identify a lunchroom problem, propose a solution to the cafeteria manager, and evaluate the result two weeks later.

title: Economic Decision-Making Grid (K–5 Economics)
description: A simple K–5 routine for teaching opportunity cost and trade-offs — the heart of elementary economics. Students list options, list what they'd gain and give up for each, and defend a choice. Aligns with Council for Economic Education standards and financial-literacy research.
howTo:
Frame a real choice ('Our class earned $20 — what should we buy?').
List 3 options in a grid: Option / What we gain / What we give up.
Small groups fill in the grid using evidence (prices, class needs, fairness).
Each group defends its recommended choice — the class votes.
Explicitly name 'opportunity cost' — 'The next-best thing you gave up.'
Repeat the routine across the year with different scenarios (community, historical, personal).

Classroom example: 3rd graders decide whether their earned class funds should go toward books, a field trip, or a class pet. They complete the grid, defend their choice, and confront the opportunity cost of whichever option loses.

title: The Turner Standard — Support and Accountability Travel Together
description: The building's professional expectation, adopted from Turner's Guide to Teaching and Learning: every classroom is held to the same instructional standard — not to each teacher's preference, and not to a vendor's product. Support comes first (scripts, models, planning tools, coaching, demonstration lessons, feedback, honest time to improve) and accountability follows, because a school that gives one without the other cheats the other one.
howTo:
State the bargain plainly and repeat it: support and accountability travel together.

The Turner Standard is not a checklist of behaviors to be caught doing. It is the process by which an ordinary teacher becomes a great one, and by which a great one stays that way:
  • Run the six moves daily so that every student notices, reads, talks, solves, defends, and revises.
  • Hold the thinking at Level 3, and make the student the one who gets it there.
  • Build the room where students are known and where demand and support arrive together.
  • Collect evidence before the bell, read it, and let it change tomorrow.
  • Repeat until it is habit, and then teach it to the next teacher.

The walkthrough lens, the rubrics, and the milestone tables show where in the process a classroom is — and what the next move should be. They do not label the teacher.

One line protects the whole arrangement: coaching and evaluation are separate lanes, and they do not cross. Walkthrough notes, practice attempts, and coaching conversations are never evaluation evidence. Accountability runs through the formal supervision lane, on its own record, against the same published standards. Coaching stays safe so practice stays honest.

A book that asked teachers to take real risks without protecting them while they learn would not deserve to be followed. The Standard tries to earn the ask.

title: Rigor Is Not — Six Clarifications
description: Rigor is the level of thinking a task demands, and whether the student is the one doing it. The book uses Costa's three levels as its only measure: Level 1 gather, Level 2 process, Level 3 apply and judge. A lesson is rigorous when it reaches Level 3 and the student is the one who gets it there. These six clarifications keep the term honest.
howTo:
Rigor is NOT difficulty.
  Difficulty is how much a task costs in effort or time; rigor is what level of thinking it requires. Fifty problems are harder than ten. Ten problems with a justification are more rigorous than fifty.

Rigor is NOT pace or coverage.
  Moving faster through more standards usually lowers the level of thinking, because there is no time left for Level 3.

Rigor is NOT a surface signal.
  A quiet room, a busy room, a laptop on every desk, students in groups — none of these tells you the level of thinking in the room. Only the student work does.

Rigor is NOT correctness.
  A right answer copied from the model, or produced through heavy prompting, is Level 1 wearing Level 3 clothes. Checking one case is not proving the claim.

Rigor is NOT harshness.
  Refusing to scaffold, grading strictly, and letting students sink or swim are not rigor; they are the absence of teaching. Direct instruction of the background knowledge a student needs to read a demanding text is not a retreat from rigor. It is what makes rigor reachable.

Rigor is NOT a property of the roster.
  It belongs to the task. An advanced class completing a worksheet is at Level 1. A Tier 1 class defending a claim from a single primary source is at Level 3. The right response to a student who is not yet there is to change the ramp, never the destination.

The book's second bargain: on-ramps and rigor travel together. Every chapter carries both.

title: The One Idea, in Six Moves — Turner Engagement Cycle
description: The single instructional arc that underlies every chapter of the book and every strategy in this Toolkit. Not a script to perform in order — strong lessons revisit, combine, and compress its phases. It is a checklist of the six things a lesson has to make room for if every student is going to think and not just receive.
howTo:
The six moves: Notice. Read. Talk. Solve. Defend. Revise.

Where each move lives on Costa's Levels:
  • Notice — Level 1 (gather). Lowers the cost of starting so the reluctant student starts.
  • Read — Level 1 (gather). Puts evidence on the desk before anyone asks for a conclusion.
  • Talk — bridging Level 1→2. Lets the quiet student say the thing once, in private, before saying it in public.
  • Solve — Level 2 (process). Compare, infer, explain why, analyze.
  • Defend — Level 3 (apply and judge). Written claim + named evidence + reasoning a stranger could check.
  • Revise — Level 3 (apply and judge). Update the claim when a second source pushes back.

Subject-specific sentence-shaped destinations (same demand, different clothes):
  • Social Studies — claim, evidence, corroborating second source.
  • English — claim, quoted line, warrant for why the words mean that.
  • Science — claim, cited data, reasoned mechanism, tested.
  • Mathematics — claim, rule that justifies it, check by a different route.

Do not skip the first three moves and go straight to 'defend your claim.' That is not more rigorous. It is Level 3 from the front row and Level 1 from everyone else. Notice, Read, and Talk make the demand survivable for every student in the room, not just the six who would have met it anyway.

Defend and Revise are the two moves that cannot be cut when time runs short. They are also the two that are cut first.

title: PIES Non-Negotiable — Cooperative Learning That Produces Individual Achievement
description: The building's cooperative-learning standard, adopted from the book: use PIES (Positive interdependence, Individual accountability, Equal participation, Simultaneous interaction) in every discipline. Group consensus never replaces individual evidence.
howTo:
PIES — the four requirements every cooperative structure must meet:
  • Positive interdependence — students need each other to complete the task.
  • Individual accountability — every student produces something recorded in their own hand or voice.
  • Equal participation — the structure requires each member to contribute (roles, rounds, tokens), not just permits it.
  • Simultaneous interaction — at any moment, roughly half the room is doing the thinking work, not one student at a time.

The Non-Negotiable (stated in the book, verbatim): 'Group consensus never replaces individual evidence. Every routine ends with an individual written product, an individual response, or readiness for any student to explain the team's reasoning.'

Why this matters:
  • A group answer with one student doing the thinking hides the four students who did not.
  • The teacher cannot check learning she cannot see on paper.
  • The 'Defend' and 'Revise' moves of the Engagement Cycle require individual output.

Subject-specific ending products:
  • Social studies — the sourced paragraph, in each student's notebook.
  • English — the individual annotated line and warrant.
  • Science — the CER on each student's page.
  • Math — the individual justification and check-by-a-different-route.

If the routine does not end with individual evidence, redesign the routine.

title: Ask Three Before Me
description: A taught classroom routine: before a student asks the teacher a procedural or task-clarification question, they check three sources first — usually their own work or notes, a nearby classmate, and a posted resource (anchor chart, board, directions). Frees the teacher from repeating routine questions and turns peer talk into a live formative-assessment signal: if three students on a table can't answer, the whole class likely needs a reteach.
howTo: Teach and rehearse it like a routine. (1) Name the three sources students must check before you (self/notes → nearby peer → posted resource or directions). (2) Model it: raise a hand, walk through the three checks aloud, then ask the teacher. (3) When a student asks a procedural question, respond first with "Did you ask three before me?" and defer to peers. (4) Listen actively as you circulate — when a question keeps coming back after three peers, that's a whole-class reteach signal, not a discipline issue. (5) Make it explicit when Ask Three does NOT apply (during silent work, quizzes, direct instruction, or when a student is in genuine distress). Post the three checks on the wall.
sourceName: Edutopia (60-Second Strategy)
videoTitle: 60-Second Strategy: Ask 3 Before Me
example: During independent practice on a math task, a student raises a hand. The teacher walks over and asks, "Did you ask three before me?" The student checks the directions on the board, asks the two students on either side, and then re-reads their own work. When they still get stuck, the teacher answers — and notices that when three students on that table all had the same confusion about step 2, the teacher pauses the class for a 90-second reteach of step 2 instead of answering the same question six times.
weeklyProduct: A posted "Ask Three Before Me" anchor chart in the room, plus a one-line note in the teacher's plans each day capturing any question that came back after three peers — those are candidates for a whole-class reteach or a formative check the next day.
